title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Decrease the Rate of Rupture, Cardiac Events, and Death in Patients with Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms.
abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a degenerative condition involving several processes including inflammation, matrix remodeling, disruptions of vascular smooth muscle cells, and thrombus formation all leading to progressive dilatation of the aorta and eventual rupture. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) are now considered part of the frontline therapeutic options to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus and have also been validated as having compelling anti-inflammatory and cardiovascular protective properties. Data is limited on the impact of GLP-1RA on outcomes of patients with AAA. The aim of this study is to examine the association and possible impact of GLP-1RA on patients with AAA. Data was sourced from the TriNetX research network, encompassing 123 health care organizations. Utilizing ICD-10 and CPT codes, we identified patients with AAA who received abdominal imaging every six months. Group 1 was comprised of patients who were treated with GLP-1RA while Group 2 patients were not. Propensity-score-matching (PSM) was used in a 1:1 fashion using age, sex, diabetes, metformin use, hypertension, cardiac disease, tobacco use, chronic kidney disease, and pulmonary disease as covariates. Primary outcomes were aneurysm rupture or repair. Secondary outcomes include mortality and major adverse cardiac events (MACE; myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure). Standard statistical methods were used as appropriate. We identified 412,490 patients with diagnosis of AAA who were undergoing 6-month surveillance between June 1, 2010 and April 16, 2024. After PSM, the GLP-1RA group (N=13,722) underwent fewer elective repairs at each timepoint (1.5% vs 2.3% at 2 years, 2.1% vs 3.0% at 5 years, P<.01) and had significantly fewer ruptures at two years (1.1% vs 1.8%, P<.01) and five years (1.6% vs 2.4%, P<.01) when compared to Group 2 (N=13,722). Group 1 also experienced significantly fewer MACE and all-cause mortality at two and five years. On multivariate analysis, GLP-1RA significantly reduced the risk of undergoing elective repair (HR 0.757, 95% CI [0.636-0.902], P<.01), rupture (HR 0.538, 95% CI [0.418-0.691], P<.01), all-cause mortality (HR 0.474, 95% CI [0.439-0.511], P<.001), and MACE (HR 0.825, 95% CI [0.794-0.857], P<.01) at 5 years. The use of GLP-1RA in patients with AAA is associated with fewer ruptures, elective repairs, and improved rates of MACE and death. A prospective analysis may further elucidate if GLP-1RA should be prescribed to reduce the rate of aneurysm growth.

title: Associations of glucose- and lipid-lowering medications with incident or first-recorded psoriasis: a systematic review of real-world observational studies.
abstract: Glucose-lowering and lipid-lowering medications may influence psoriasis development through metabolic, inflammatory, and immune pathways, but real-world evidence remains inconsistent. To systematically evaluate associations between these medications and the risk of incident or first-recorded psoriasis, with particular attention to comparator choice, outcome definition, study design, and data-source overlap. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 1 July 2026, with an updated search conducted on 11 September 2026 during manuscript revision. Longitudinal observational studies evaluating glucose-lowering or lipid-lowering medication use and incident or first-recorded psoriasis were included. Evidence was grouped by medication class, comparator, and outcome type and synthesized narratively. Psoriasis-specific outcomes and broader or composite psoriatic-disease outcomes were treated as distinct evidence categories. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I. Meta-analysis was not performed because sufficiently comparable and mutually independent estimates were unavailable within most medication-comparator-outcome strata. Eighteen reports were included. Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor estimates were generally below 1; in an active-comparator study using a broader psoriasis-related outcome including psoriatic arthritis codes, the hazard ratio versus sulfonylureas was 0.422 (95% confidence interval, 0.273-0.716). Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist estimates were notably comparator dependent: estimates were above 1 in comparisons with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors, approximately null in comparison with sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, and inconsistent across comparisons with GLP-1RA nonuse. Most sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor estimates were near or above the null. Metformin and thiazolidinediones yielded lower estimates in some studies, whereas statins showed no consistent association or exposure-response gradient. Of the 18 report-level ROBINS-I assessment anchors, 13 (72.2%) had a serious overall risk of bias and five (27.8%) had a moderate risk; none had a low risk of bias. Several reports may also have included overlapping populations and were therefore not interpreted as independent replications. The available observational evidence does not establish causal effects of glucose-lowering or lipid-lowering medications on incident or first-recorded psoriasis. This review does not support choosing or avoiding these medications solely to prevent psoriasis or modifying standard diabetes or cardiovascular treatment on the basis of the reported associations. The findings remain hypothesis-generating because of confounding by indication, other risks of bias, and limited independent evidence. https://doi.org/10.37766/inplasy2026.7.0070, identifier INPLASY202670070.

title: Combination Therapy Potential of HTD1801 (Berberine Ursodeoxycholate) in MASLD/MASH and Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Disease: A Narrative Review.
abstract: The cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) continuum is characterized by the close interrelatedness of metabolic, hepatic, cardiovascular, and renal disease, making multidomain therapies particularly relevant to MASLD/MASH. HTD1801, an investigational ionic therapeutic, combines berberine's metabolic effects with the hepatoprotective effects of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), making it a potential multidomain therapy within this setting. This review had two related goals: first, to synthesize the mechanistic and clinical evidence for HTD1801 itself; and second, to evaluate the rationale and available evidence for extending this complementary-action approach through combination with other therapies relevant to MASLD/MASH and CKM disease. PubMed/MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, conference abstracts, and selected regulatory or sponsor sources were reviewed through 9 August 2026. Six CKM-relevant therapeutic classes were selected for their human evidence of multidomain benefit: metformin, GLP-1 receptor agonists, statins, SGLT2 inhibitors, PPAR agonists, and resmetirom. Studies of both HTD1801 and its individual components, berberine and UDCA, were included. A systematic review or meta-analysis was not feasible due to the limited and heterogeneous evidence base, instead necessitatinganarrative review. Across seven completed HTD1801 clinical studies with publicly reported results, treatment showed multidomain metabolic and hepatic benefits across the CKM spectrum, including improvements in HbA1c, LDL-C, MRI-PDFF hepatic fat, ALT, AST, and GGT. Direct human evidence: HTD1801 + metformin, supported by a Phase 3 randomized add-on trial. Indirect human evidence: HTD1801 + SGLT2 inhibitors. Preclinical evidence: HTD1801 + GLP-1 receptor agonists; berberine + statins. Theoretical mechanistic rationale only: HTD1801 + PPAR agonists; HTD1801 + resmetirom. Overall, mechanistic and preclinical rationale has advanced further than direct human validation, and evidence remains centered largely on surrogate rather than definitive clinical outcomes. HTD1801 has demonstrated multidomain metabolic and hepatic activity, but direct human evidence supporting its use with other CKM therapies remains limited and is currently established only for metformin. The principal next step is to test HTD1801 in dedicated combination RCTs for clinically meaningful benefit. Further studies should characterize combination-specific safety and tolerability and compare HTD1801 with separate berberine and UDCA administration.

title: Weight Regain After Discontinuation of GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Weight regain and loss of cardiometabolic benefit commonly follow the withdrawal of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/GLP-1 receptor agonists, yet maintenance strategies are incompletely characterized. We conducted a systematic review reported according to PRISMA 2020 of primary studies in adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes. PubMed/MEDLINE, Europe PMC and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to September 2026, supplemented by backward/forward citation searching and cross-checking of recent systematic reviews. Eligible reports quantified weight or cardiometabolic outcomes at least 12 weeks after planned or unplanned treatment cessation, or tested a post-cessation maintenance strategy. Randomized reports were assessed with RoB 2 and non-randomized reports with ROBINS-I. Owing to incompatible estimands, follow-up schedules, cointerventions and overlapping trial families, results were synthesized narratively without a new pooled estimate. Eighteen reports representing 16 study families were included. Randomized withdrawal trials showed renewed weight gain after treatment cessation: +6.9% over 48 weeks after switching from semaglutide to placebo in STEP 4, and +14.0% over 52 weeks after switching from tirzepatide to placebo in SURMOUNT-4. In the STEP 1 extension, participants regained 11.6 percentage points over one year, approximately two-thirds of their prior loss, while several cardiometabolic measures moved toward baseline. Real-world estimates were smaller and more variable because discontinuation was often inferred from prescriptions, follow-up weights were missing, and many patients restarted or switched therapy. Cardiometabolic rebound was associated with the degree of weight regain, but clinical cardiovascular events were not evaluated. Evidence for maintenance strategies was sparse: one randomized post-treatment study supported supervised exercise, with the exercise-plus-liraglutide group retaining an additional 5.1 kg of weight loss one year after both interventions ended compared with liraglutide alone; a small pilot supported sitagliptin plus metformin after liraglutide in polycystic ovary syndrome. No eligible controlled trial isolated a specific diet after cessation. Weight regain is frequent after stopping GLP-1-based therapy, although magnitude varies by drug, design, follow-up and subsequent treatment. Structured exercise may help reduce regain and preserve lean mass, but evidence for dietary, behavioral, tapering or pharmacologic transition strategies remains limited. Discontinuation should therefore be planned as part of chronic obesity care, with explicit monitoring and shared decision-making, rather than presented as a predictable short course.

title: Metformin, SGLT2 Inhibitors, and Intermittent Fasting: Convergent Pathways to Healthspan Extension, Cardiovascular Longevity, and Cancer Prevention-A Narrative Review.
abstract: The biology of aging and the epidemiology of cardiovascular disease share a common molecular pathway expressed through nutrient-sensing kinases, mitochondrial redox state, and chronic inflammation. Three interventions have independently emerged as translators of that interconnection into clinical benefit: metformin, a biguanide that has evolved from a first-line anti-diabetic into the world's most extensively studied putative geroprotector; the sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is), pharmacological generators of a fasting-mimetic state that has reshaped heart failure outcomes across the ejection-fraction spectrum; and intermittent fasting (IF), the evolutionary archetype from which both agents partially derive their effects on longevity. Based on the synthetized evidence, we propose a stage-stratified clinical framework for integrated deployment. To find the manuscripts relevant for our narrative review, we searched the medical literature by using key words ("metformin"; "SGLT2i"; "intermittent fasting"; "health span"; "cardiovascular longevity"; "cancer chemoprevention"; "gut microbiome"; "geroprotection"; "heart failure") combined through Boolean operators (AND/OR). This narrative review integrates preclinical mechanistic evidence, landmark randomized controlled trial data, and emerging data on cancer chemoprevention and gut microbiome remodeling to provide a rigorous, side-by-side analysis of all three strategies. We delineate molecular convergence on adenosine monophosphate kinase (AMPK) activation, mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) suppression, enhanced autophagy, mitochondrial renewal, inflammatory responses, and anti-cancer biology, while mapping critical divergences in specific populations, lifespan timing, combinability, and safety. Our proposed framework has to be treated with caution, as it is based on the current evidence base, which lacks dedicated outcome trials for IF and published randomized clinical trial data for metformin in non-diabetic adults.

title: MetCool ACS: study protocol for a multicentre quasi-randomised trial of metformin in patients without diabetes after acute coronary syndrome in Poland.
abstract: Despite advances in coronary intervention and secondary prevention, patients without diabetes who experience acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remain at elevated cardiovascular risk. Metformin has pleiotropic cardiovascular effects beyond glucose lowering, but its role after ACS in people without diabetes is uncertain. MetCool ACS is a multicentre, prospective, quasi-randomised, open-label trial enrolling 1000 adults without diabetes hospitalised for ACS and treated with successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stent implantation. Allocation is determined by the second digit of the Polish national identification number: even digits allocate to metformin and odd digits to standard care (allocation 1:1). Participants allocated to metformin will receive dose-escalated therapy to 850 mg three times a day (2550 mg/day) for 24 months, followed by 6 months of post-treatment follow-up (total 30 months). The primary endpoint is unplanned coronary revascularisation (PCI or coronary artery bypass grafting) within 30 months after the index ACS-related revascularisation. Secondary endpoints include cardiac death, all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke and safety outcomes. Time-to-event outcomes will be analysed using appropriate survival analysis methods, including Kaplan-Meier estimates, log-rank testing and Cox proportional hazards models, with competing-risk methods applied where appropriate. Detailed statistical methods will be prespecified in the statistical analysis plan. Protocol version: 3.1/2023 (10 January 2023). The study was approved by the Bioethics Committee at the Military Institute of Medicine (Resolution 55/WIM/2020; 18 November 2020) and the Bioethics Committee at the Military Chamber of Physicians (Resolution 31/23; 27 October 2023). All participants provide written informed consent. Results will be disseminated primarily through peer-reviewed publication and scientific meetings. The trial is covered by clinical trial insurance, including coverage for potential claims arising from harm related to participation in the trial. Any compensation for trial-related harm will be provided in accordance with applicable regulations and the terms and conditions of the insurance policy. EudraCT 2020-004962-21; EU CT 2024-516589-13-00; NCT05305898.

title: Trends in Diabetes Medications After Metformin in Patients at High Versus Moderate Cardiovascular Risk: The BESTMED Consortium 2014-2022.
abstract: To compare nationwide prescription trends in medications (dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors [DPP-4i], glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists [GLP-1 RAs], sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors [SGLT2i], or sulfonylureas [SUs]) after treatment with metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) at high versus moderate cardiovascular risk by key sociodemographic and health characteristics. Electronic health records and insurance claims from 2014 to 2022 from 10 health systems and two insurance plans from different U.S. regions were evaluated. Risk-stratified multinomial log-linear models were used to model trends in prescribing patterns, adjusted for sociodemographic variables. A total of 104,474 patients were included (28% at high and 72% at moderate cardiovascular risk). Among those at high cardiovascular risk, DPP-4i (2014 24.0%; 2022 11.0%) and SU (66.4%; 35.7%) prescriptions declined, whereas GLP-1 RA (4.4%; 20.5%) and SGLT2i (5.2%; 32.8%) prescriptions increased. Among those at moderate cardiovascular risk, DPP-4i (23.7%; 11.7%) and SU (63.7%; 31.5%) prescriptions declined, whereas GLP-1 RA (5.7%; 30.0%) and SGLT2i (6.9%; 26.8%) prescriptions increased. Annual increases differed by high versus moderate cardiovascular risk for GLP-1 RAs (+2.5% vs. +3.6%/year; P P P < 0.01). Greater increases in SGLT2i prescriptions occurred among Black patients, and greater increases in GLP-1 RA prescriptions occurred among those of Hispanic ethnicity at moderate cardiovascular risk. Prescribing patterns for second-line T2D therapies in those at moderate cardiovascular risk are approaching guideline recommendations for those at high risk. Some trends are potentially clinically explainable, whereas certain racial/ethnic differences may warrant exploration. Video 1.Video abstract3e51f820-63ec-4c76-86f4-002f78d7c5f0doc260027video1.

title: Metabolic and oncological effects of metformin added to ADT in prostate cancer: systematic review and meta-analysis including STAMPEDE.
abstract: Androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) is the cornerstone of advanced prostate cancer treatment but induces a metabolic syndrome phenotype that heightens cardiovascular risk. Metformin, an insulin-sensitising biguanide with emerging anticancer properties, is a rational ADT adjunct. Following STAMPEDE's 2025 publication, we aimed to quantify metformin's metabolic benefit and characterise its oncological signal by disease volume. This PRISMA 2020-guided review (PROSPERO CRD420261384520) searched five databases through 12 May 2026. Eligible RCTs compared metformin plus ADT versus ADT alone in prostate cancer. Primary metabolic outcomes were body weight, waist circumference, HbA1c, fasting glucose, and LDL cholesterol. Secondary (exploratory) oncological outcomes were overall survival (OS) and castration-resistant prostate cancer-free survival (CRPC-FS), derived predominantly from a single trial. Random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp correction were used; GRADE assessed certainty. Six trials enroling 2415 participants (78% from STAMPEDE) were included: STAMPEDE (n = 1 874), PRIME (n = 166), PREMIUM (n = 83), MANSMED (n = 124), Mahalingam (n = 36), and Alagizy (n = 132). Disease status ranged from metastatic (STAMPEDE, Alagizy, majority MANSMED) to locally advanced or biochemically recurrent (PREMIUM, PRIME, Mahalingam); all excluded diabetes mellitus except MANSMED ( ~ 20%). At 12 months, metformin significantly reduced waist circumference (MD -1.12 cm; p = 0.014), HbA1c (MD -0.070%; p = 0.029), and fasting glucose (MD -0.100 mmol/L; p = 0.031). Body weight and LDL cholesterol reductions were non-significant (MD -1.60 kg; p = 0.090 and MD -0.130 mmol/L; p = 0.343, respectively). In STAMPEDE, metformin did not improve OS (HR 0.91; p = 0.15); the high-volume subgroup showed a survival benefit (HR 0.79; p = 0.007; volume interaction p = 0.12, non-significant). In MANSMED, CRPC-free survival was significantly prolonged (HR 0.50; p = 0.01), though this signal derives from a single small, open-label trial. Metformin added to ADT produces moderate-certainty reductions in waist circumference and HbA1c. Oncological benefit in unselected patients was not demonstrated; the hypothesis-generating STAMPEDE high-volume subgroup signal, derived from a single trial, warrants evaluation in a prospective, volume-stratified RCT.

title: Can metformin prolong pregnancy in preterm pre-eclampsia? Study protocol for a Nordic multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (PI4).
abstract: Pre-eclampsia affects 2–8% of all pregnancies and remains a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. A randomised trial in South Africa suggested metformin used to treat preterm pre-eclampsia (26–32 weeks’ gestation) may prolong pregnancy by 7 days compared with standard care. However, this finding was borderline significant and requires validation in higher-resource settings and in diverse populations. Here, we present a Nordic multicentre trial protocol designed to evaluate whether extended-release metformin can prolong gestation in women with preterm pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia Intervention 4 trial is a phase III, double-blind, multicentre randomised controlled trial conducted in Sweden, Norway and Finland aiming to investigate whether metformin can prolong gestation in preterm pre-eclampsia. A total of 294 women between 22+0 and 33+6 weeks of gestation with pre-eclampsia and planned to undergo expectant management will be enrolled. Participants are randomised to receive one gram of extended-release metformin or matching placebo three times daily. The primary outcome is prolongation of gestation defined as time from randomisation to birth. Secondary outcomes include length of neonatal hospital stay and neonatal birth weight. Adverse events will be reported in line with current clinical trial guidelines. All efficacy analyses will be conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle. The trial is conducted in accordance with Good Clinical Practice, as defined by the International Council for Harmonisation. The protocol, including amendments, was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority and the Swedish Medical Products Agency in accordance with national legislation, and authorised for Finland and Norway through the Clinical Trials Information System in accordance with the EU Clinical Trials Regulation. Results will be disseminated at international conferences and published in peer-reviewed journals and communicated via popular science outlets, media, patient organisations and the trial website: https://www.preeclampsiaresearch.com/pi-trials. NCT06033131.

title: Preconception incretin therapy reduces pregnancy and cardiometabolic outcomes in polycystic ovary syndrome.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), now polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), is associated with reproductive and cardiometabolic complications. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) receptor agonists (RAs) improve obesity-related outcomes, but their impact on pregnancy outcomes in PMOS remains unclear. We conducted a target trial emulation using the TriNetX global federated health research network. Women ≥18 years with PCOS/PMOS receiving pre-conception GLP-1/dual GLP-1/GIP RA therapy (liraglutide, semaglutide or tirzepatide) were compared with metformin. Propensity score matching (1:1) accounted for demographics, anthropometrics, comorbidities and medications. The primary outcome was a composite of adverse pregnancy outcomes (hypertensive, glycaemic, placental, delivery, labour, foetal growth, preterm and early pregnancy complications) over two years. Individual pregnancy endpoints, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) were exploratory secondary outcomes. Cox regression generated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). After matching, 48,126 patients were included per group. Pre-conception GLP-1/GIP RA use was associated with lower risk of the composite pregnancy outcome (HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.34-0.41). Exploratory analyses also demonstrated lower risks of individual pregnancy endpoints, MACE (HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.81-0.95) and T2D (HR 0.31; 95% CI 0.30-0.33). Associations varied across some sensitivity analyses. Pre-conception GLP-1/GIP RA use in women with PCOS/PMOS was associated with lower risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes and cardiometabolic disease compared with metformin, consistent with potential benefits of pre-conception metabolic optimisation. This study cannot evaluate in-pregnancy safety or efficacy, and these findings do not support GLP-1/GIP RA use during gestation.

title: From PCOS to PMOS: reframing the clinical pathway around insulin sensitivity and weight-neutral metabolic risk.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a heterogeneous condition associated with reproductive, metabolic, pregnancy, and psychological morbidity across the life course. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) was recently proposed through a multistep global consensus process, with implementation across guidelines and health systems still under way. This Perspective argues that the clinical value of the naming proposal will depend on whether it redirects care beyond ovarian morphology and body size. Insulin resistance can serve as an actionable management hub linking reproductive endocrine dysfunction with longer-term metabolic risk in a substantial subgroup, but it is neither universal, the sole cause of the syndrome, nor a diagnostic criterion. Routine fasting insulin measurement or homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance should therefore not be introduced as diagnostic requirements. Instead, we propose a weight-neutral, insulin-sensitivity-centered, life-course pathway aligned with existing guideline recommendations. Glycemic status, lipids, blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, pregnancy planning, psychological health, and risk-directed liver assessment should be considered according to clinical guidance without using BMI as an exclusion criterion. Lifestyle intervention should be evaluated through metabolic, functional, reproductive, and quality-of-life outcomes, not weight change alone. Metformin and GLP-1 receptor agonists should remain confined to guideline-supported indications and evidence limitations. Whether PMOS improves risk recognition, guideline adherence, patient experience, or continuity of care remains to be established.

title: Impact of Metformin on the Incidence of Thrombosis in Older Adults with Polycythemia Vera or Essential Thrombocythemia and Diabetes.
abstract: Individuals with myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) have an increased thrombotic risk, particularly in the presence of cardiovascular comorbidities such as diabetes (DM). Metformin (MET) has been associated with a reduced incidence of MPNs; however, data on its association with thrombotic outcomes in polycythemia vera (PV) and essential thrombocythemia (ET) are limited. We conducted a retrospective study using the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results-Medicare-linked database to evaluate the association between MET use and thrombotic risk in patients with MPNs and DM. We included patients with DM aged ≥66 years diagnosed with PV or ET between 2008-2019, continuously enrolled in Medicare Parts A/B/D, and followed for ≥6 months after diagnosis. Adjusted competing risk models were used to evaluate the association between MET and thrombotic risk. Among 1153 eligible patients (PV, n=528; ET, n=629), 846 (73.4%) had mild and 307 (26.6%) had severe DM. A total of 431 (37.4%) used MET. Overall, 485 (42.1%) patients experienced thrombosis after MPN diagnosis. MET use was independently associated with a reduced thrombotic risk (hazard ratio [HR]=0.78, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.64-0.95; p=0.02), especially among patients with severe DM (HR=0.58, 95% CI: 0.38-0.89; p=0.01), and those without prior thrombosis (HR=0.78, 95% CI: 0.62-0.97; p=0.02), but not among those with mild DM (HR=0.87, 95% CI: 0.68-1.11; p=0.27). When evaluating thrombotic event types separately, this benefit applied to arterial, but not venous thrombosis. MET use was associated with a lower thrombotic risk in older patients with PV/ET, primarily in individuals with severe DM.

title: Early insulin combined with metformin therapy and long-term risks of cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and cancer in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes: a real-world cohort study in China.
abstract: To evaluate the longitudinal associations of early insulin combined with metformin therapy, compared with metformin monotherapy, with subsequent risks of stroke, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and cancer among adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes using real-world data. We conducted an active-comparator new-user cohort study using the Cheeloo LEAD electronic health record database (Shandong, China; 2014-2021). Adults aged 40-85 years who initiated early insulin combined with metformin therapy or metformin monotherapy during 2014-2017 were included in the common parent cohort (n=19,908; 4,304 [21.6%] and 15,604 [78.4%], respectively). Follow-up began at each treatment strategy initiation date (t0). Four independent outcome-specific subcohorts excluded patients with the corresponding pre-existing outcome and those with the outcome recorded within 30 days after t0. The combination group required at least 14 days of overlapping insulin and metformin use. L1-regularized propensity score matching and Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) over up to 1,500 days. Sensitivity analyses used a 180-day outcome-exclusion window. Compared with metformin monotherapy, early insulin combined with metformin therapy was associated with a lower hazard of stroke (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.78-0.99) and higher hazards of heart failure (HR 1.18, 95% CI 1.02-1.36), chronic kidney disease (HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.03-1.83), and cancer (HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.14-1.66). Exploratory subgroup estimates varied by age and sex; no formal interaction tests were performed. Results were broadly consistent in sensitivity analyses. Early insulin combined with metformin therapy and metformin monotherapy showed different longitudinal associations with the four outcomes. These findings should be interpreted in light of residual confounding by baseline disease severity and treatment indication and may inform risk monitoring in routine care.

title: A 52-Week Efficacy and Safety Study of Teneligliptin, as an Add-On to Empagliflozin and Metformin in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Randomised, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Phase 3 Trial (TERA305 Study).
abstract: To evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of teneligliptin add-on in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) inadequately controlled with metformin and empagliflozin. In this randomised, double-blind, phase 3 trial, 214 patients received teneligliptin 20 mg (n = 107) or placebo (n = 107) once daily for 24 weeks, in addition to metformin (≥ 1000 mg/day) and empagliflozin (25 mg/day). In a subsequent 28-week open-label extension, all patients received teneligliptin 20 mg/day. The primary endpoint was HbA1c change from baseline to week 24. At week 24, the least squares mean (LSM) change in HbA1c from baseline was -0.70% ± 0.06% in the teneligliptin group and -0.03% ± 0.06% in the placebo group, with a placebo-adjusted LSM change of -0.67% (95% CI, -0.84 to -0.49; p < 0.0001), demonstrating the superiority of teneligliptin. A significant between-group difference was already evident at week 4 (placebo-adjusted LSM change, -0.36%; p < 0.0001). Significant reductions in fasting plasma glucose and glycated albumin and improvement in pancreatic β-cell function were observed at week 24. During the open-label extension, glycaemic improvements were maintained through week 52, although no concurrent randomised control was available beyond week 24. Placebo-group patients achieved a similar benefit after switching to teneligliptin. Safety outcomes did not differ between groups. Adding teneligliptin to metformin and empagliflozin in patients with inadequately controlled T2DM significantly improved glycaemic control and β-cell function over 24 weeks and was well tolerated through 52 weeks. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05504226.

title: Cardiovascular safety of orforglipron versus insulin glargine in adults with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk (ACHIEVE-4): a phase 3, event-driven, randomised, open-label, non-inferiority, active comparator trial.
abstract: Orforglipron is an oral, non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist. While some peptide GLP-1 receptor agonists have established cardiovascular benefit, the cardiovascular safety of non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonists has not been studied. This study aimed to compare the effect of orforglipron with insulin glargine on the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events in individuals with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight who are at increased risk for cardiovascular events. This event-driven, phase 3, multicentre, randomised, open-label, active comparator, parallel-group study was conducted in 317 sites across 16 countries and territories. Adults with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk with glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) concentrations between 7·0% and 10·5% (53-91 mmol/mol) and a BMI of 25 kg/m2 or more, treated with up to three glucose-lowering medications (metformin, a sulfonylurea, and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor), were randomly assigned (1:1) to oral orforglipron maximum tolerated dose (up to 36 mg capsule [equivalent to 17·2 mg tablet]) or injectable titrated insulin glargine, each administered once daily. All participants had established cardiovascular or chronic kidney disease. The primary outcome was time to occurrence of four-component major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE-4), including cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, or hospitalisation for unstable angina. Non-inferiority of orforglipron to insulin glargine was declared if the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the hazard ratio (HR; orforglipron vs insulin glargine) was less than 1·8. The primary endpoint and other safety endpoints were assessed in all participants who took at least one dose of assigned treatment using all datapoints from baseline until withdrawal or study completion, regardless of treatment adherence. This trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05803421) and is completed. Between May 1, 2023, and Sept 5, 2024, 2749 participants were randomly assigned (1371 to orforglipron and 1378 to insulin glargine). 1032 (38%) participants were female and 1717 (62·5%) male. 2362 (85·9%) participants had established cardiovascular disease and 1033 (37·6%) had chronic kidney disease. Mean baseline age, HbA1c, and BMI were 63·1 years (SD 9·9), 8·2% (1·0), and 33 kg/m2 (6·2), respectively. Over a median follow-up of 2 years, the primary outcome occurred in 57 (4·2%) of 1358 orforglipron participants and 67 (5·0%) of 1343 insulin glargine participants, showing non-inferiority to insulin glargine for MACE-4 (HR 0·84; 95% CI 0·59-1·20; p<0·0001 for non-inferiority). Gastrointestinal adverse events were reported in 851 (62·1%) of 1371 orforglipron participants and 193 (14·2%) of 1355 insulin glargine participants; clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia (glucose <3 mmol/L [54 mg/dL]) occurred in 93 (6·8%) of 1371 orforglipron participants and 260 (19·2%) of 1355 insulin glargine participants. 62 deaths were reported during the study: 19 (1·4%) of 1371 participants receiving orforglipron and 43 (3·2%) of 1355 participants receiving insulin glargine; all deaths except one (in the insulin glargine group) were deemed unrelated to treatment. In people with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk, the cardiovascular safety of orforglipron was confirmed by demonstrating non-inferiority to insulin glargine for MACE-4. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent adverse event and most common reason for orforglipron treatment discontinuation with orforglipron, while clinically significant hypoglycaemia occurred less frequently with orforglipron than with insulin glargine. These findings support orforglipron as a potential once-daily, oral treatment option with established cardiovascular safety in people with type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk. Eli Lilly and Company.

Adults with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk with glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) concentrations between 7·0% and 10·5% (53-91 mmol/mol) and a BMI of 25 kg/m2 or more, treated with up to three glucose-lowering medications (metformin, a sulfonylurea, and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor), were randomly assigned (1:1) to oral orforglipron maximum tolerated dose (up to 36 mg capsule [equivalent to 17·2 mg tablet]) or injectable titrated insulin glargine, each administered once daily. All participants had established cardiovascular or chronic kidney disease. The primary outcome was time to occurrence of four-component major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE-4), including cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, or hospitalisation for unstable angina. Non-inferiority of orforglipron to insulin glargine was declared if the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the hazard ratio (HR; orforglipron vs insulin glargine) was less than 1·8. The primary endpoint and other safety endpoints were assessed in all participants who took at least one dose of assigned treatment using all datapoints from baseline until withdrawal or study completion, regardless of treatment adherence. This trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05803421) and is completed.

abstract_sections.label: Findings
abstract_sections.text: Between May 1, 2023, and Sept 5, 2024, 2749 participants were randomly assigned (1371 to orforglipron and 1378 to insulin glargine). 1032 (38%) participants were female and 1717 (62·5%) male. 2362 (85·9%) participants had established cardiovascular disease and 1033 (37·6%) had chronic kidney disease. Mean baseline age, HbA1c, and BMI were 63·1 years (SD 9·9), 8·2% (1·0), and 33 kg/m2 (6·2), respectively. Over a median follow-up of 2 years, the primary outcome occurred in 57 (4·2%) of 1358 orforglipron participants and 67 (5·0%) of 1343 insulin glargine participants, showing non-inferiority to insulin glargine for MACE-4 (HR 0·84; 95% CI 0·59-1·20; p<0·0001 for non-inferiority). Gastrointestinal adverse events were reported in 851 (62·1%) of 1371 orforglipron participants and 193 (14·2%) of 1355 insulin glargine participants; clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia (glucose <3 mmol/L [54 mg/dL]) occurred in 93 (6·8%) of 1371 orforglipron participants and 260 (19·2%) of 1355 insulin glargine participants. 62 deaths were reported during the study: 19 (1·4%) of 1371 participants receiving orforglipron and 43 (3·2%) of 1355 participants receiving insulin glargine; all deaths except one (in the insulin glargine group) were deemed unrelated to treatment.

abstract_sections.label: Interpretation
abstract_sections.text: In people with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk, the cardiovascular safety of orforglipron was confirmed by demonstrating non-inferiority to insulin glargine for MACE-4. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent adverse event and most common reason for orforglipron treatment discontinuation with orforglipron, while clinically significant hypoglycaemia occurred less frequently with orforglipron than with insulin glargine. These findings support orforglipron as a potential once-daily, oral treatment option with established cardiovascular safety in people with type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk.

title: Aldosterone synthase inhibition for treatment of people with chronic kidney disease.
abstract: Aldosterone contributes to the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) not only through its effects on blood pressure (BP) but also by promoting inflammation and fibrosis in the kidney and cardiovascular system. Despite contemporary treatment with renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, residual risk persists for adverse kidney and cardiovascular outcomes. Aldosterone synthase inhibition (ASI) has emerged as a potent strategy to directly suppress aldosterone production. Several selective inhibitors, including baxdrostat, lorundrostat, and vicadrostat, have been shown to lower aldosterone levels without affecting cortisol synthesis in a clinically meaningful manner. Clinical studies in hypertension consistently show a decrease in systolic BP with these agents. In a CKD population, vicadrostat dose-dependently reduced the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio with additional BP lowering, and possibly greater albuminuria reduction when combined with empagliflozin. Similar findings have been observed with lorundrostat and baxdrostat in patients with CKD and uncontrolled hypertension. Median increases in serum potassium of ∼0.3 mmol/l that have been observed with ASI were generally manageable in clinical trial populations. Emerging evidence from clinical trials and meta-analyses suggests that concomitant SGLT2 inhibitor therapy may mitigate the risk of clinically significant hyperkalaemia, also supporting the use of combination therapy. Overall, ASI provide a potentially beneficial approach to reduce residual risks of CKD. Several phase 3 trials testing vicadrostat or baxdrostat across different populations with CKD, hypertension, or cardiovascular disease will determine whether favourable effects on albuminuria translate into improved kidney and cardiovascular outcomes.

title: Effects of SGLT2 inhibition on cardiac remodeling and heart failure development in aortic stenosis rats.
abstract: Aortic stenosis (AS) is increasingly prevalent in ageing populations, yet no pharmacological therapy has been shown to modify its progression to heart failure (HF). Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors improve outcomes in HF, but their effects in pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling remain unclear. Here, we show that rats with long-term AS develop HF features, left ventricular dilation, and systolic and diastolic dysfunction, accompanied by increased oxidative stress, impaired antioxidant defenses, myocardial fibrosis, and transcriptional remodeling. Empagliflozin (10 mg/kg/day for 8 weeks) attenuated cardiac dysfunction and reduced HF features. At molecular level, empagliflozin prevented increase in lipid peroxidation, and decreased interstitial collagen deposition, while increasing glutathione peroxidase and matrix metalloproteinase-2 activity. Transcriptomic analysis identified 1,078 differentially expressed genes and revealed enrichment of pathways associated with extracellular matrix organization and signal transduction in AS. Empagliflozin predominantly regulated genes involved in cardiac contraction, mitochondrial membrane organization, apoptosis, and cell survival. Profibrotic and remodeling-associated genes were upregulated in AS, while empagliflozin induced a distinct transcriptional program associated with improved myocardial homeostasis. AS was associated with reduced activity of energy metabolism enzymes, which was not restored by empagliflozin. Collectively, these findings identify oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, and transcriptional reprogramming as mechanisms underlying cardiac dysfunction in AS. Empagliflozin mitigates cardiac remodeling and HF progression and modulates fibrosis and gene networks regulating cardiac function. These data highlight SGLT2 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy in pressure overload-induced heart failure.

title: Medicare Part D formulary coverage of SGLT2 inhibitors across cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic indications, 2019-2026.
abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) carry Class I, Level A recommendations for type 2 diabetes (T2D), heart failure (HF), and chronic kidney disease (CKD) but remain underused outside T2D, with formulary restrictions commonly cited as a contributing cause. We assessed whether Medicare Part D formulary restrictions account for this gap and whether the restrictions differ across cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) indications. Cross-sectional analysis of national Medicare Part D formulary files for plan years 2019-2026, using the January/February snapshot (410 formularies in 2019, 330 in 2026; 13,726 SGLT2i monotherapy entries). We measured entry-level prior authorization (PA) and step-therapy prevalence, the proportion of formularies offering at least one and at least two unrestricted SGLT2i drugs, and tier distribution, across three indication groups reflecting cumulative regulatory approvals. PA was uncommon across all indications and years, never exceeding 1.6%, and at least 98% of formularies offered a PA-free SGLT2i in every indication group-year. Step therapy fell to zero by 2025 then rebounded in 2026, concentrated on empagliflozin, whose entry-level step therapy rate rose from 0.00% to 18.18%, coincident with the effective date of its negotiated maximum fair price; co-negotiated dapagliflozin showed no comparable increase (1.21%). Tier 3 was the dominant placement (61.9-78.7%). Canagliflozin coverage fell from 58.3% of formularies in 2019 to 5.8% in 2026, and only 5.8% offered two step-free SGLT2i for CKD by 2026. Formulary restrictions do not appear to be a major barrier to SGLT2i use among Medicare beneficiaries, redirecting attention toward clinician- and system-level factors. Narrowing CKD-indication approved options and an emergent step-therapy rebound warrant monitoring.

title: Network and pairwise meta-analysis of the effects of novel hypoglycemic agents on cardiorenal outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes and heart failure.
abstract: This study aims to evaluate the cardiovascular and renal benefits of novel hypoglycemic agents, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4is), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is), and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 dual receptor agonists (GIP/GLP-1RAs) in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and heart failure (HF). Systematic literature searches were conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) from inception to 30 April 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for cardiovascular outcomes (CVOTs) or post hoc analyses of CVOTs comparing SGLT-2is, DPP-4is, GLP-1RAs, or GIP/GLP-1RAs in patients with T2DM and HF were selected. Network meta-analysis was used for indirect comparisons, with results presented as hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A total of 10 RCTs and two post hoc analyses of CVOTs involving 13,886 patients were included. Compared with placebo, SGLT-2is (HR [95% CI]: 0.75 [0.68, 0.82]) and GLP-1RAs (HR [95% CI]: 0.77 [0.61, 0.97]) both significantly reduced the risk of HF-related composite endpoints in patients with T2DM and HF. No statistically significant difference was observed between SGLT-2is and GLP-1RAs (HR [95% CI]: 0.98 [0.76, 1.25]). SGLT-2is also reduced the risk of HF worsening (HR [95% CI]: 0.72 [0.53, 0.96]), HF hospitalization (HR [95% CI]: 0.74 [0.66, 0.83]), and cardiovascular (CV) death (HR [95% CI]: 0.87 [0.77, 0.98]). For all-cause death, SGLT-2is showed a trend toward reduced risk compared to placebo, but this difference did not reach statistical significance (HR [95% CI]: 0.83 [0.67, 1.02]). For the renal composite outcome, SGLT-2is did not demonstrate a statistically significant benefit (HR [95% CI]: 0.76 [0.51, 1.14]). Optimal clinical management of T2DM requires a comprehensive assessment of cardiovascular and renal comorbidities. This network meta-analysis indicates that SGLT-2is significantly reduce the risk of HF-related composite endpoints and CV death in T2DM patients with HF, although their renoprotective effect does not reach statistical significance. GLP-1RAs also demonstrate beneficial effects on HF-related composite endpoints. These findings suggest that both SGLT-2is and GLP-1RAs are preferred glycemic control strategies for improving cardiovascular outcomes in T2DM patients with HF, while further evidence is needed to confirm their definitive renal benefits. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42026142123, identifier: CRD420261421235.

title: Real-world safety of vericiguat as a fifth-line agent in heart failure: a pharmacovigilance study of quintuple therapy.
abstract: Vericiguat, a novel soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulator, is indicated for high-risk worsening heart failure (HF). However, its real-world reporting profile when added to contemporary quadruple guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)-effectively creating a "quintuple" regimen-remains largely unexplored, particularly regarding cardiorenal and hematologic adverse-event reporting patterns. We conducted a retrospective pharmacovigilance study using the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database (2021 Q1-2025 Q4). HF reports were strictly stratified into an expanded quadruple GDMT cohort [renin-angiotensin system inhibitor + beta-blocker + mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist [MRA] + sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor [SGLT2i]] and a quintuple cohort (GDMT + vericiguat). Disproportionality analysis utilized a dual-algorithm approach: the frequentist Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) and the Bayesian Information Component (IC) derived from the Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN). SGLT2i-stratified analyses and formal interaction testing were also performed. The final cohort comprised 5,524 reports (5,459 quadruple; 65 quintuple). No ROR signals were identified for hypotension (ROR = 1.66, 95% CI: 0.90-3.06), syncope (ROR = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.21-3.49), or acute kidney injury (ROR = 0.61, 95% CI: 0.26-1.41). Anemia met the frequentist ROR signal criterion (ROR = 2.61, 95% CI: 1.03-6.58), but not the BCPNN criterion (IC = 0.96, IC-2SD = -0.29). The anemia ROR was 2.61 (95% CI: 1.03-6.58) with an SGLT2i background and 1.82 (95% CI: 0.42-7.88) without an SGLT2i background; formal interaction testing did not demonstrate significant effect modification (P for interaction = 0.683). No statistically significant differences were detected in reported serious outcomes between groups. In this FAERS analysis, no robust reporting signals were identified for hypotension, syncope, or acute kidney injury after vericiguat was added to contemporary quadruple GDMT. Although anemia met the frequentist ROR criterion, the finding was not supported by Bayesian signal detection, and formal analyses did not demonstrate significant effect modification by background SGLT2i use. Given the small vericiguat-exposed cohort, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger longitudinal studies.

title: Contraindication-adjusted prescription omission patterns of RASi, beta-blockers, and MRAs in hospitalized heart failure: associations with 30-day and 1-year mortality.
abstract: Guideline directed therapy is still underused in heart failure and little is known about how missing specific medications near discharge relates to survival. The aim of this study is to examine whether study-defined omission patterns of RASi (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or ARNIs), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) in the final 48 h before discharge were associated with short-term and 1-year mortality among hospitalized adults with heart failure. Adult admissions with a recorded heart failure diagnosis were identified using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes. The three classes were RASi, beta-blockers, and MRAs (SGLT2 inhibitors were not included). A contraindication-adjusted operational framework was used to identify admissions without selected laboratory or hemodynamic barriers to these therapies and to classify late-hospital prescription omission patterns. Final-48-h orders were a proxy for treatment near discharge, not a reconciled discharge list. This framework did not establish heart failure phenotype-specific guideline eligibility. Associations with mortality within 30 and 365 days after discharge were evaluated using multivariable regression models. The final analytic cohort included 57,098 admissions from 24,922 patients. The reference group with prescriptions for all three study classes was small whereas omission of 2 or 3 therapies was substantially more common across the cohort. Admissions with prescriptions for all three study classes had the lowest 365-day mortality (13.88%). Crude 365-day mortality was higher in all omission groups, reaching 30.84% when RASi and beta-blocker were omitted and 27.50% when all three classes were omitted. In adjusted analyses, omission of all 3 therapies was associated with higher 30-day mortality (OR = 1.67). For 365-day mortality, the strongest adverse association was observed for omission of renin-angiotensin system inhibitor plus beta-blocker (HR = 1.33). Late-hospital omission patterns involving RASi and omission of all three study therapies were associated with higher post-discharge mortality. As heart failure phenotype and left-ventricular ejection fraction were not incorporated into the eligibility definition, these findings should be interpreted as prognostic associations of prescribing patterns rather than causal effects of withholding guideline-indicated HFrEF therapy.

title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: From pathophysiology to a practical approach to diagnosis and treatment.
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a heterogeneous syndrome with increasing prevalence, driven by aging and cardiometabolic comorbidities. It is better understood as a disorder of elevated filling pressures, impaired cardiovascular reserve, recurrent congestion, and systemic multiorgan dysfunction than as heart failure with normal systolic function. Diagnosis remains probabilistic and requires integration of symptoms, natriuretic peptides, echocardiographic structural and functional abnormalities, and, when resting findings are inconclusive, exercise or invasive hemodynamic testing. Treatment has evolved from symptom control toward phenotype-oriented care. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are foundational therapy, finerenone expands options for selected patients, and obesity is now a modifiable therapeutic target. This review summarizes current mechanisms, diagnostic pathways, and treatment strategies, with emphasis on practical clinical decision-making.

title: Prescribing SGLTis and GLP-1 RAs for Patients With Type 2 Diabetes, Guideline Updates, and Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment Scores.
abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce cardiovascular and kidney events in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) who have established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, yet prescribing to these patients remains low. To describe temporal patterns in SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA prescribing before and after the 2019 American Diabetes Association (ADA) guideline update and to assess whether these patterns differed across physicians with subsequently measured different first-year American Board of Internal Medicine Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment (LKA) scores. This serial cross-sectional study was conducted from October 2025 through January 2026, using 2017 to 2022 traditional Medicare claims. Endocrinologists first participating in the 2022 to 2023 LKA and the Medicare beneficiaries with T2D they treated were included. Time relative to the 2019 ADA guideline update. The annual patient-year SGLT2i and GLP-1RA guideline-targeted and nontargeted patient fill rates were the main outcome. Linear physician, year, and target subgroup fixed-effects regression models were estimated, with patient demographic and health risk controls to evaluate within-physician associations between guideline-targeted vs nontargeted patient-year fill rates each year relative to 2018 (the year before the guideline update). The variation in these associations across first-year LKA score quartiles was also evaluated. title: Cardiorenal Syndrome: Pathophysiology, Management, and the Challenge of Therapeutic Inertia.
abstract: Cardiorenal syndrome describes the clinical consequences of the bidirectional influence that cardiac and renal dysfunction exert on each other-a domain in which single-organ care proves insufficient. A 2024 meta-analysis estimated the pooled prevalence of chronic kidney disease among patients with heart failure at 49%. Across individual cohorts, this figure ranges between 30% and 60%, with the spread reflecting the population studied and the threshold used to define kidney disease. Among acute heart failure admissions, 64% of cases have an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and mortality reaches 7.6% once it falls into the severe range (15-29 mL/min/1.73 m2). The same can be described in the other "direction": congestive heart failure is reported in 28% of adults aged 66 years or older with chronic kidney disease, compared to 6% of those without. The Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative distinguishes a five-subtype framework by direction and chronicity of organ injury, and each subtype shows characteristic prescribing failure patterns. In types 1 and 2, the dominant problem is premature de-escalation of neurohormonal therapy at the first creatinine rise. In type 4, the failure is upstream in the cascade: cardiovascular surveillance lags behind the increasing rate of chronic kidney disease. Randomized trials over the past decade have expanded the therapeutic options. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors showed cardiorenal benefit across every ejection fraction studied and at estimated glomerular filtration rate values down to 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. These findings have expanded treatment eligibility to patients with advanced CKD. The FINE-HEART pooled analysis of finerenone suggested a nominal reduction in all-cause mortality, alongside fewer heart failure hospitalizations and improvement in the kidney composite outcome. In the FLOW trial, semaglutide showed a reduction in the composite of major kidney events and cardiovascular death in diabetic adults with chronic kidney disease. In this cohort, the estimated glomerular filtration rate slope was slower in the active arm and secondary outcomes showed reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events and in all-cause mortality. However, observational registries show that these classes of drugs are less used in patients with the highest baseline risk, with advancing renal disease identified as an independent predictor of under-prescription. Therapeutic inertia in this setting reflects determinants at the patient, clinician, and system levels, which is compounded because each prescribing decision must be justified for both the heart and the kidney. The primary objective of the present narrative review is the therapeutic inertia that separates this evidence from routine prescribing: the sections on pathophysiology, imaging and biomarker tools, and subtype-specific pharmacotherapy supply the clinical rationale, and the closing sections cover the implementation strategies and the multidisciplinary framework required to act on the trial findings.

title: Drug Therapies and Incident Heart Failure in Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF), the most common cardiac arrhythmia, significantly elevates the risk of new-onset heart failure (HF). We aimed to systematically map and appraise available evidence on drug therapies and incident HF in patients with AF. We searched Medline, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Scopus up to 16 September 2026 for relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs), sub-analyses of RCTs, and observational/cohort studies. Seventeen studies (397,991 participants) were included. The only randomized signal came from a prespecified subgroup of the ACTIVE-I trial, in which irbesartan was associated with fewer first HF hospitalizations than the placebo (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.69-0.96; moderate certainty). Observational studies showed an association with lower first HF hospitalization for sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors in patients with type 2 diabetes (pooled HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.48-0.95; two studies; low certainty) and lower incident HF diagnosis in a larger cohort that included patients without diabetes (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.82-0.89). The remaining cohort evidence largely reflected prescribing patterns rather than drug effects. Statins showed an inconsistent association. The higher HF incidence among users of diuretics, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, digoxin and renin-angiotensin system inhibitors was consistent with confounding by indication (very low certainty). Evidence on drug therapies to prevent HF in AF is limited to one randomized subgroup signal for irbesartan. The remaining findings were associations rather than demonstrated treatment effects. High-quality research, including RCTs in broader AF populations, is needed. PROSPERO Registration: CRD42024587926.

title: Clinical Characteristics, Cardiometabolic Risk Burden and Therapeutic Patterns in Patients Attending Cardiology Clinics in Spain: The RIESCAR Study.
abstract: Contemporary data on patients attending cardiology outpatient clinics in Spain are scarce. We aimed to characterise cardiovascular conditions, cardiometabolic burden, risk-factor control and treatment patterns. RIESCAR is a national, multicentre, observational study. This analysis included 2808 adults evaluated in 50 general cardiology outpatient clinics. Hypertension was present in 60.3%, dyslipidaemia in 58.9%, type 2 diabetes mellitus in 24.7%, obesity in 32.4%, and central obesity in 48.7%. Established cardiovascular disease was documented in 59.7%, with coronary artery disease (30.0%), atrial fibrillation (18.2%) and heart failure (11.7%) being the most frequent conditions. Among hypertensive patients, 42.6% had blood pressure ≥ 140/90 mmHg. In patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), 37.2% achieved LDL-C < 55 mg/dL. Patients received a high number of cardiovascular drugs (mean 3.9). Among patients with a potential clinical indication for contemporary cardiometabolic therapies, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists were used in 35.4% and 8.6%, respectively. Patients attending cardiology clinics in Spain have a high cardiometabolic burden, with important gaps in blood-pressure and LDL-C target attainment. Use of contemporary cardiometabolic therapies remains variable, highlighting opportunities to strengthen cardiovascular prevention in routine practice.

title: Impact of Functional Frailty Measured by Short Physical Performance Battery Test on the Effectiveness of SGLT2 Inhibitors in Elderly Patients with Acute Heart Failure:PROFUND-IC Registry.
abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) is the leading cause of hospitalization among patients over 65 years and is frequently associated with frailty. Sodium-glucose cotransporter type 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) currently represent the only drug class recommended across the entire ejection fraction spectrum, although evidence regarding their effectiveness according to frailty status remains limited. To determine whether functional frailty, measured by the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) test, influences the effectiveness of SGLT2i in reducing hospital readmission and mortality in elderly patients with AHF. Observational study of 794 polypathological patients admitted to Internal Medicine with AHF. An interaction analysis assessed whether SPPB, as a continuous variable, modified the association between SGLT2i and the composite outcome (hospital readmission or death), using a Cox model. The sample was further divided by SPPB test score (below 4 (N = 477) or ≥4 (N = 317)) for exploratory analyses. Descriptive and comparative analyses were performed according to SGLT2i administration, using the chi-squared test for qualitative variables and Student's t-test for quantitative ones (Fisher's and Mann-Whitney U test as appropriate). Survival analysis was done using Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression, with multivariable adjustment for confounders. No significant interaction was found between SPPB score and SGLT2i (p = 0.506). When SPPB was dichotomised, SGLT2i treatment was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (3.7% vs. 12.0%; p = 0.018) and readmission (30.3% vs. 45.2%; p = 0.021) in SPPB ≥ 4, with mortality and readmission also numerically lower, without reaching statistical significance, in SPPB p = 0.410; readmission 34.5% vs. 42.0%, p = 0.220). After adjustment, SGLT2i treatment in the SPPB ≥ 4 group remained associated with a numerically lower hazard for the composite outcome (HR 0.652; 95% CI 0.418-1.018; p = 0.060). No evidence was found that functional frailty modifies the effectiveness of SGLT2i in elderly polypathological patients with AHF. An exploratory analysis suggested a possible gradient of greater association with SPPB ≥ 4, although this should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.

title: Early Initiation of Dapagliflozin in Acute Heart Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: Dapagliflozin is a foundational chronic heart failure therapy, but whether it retains benefit when initiated early during hospitalization for acute heart failure (AHF) remains uncertain. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and CENTRAL from inception to 26 January 2026 for randomized trials comparing early initiation of dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily with standard therapy in adults hospitalized for AHF (PROSPERO CRD420261364466). Two reviewers independently performed screening, extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Outcomes were pooled under random-effects models with Knapp-Hartung adjustment. Ten trials enrolling 3507 participants (1769 in the dapagliflozin group and 1738 in the control group) were eligible. Dapagliflozin significantly reduced all-cause mortality (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.52-0.86) and urinary tract infections (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.35-0.76), while no significant differences were observed in cardiovascular death, MACEs, heart failure hospitalization, all-cause readmission, length of hospital stay, or body weight. Dapagliflozin was not associated with a significant increase in acute kidney injury, hypotension, or hypoglycemia, supporting a favorable safety profile. In adults hospitalized with acute heart failure (AHF), dapagliflozin significantly reduced all-cause mortality but not heart failure hospitalization during follow-up. Larger, adequately powered trials in patients with AHF, with prespecified analyses according to the timing of dapagliflozin initiation, are warranted.

title: Comparative risk assessment of cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes using cystatin C and creatinine in DECLARE-TIMI 58.
abstract: The relationship between cystatin C and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes is not well explored in individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and normal or mild kidney dysfunction. This nested prospective biomarker study included patients enrolled in DECLARE-TIMI 58. Participants were categorized into quartiles of CysC/creatinine and eGFRCysC/eGFRCr and classified according to Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) risk categories. Hazard ratios were estimated for a composite of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure (CVD/HHF), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and a kidney-specific composite outcome (persistent ≥40% decrease in eGFR, end-stage renal disease, or renal death). Among 1899 placebo-treated patients, higher baseline CysC was associated with higher risk for CVD/HHF, MACE, and the kidney-specific composite outcome. A gradient of risk across quartiles was observed for CVD/HHF [Q4 v Q1: 1.33 (0.98-1.80), p-trend = 0.016]; MACE [1.34 (1.06-1.69), p-trend = 0.013]; and kidney-specific composite outcome [1.95 (0.95-3.99), p-trend = 0.036]. When compared with creatinine, CysC showed more pronounced and statistically significant risk gradients (CVD/HHF: KDIGO-CysC p-trend 0.05). In patients with T2D and predominantly preserved Cr-based eGFR, CysC was associated with increased cardiovascular and kidney risk. Although discrimination assessed by c-statistic was similar for CysC and Cr, risk gradients seen with CysC became attenuated and no longer statistically significant when using Cr-based analogs. The effect of dapagliflozin was consistent irrespective of baseline CysC. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01730534.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Obese Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction.
abstract: To evaluate whether GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), compared with DPP4 (dipeptidyl peptidase-4) inhibitors or sulfonylureas, are associated with reduced all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalizations in patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. PRAISE-HFpEF (Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist in Obese Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction) was a nationwide multicenter cohort study using a new-user, active-comparator design within the national Veterans Affairs Health System (170 US hospitals). Adults with type 2 diabetes between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2021, were identified from centralized electronic health records. Patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and a body mass index ≥30 kg/m2 were selected using a validated diagnostic algorithm. Exposure was initiation of a GLP-1RA versus DPP4 inhibitors/sulfonylurea from January 1, 2015 to December 31, 2021. The primary outcome was time to all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization. Inverse probability of treatment weighting based on the propensity score was used to balanced baseline characteristics. Among 179 288 patients with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, 1024 GLP-1RA users and 796 DPP4 inhibitors/sulfonylurea users met inclusion criteria. Over a median follow-up of 1.5 years, GLP-1RA use was associated with a lower risk of the primary outcome (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.64-0.95], P=0.01). Weight loss was modestly greater with GLP-1RAs compared with DPP4 inhibitors/sulfonylurea (-12.9% versus -10.1%). Among patients with obese heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and type 2 diabetes, GLP-1RA initiation was associated with a lower incidence of death or heart failure hospitalization compared with alternative oral agents.

title: From metabolic therapy to addiction care: a clinical pharmacology roadmap for GLP-1 receptor agonists in substance use disorders.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), established treatments for type 2 diabetes and obesity, are being investigated for substance use disorders (SUDs). Randomized evidence is emerging in alcohol use disorder (AUD), while evidence for opioid, nicotine, cocaine, cannabis, and stimulant use disorders remains mixed, observational, or investigational. This targeted narrative review integrates PubMed/MEDLINE literature, US Food and Drug Administration guidance and labeling, and ClinicalTrials.gov records available through 15 July 2026, with targeted literature and registry updates through 20 October 2026. It evaluates mechanistic plausibility, randomized and real-world human evidence, agent- and dose-specific pharmacology, co-treatment with established SUD medications, safety, adherence, benefit-risk assessment, harm reduction, equity, and trial design. The evidence is sufficient to justify indication-specific clinical development, especially for AUD, but currently insufficient for routine off-label treatment of SUDs for patients without an approved metabolic indication. Near-term research should test GLP-1 RAs as adjuncts rather than replacements for established SUD care, distinguish direct reward effects from weight loss and adverse-effect pathways, and embed risk minimization, patient-important outcomes, and equitable access into development from the outset.

title: Urological manifestations in obesity.
abstract: The global prevalence of obesity continues to rise, with effects ranging across urology. This review summarizes recent evidence on obesity and its impact on various urological conditions, including malignancy, infections, stone disease, functional urology and male reproductive health, chronic kidney disease, and pediatric urology, to guide comprehensive management in this population. Obesity has a paradoxical survival benefit in patients with renal cell carcinoma, while its impact drives aggressive prostate cancer. Obesity increases kidney stone risk, with sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists showing divergent effects on lithogenesis and urinary tract infections. It is a modifiable risk factor for overactive bladder and stress urinary incontinence, both of which improve with weight loss/ bariatric surgery. Robotic surgery mitigates obesity-related perioperative risk. Hypogonadism secondary to obesity is a major reversible cause of male infertility. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) reverse metabolic hypogonadism and helps in slowing chronic kidney progression. Maternal and childhood obesity may impair testicular descent and can also increase the risk of nocturnal enuresis. Obesity's urological effects are heterogeneous, paradoxical from pediatric to adults, mediated by insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and hormonal dysregulation. Weight loss and the use of GLP-1 RA may offer a unique strategy for optimizing and treating urological conditions.

title: Obesity and skeletal fragility: revisiting an old paradigm.
abstract: Obesity has traditionally been considered protective against osteoporosis because of its association with higher bone mineral density (BMD). However, emerging evidence demonstrates that individuals with obesity remain at increased risk of peripheral fractures despite preserved BMD. This review summarizes current evidence on the complex relationship between obesity and skeletal health, including underlying mechanisms, fracture patterns, assessment strategies, and management considerations. Studies indicate that fracture risk in obesity is site-specific, with a greater propensity for peripheral fractures. Visceral adiposity, bone marrow adipose tissue, chronic low-grade inflammation, altered adipokine signaling, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and obesity-related comorbidities contribute to impaired bone quality and skeletal fragility. Conventional Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) may underestimate skeletal risk in obesity, while newer tools such as trabecular bone score (TBS) version 4.0, peripheral quantitative computerized tomography (pQCT) may improve risk assessment. Weight-loss interventions, including lifestyle modification, Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA), and bariatric surgery, provide substantial metabolic benefits but may increase fracture risk if skeletal health is not adequately addressed. Obesity should no longer be regarded as protective for bone health. Although BMD is often normal or elevated, obesity is associated with alterations in bone quality and increased fracture susceptibility. Comprehensive skeletal assessment, incorporation of lifestyle measures to preserve bone health, and appropriate osteoporosis therapy are essential. Future research should focus on obesity-specific fracture prediction tools, advanced imaging modalities, and dedicated clinical guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, and management of osteoporosis in individuals with obesity.

title: The pharmacist's role in enhancing adherence to GLP1 based anti-obesity medications through comprehensive side effect management.
abstract: The emergence of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP1) and GLP1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonists (hereinafter GLP1-RAs, GLP1-GIP-RAs) have transformed obesity treatment. These agents offer substantial weight loss and notable cardiometabolic and other health benefits. Yet, their success relies on long-term adherence and careful management of side effects. Common adverse events - especially gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances - often lead to treatment discontinuation, weight regain and reduced effectiveness. As healthcare providers with multiple patients' interactions, pharmacists provide continuous care throughout the entire treatment journey, from initiation through titration phase and long-term maintenance. The unique position of pharmacists' interactions with patients enables them to address the high rates of non-adherence commonly observed with GLP1 based medications, which often stem from GI side effects, medication complexity, and patient education gaps. Treatment persistence and patient outcomes can be significantly improved through structured, pharmacist-led strategies, including comprehensive patient education, lifestyle modifications, and judicious use of over-the-counter interventions and vitamin/mineral/supplement therapies. Critical emphasis is placed on the pharmacist's role in preventing and managing serious complications associated with rapid weight loss, particularly sarcopenia and nutrient deficiencies, while maintaining vigilance for "red flags" that signal serious complications requiring physician intervention. This manuscript delineates the rationale for pharmacist involvement through the phases of adherence: initiation, titration, persistence, and discontinuation. It provides side-effect incidence and management tables, possible lifestyle and treatment options in each phase, red-flag and referral criteria, strategies to prevent sarcopenia and nutrient deficiency. Implementing these pharmacist-driven interventions can significantly improve tolerability, adherence, and long-term clinical outcomes in obesity pharmacotherapy.
