title: Gastric residual volume in patients with obesity receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists: A comparative gastric ultrasound pilot study.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) enhance insulin secretion, suppress glucagon release, promote satiety, and may slow gastric emptying. Introduced in 2005 for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity, these agents have prompted interest in assessing delayed gastric emptying as a potential biomarker to predict treatment response and to guide decisions regarding long-term therapy. Point-of-care gastric ultrasound (POCUS) offers a bedside method to assess gastric contents. To compare gastric residual volume (GRV) on gastric ultrasound among patients with obesity receiving GLP-1 RAs and nonusers and those with prior weight loss surgeries. In this comparative cross-sectional pilot study, gastric POCUS was done on patients with obesity who took GLP-1 RAs and other patients with obesity with no history of taking GLP-1 RAs prior to surgery in the supine and lateral decubitus positions. Antral cross-sectional area and GRV were measured using validated mathematical models. Patients receiving GLP-1 RAs demonstrated higher estimated GRV compared with nonusers. A higher proportion of GLP-1 RA users met ultrasound criteria for a full stomach. Among patients with obesity, GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with enlargement of the gastric antrum, increased gastric volume, and greater residual gastric contents, leading to an elevated estimated risk of aspiration. This increased risk is primarily determined by gastric ultrasound findings rather than patient characteristics, comorbidities, or duration of treatment. Gastric ultrasound may support individualized perioperative decision-making regarding aspiration precautions.

title: Single or multiple nutritional hormone receptor modulators for chronic kidney disease.
abstract: The global rise in obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) has contributed substantially to the increasing burden of chronic kidney disease (CKD), cardiovascular disease, and heart failure, highlighting the need for therapeutic strategies capable of addressing multiple components of the cardio-renal-metabolic axis. Incretin-based therapies have undergone an evolution from glucose-lowering agents to treatments with broad metabolic, cardiovascular, and renal effects. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have demonstrated clinically meaningful reductions in cardiovascular events and have emerged as important therapies for kidney protection. Evidence from cardiovascular and kidney outcome trials, culminating in the FLOW study, has established semaglutide as a clinically relevant strategy for reducing kidney and cardiovascular risk in patients with T2DM and CKD. Beyond single-receptor agonism, the development of dual and triple incretin receptor agonists has expanded the therapeutic possibilities. Tirzepatide, a dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist, has demonstrated favourable kidney outcomes compared with dulaglutide, while early studies of the dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist cotadutide suggest additional benefits on albuminuria and cardiorenal risk markers. Retatrutide, a triple GLP-1/GIP/glucagon receptor agonist, has shown promising effects on kidney-related parameters, although the mechanisms underlying observed increases in estimated glomerular filtration rate remain uncertain. Accumulating evidence suggests that incretin-based therapies may exert renoprotective effects through pathways extending beyond glycaemic control and weight reduction, including improvements in endothelial function, microvascular integrity, inflammation, fibrosis, and renal haemodynamics. Nevertheless, important questions remain regarding the mechanisms of kidney protection, the interpretation of kidney function changes in the setting of substantial weight loss, and the long-term renal benefits of multi-receptor modulators. Ongoing mechanistic studies and dedicated outcome trials will further define the role of incretin biology in the prevention and treatment of CKD.

title: Reproductive and Gynecologic Effects of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Women With Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder characterized by metabolic dysfunction, hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and infertility. Although glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have demonstrated efficacy in promoting weight loss and improving insulin resistance, their effects on reproductive and gynecologic outcomes in women with PCOS have not been comprehensively summarized. This scoping review aimed to evaluate the available evidence regarding the reproductive and gynecologic outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA therapy in women with PCOS. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Nursing & Allied Health Premium. Original studies evaluating GLP-1 RA therapy in women with PCOS and reporting reproductive or gynecologic outcomes were eligible for inclusion. Following duplicate removal, studies underwent title/abstract screening, full-text review, and standardized data extraction. Outcomes of interest included menstrual function, ovulation, fertility and pregnancy outcomes, hyperandrogenism, reproductive hormone profiles, ovarian function, and secondary metabolic outcomes. Twenty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Across the available literature, GLP-1 RA therapy was consistently associated with improvements in biochemical markers of hyperandrogenism, including reductions in total testosterone, free testosterone, free androgen index, and androstenedione, and increases in sex hormone-binding globulin. Improvements in menstrual regularity and reductions in amenorrhea were also frequently reported. Evidence regarding ovulation, fertility, and pregnancy outcomes was more limited but generally suggested improved ovulation rates and increased pregnancy rates in selected populations, particularly when GLP-1 RAs were combined with metformin. Nearly all included studies also demonstrated significant improvements in body weight, body mass index, and insulin resistance. Considerable heterogeneity in study design, interventions, and reported outcomes precluded quantitative synthesis. The overall findings suggest that GLP-1 RAs may provide reproductive and gynecologic benefits in women with PCOS in addition to their established metabolic effects. The most consistent improvements were observed in hyperandrogenism and menstrual function, whereas evidence supporting effects on fertility and pregnancy outcomes remains comparatively limited. Further high-quality prospective studies with standardized reproductive outcome measures are needed to better define the role of GLP-1 RAs in the management of PCOS.

title: Obesity Medications in Older Adults: A Geriatrics 5Ms Framework for Safe and Patient-Centered Prescribing.
abstract: Obesity medications that act through gut-derived hormonal pathways include glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1), dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1/GIP), and emerging triple glucagon-like peptide-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon receptor agonists. These therapies are increasingly prescribed for weight management and glycemic control, as well as for their cardiometabolic and renal benefits. While these medications offer substantial benefits to patients across multiple health conditions, their use in older adults warrants heightened scrutiny. Older adults face increased risks of sarcopenia and frailty, and evidence from major clinical trials suggests that a substantial proportion of medication-associated weight loss agents may result in loss of lean mass, potentially posing risks for this population. Other adverse effects that may be more consequential in older adults include dehydration, malnutrition, perioperative aspiration, and fat-predominant weight regain after discontinuation. This paper provides a clinically oriented framework to guide prescribing decisions for older adults. Drawing on patient scenarios from common geriatric contexts, including frailty, cognitive impairment, glucocorticoid use, and surgical planning, we propose prescribing approaches that optimize therapeutic benefits while mitigating potential harms. We integrate these recommendations within the Geriatrics 5Ms Framework (Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most) to contextualize treatment within geriatrics practice. Lifestyle co-interventions, particularly resistance training, adequate protein intake, and ongoing functional monitoring, emerge as essential components for older adults receiving these therapies. We also discuss identifying priority areas for future research, including age-stratified clinical trials and the routine inclusion of body composition and physical function outcomes.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and the Diabetic Foot: Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence, and Practical Considerations.
abstract: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a major complication of diabetes and are associated with impaired healing, lower-extremity amputation, and substantial morbidity and mortality. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are increasingly used in the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity, with emerging evidence suggesting potential effects on diabetic foot health beyond glycemic control. This review examines the mechanistic and clinical evidence linking GLP-1RA therapy to DFU development, healing, and lower-extremity outcomes. Experimental studies demonstrate anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, improved endothelial function and angiogenesis, enhanced cellular repair, and potential neuroprotective effects. Clinical studies further suggest favorable associations with incident DFU, lower-extremity amputation, wound-related complications, and mortality, although findings are not uniform and most evidence is observational. Emerging data also suggest potentially favorable postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing diabetic foot and lower-extremity procedures. Comparative studies across glucose-lowering therapies demonstrate heterogeneous findings and do not establish a consistent advantage of one drug class across diabetic foot outcomes. Substantial GLP-1RA-associated weight loss may be accompanied by reductions in lean mass and nutritional intake and may raise additional concerns regarding peripheral neuropathy, wound healing, and foot biomechanics. However, direct evidence linking GLP-1RAs to plantar fat-pad loss, altered plantar pressure, or impaired DFU healing is lacking. Overall, GLP-1RAs may offer benefits relevant to diabetic foot health, but prospective studies using validated wound-healing endpoints are needed to determine whether these therapies directly improve DFU healing and to clarify their role in diabetic foot management.

title: Starvation-associated high-anion gap metabolic acidosis following short-term oral semaglutide use: A case report.
abstract: Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, is increasingly used for weight reduction beyond its approved indications. We report a case of starvation-associated euglycemic ketoacidosis in a previously healthy, nondiabetic young woman following short-term oral semaglutide use. A young adult woman presented with persistent nausea, vomiting, and markedly reduced oral intake after 5 days of oral semaglutide prescribed for weight reduction despite having a normal body mass index. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated a high-anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketonemia and ketonuria. Serum glucose and lactate levels were within normal limits. Urine studies showed high sodium excretion and evidence of phosphate and magnesium wasting. Semaglutide was discontinued, and the patient was treated with intravenous fluids, dextrose supplementation, and electrolyte replacement. The acid-base status normalized within 3 days, although electrolyte abnormalities required continued monitoring. This case suggests a possible association between semaglutide use and starvation-associated euglycemic ketoacidosis in nondiabetic individuals, likely mediated by reduced caloric intake and gastrointestinal intolerance of food. Increased clinical awareness is warranted, particularly in patients using glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists for off-label indications such as weight loss.

title: The Impact of Incretin-Based Therapies on Anthropometric and Metabolic Parameters in Women with Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), recently renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), affects 170 million women globally and is often accompanied by obesity and various levels of insulin resistance. Incretin-based therapies, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists liraglutide and semaglutide, and the dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) agonist tirzepatide, offer a biologically plausible mechanism for targeting metabolic dysfunction in PMOS. This review examines clinical trial evidence on the anthropometric and metabolic effects of incretin-based therapies in this population, including a focus on women of reproductive age, who face distinct challenges related to preconception planning, treatment duration, and post-discontinuation metabolic and weight management. Available literature shows that liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide produce clinically meaningful reductions in body weight, body mass index (BMI), and waist circumference, with some studies also confirming preferential effects on visceral and ectopic fat compartments. Glycaemic and insulin resistance outcomes vary across studies, while lipid and blood pressure effects remain incompletely characterized. Although emerging data suggest that higher-potency agents may yield more consistent weight-loss benefits, available PMOS-specific evidence does not establish comparative metabolic superiority among agents. Interpretation of the available evidence is limited by the predominance of short-term trials at sub-obesity doses, frequent co-administration with metformin, and the absence of phenotype-stratified data, leaving the full metabolic potential of these agents in PMOS incompletely defined. Larger, longer, and higher-dose trials are needed to fully characterize the anthropometric and metabolic potential of these agents in PMOS.

title: From pathophysiology to therapy: dual and triple agonists as a new frontier in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has emerged as the most prevalent chronic liver condition worldwide, reflecting the growing global burden of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D). The complex pathophysiology of MASLD, characterized by insulin resistance (IR), lipotoxicity, and chronic low-grade inflammation, necessitates therapeutic strategies that address systemic metabolic dysfunction rather than isolated hepatic markers. Current evidence highlights the synergistic potential of targeting multiple incretin and metabolic pathways. Dual agonists, most notably Tirzepatide (a GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist), have demonstrated profound efficacy in clinical trials (SURPASS and SURMOUNT programs), achieving significant reductions in hemoglobin A1c, body weight, and liver fat content. Furthermore, dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonists like Survodutide and Cotadutide offer complementary benefits by enhancing energy expenditure and modulating hepatic lipid metabolism. The development of triple agonists, such as Retatrutide (targeting GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors), represents a further escalation in potency, showing unprecedented results in liver fat reduction and weight loss. The integration of these multi-target agents, together with emerging pathways involving amylin analogues and pan-PPAR agonists like Chiglitazar, marks a paradigm shift toward holistic cardiometabolic management. These therapies not only target the resolution of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and fibrosis but also address the interconnected risks of cardiovascular and renal complications. This review aims to explore the evolving landscape of pharmacological interventions, focusing on the emergence of dual and triple receptor agonists as a transformative frontier in metabolic dysfunction and MASLD therapy.

title: Semaglutide and Panic Attacks: Active-Comparator Disproportionality Analysis, Temporal Assessment of Notoriety Bias and Evidence Triangulation in Post-Marketing Pharmacovigilance.
abstract: To evaluate how confounding by indication and notoriety bias shape the apparent semaglutide-panic attack signal in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and to interpret this signal using an evidence-triangulation framework integrating randomized and observational studies. We conducted an active-comparator restricted disproportionality analysis of FAERS (2018Q1-2024Q4), including individual case safety reports in which semaglutide, dulaglutide or empagliflozin was the primary suspect drug. Panic attack was identified using the MedDRA preferred term. Crude and adjusted reporting odds ratios (RORs, aRORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using logistic regression, adjusting for age, sex and indication (Type 2 diabetes, obesity/weight management). Notoriety bias was assessed using prespecified temporal analyses (analyses restricted to reports received before July 1, 2023 and a drug-by-period comparison of 2018-2022 with 2023-2024) and reporting proportions per 10 000 reports. A sensitivity analysis used all other primary-suspect drugs in FAERS as the reference set. In parallel, we conducted a systematic review (MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL to November 24, 2025) of randomized trials, cohort and cross-sectional studies, pharmacovigilance analyses and case reports reporting panic attacks or acute anxiety outcomes with semaglutide. Among 33 267 semaglutide, 54 282 dulaglutide and 25 380 empagliflozin reports, panic attacks were recorded in 87 (0.26%), 28 (0.05%) and 13 (0.05%) cases, respectively. Crude RORs were 5.08 (95% CI 3.32-7.78) versus dulaglutide and 5.12 (95% CI 2.86-9.17) versus empagliflozin, attenuating after adjustment to 2.82 (95% CI 1.74-4.56) and 2.75 (95% CI 1.41-5.36). In the pre-warning period crude RORs were 2.24 (95% CI 1.23-4.07) and 2.15 (95% CI 1.00-4.58), attenuating to 1.38 (95% CI 0.69-2.75) and 1.14 (95% CI 0.48-2.68) after adjustment. Panic-attack reports per 10 000 semaglutide reports rose from 6.7 in 2018-2022 to 42.0 in 2023-2024 (drug-by-period interaction p = 0.007). Against all other primary-suspect drugs, the aROR was 1.48 (95% CI 1.18-1.87) overall and 0.76 (95% CI 0.48-1.18) before July 1, 2023. Across 12 studies, randomized trials and active-comparator observational cohorts did not show a consistent increase in panic attacks or anxiety-related outcomes. Crude FAERS analyses suggested a semaglutide-panic attack signal that attenuated after adjustment was no longer significant before the July 2023 regulatory communication and rose sharply thereafter in a pattern consistent with notoriety bias. Triangulation with randomized trials and active-comparator observational studies does not support a consistent pharmacological association. Disproportionality analyses are hypothesis-generating and cannot estimate incidence or establish causality. This case study illustrates how active-comparator design, temporal assessment of notoriety bias and evidence triangulation can improve the interpretation of post-marketing safety signals.

title: Beyond Weight Loss and Glycemic Control: Molecular Mechanisms and Hypothesis-Generating Therapeutic Potential of Incretin-Based Therapies Against Peritoneal Fibrosis in Peritoneal Dialysis.
abstract: Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is an established kidney replacement therapy, but long-term exposure to bioincompatible dialysate, uremic toxins, recurrent peritonitis, glucose degradation products, oxidative stress, and sterile inflammation progressively remodels the peritoneal membrane and contributes to peritoneal fibrosis (PF). This review summarizes the molecular basis of PF in PD and evaluates the therapeutic rationale for incretin-based interventions beyond weight loss and glycemic control. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, translational, and clinically relevant literature on PD-associated PF, with emphasis on DPP-4 biology, GLP-1 receptor agonism, inflammatory and oxidative signaling, angiogenesis, mesothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, glycemic management in PD, and selected author-conducted translational studies interpreted alongside independent evidence. Available evidence supports a model in which DPP-4 activation, altered GLP-1/GLP-1R signaling, TGF-β/Smad3-driven mesothelial transition, NF-κB/MyD88 inflammation, ROS-mediated oxidative stress, angiogenesis, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal remodeling converge to impair peritoneal membrane integrity. DPP-4 inhibition, exendin-4, and dulaglutide attenuated these pathways in experimental models, while GLP-1 receptor agonists have established metabolic benefits in appropriate diabetic and obese populations. Direct clinical evidence that incretin-based therapies prevent or treat peritoneal fibrosis in humans undergoing PD is currently lacking. Therefore, peritoneal membrane protection, reduced ultrafiltration failure, and improved technique survival should be regarded as investigational, hypothesis-generating possibilities that require prospective clinical validation.

title: Mendelian Randomization-Based Analysis of Causal Effects Between Statins and Common Upper Gastrointestinal Diseases.
abstract: Statins are widely used for cardiovascular disease prevention and exhibit multiple pleiotropic effects, including anti-inflammatory properties. However, conclusions from observational studies regarding the causal relationship between statin use and upper gastrointestinal diseases (such as gastric cancer, gastric ulcer, and functional dyspepsia) remain controversial. This study is aimed at systematically evaluating the causal association between statin-targeted gene (HMGCR)-mediated reductions in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels and common upper gastrointestinal diseases using drug-targeted Mendelian randomization (MR). This approach seeks to uncover potential unintended effects. We extracted genetic variants associated with the HMGCR gene region from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) as instrumental variables to simulate the lipid-lowering effects of statins. Outcome data were derived from large-scale GWAS meta-analyses covering gastric cancer (n = 202,308), gastroenteritis (n = 7651), gastric ulcer (n = 361,194), gastroesophageal reflux disease (n = 462,933), and functional dyspepsia (n = 84,572). The primary analysis employed inverse variance weighting (IVW), with sensitivity assessments for heterogeneity and pleiotropy conducted via MR-Egger, weighted median, and MR-PRESSO methods. Genetically predicted HMGCR-mediated LDL-C reduction was associated with reduced risk of gastric cancer (OR = 0.588, 95% CI: 0.423-0.816, p = 0.002), gastroenteritis (OR = 0.257, 95% CI: 0.086-0.766, p = 0.015), and gastric ulcer (OR = 0.996, 95% CI: 0.993-0.998, p = 0.003). However, analysis indicated a potential increased risk of functional dyspepsia (OR = 1.437, 95% CI: 1.014-2.036, p = 0.042). No significant causal association was found between statin use and gastroesophageal reflux disease (OR = 0.999, 95% CI: 0.992-1.006, p = 0.773). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the results, with no evidence of significant level-specific multiplicity. This study provides genetic evidence supporting the potential protective effects of statins against gastric cancer, gastritis, and gastric ulcers, which may be associated with their anti-inflammatory properties. However, the potential increased risk of functional dyspepsia suggests the complexity of the drug's effects. These findings provide scientific basis for the repositioning of statins in gastrointestinal diseases and their safety assessment.

title: [From guidelines: cardiovascular risk stratification and therapeutic targets].
abstract: The linear relationship between LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) concentrations and cardiovascular risk, together with evidence of clinical benefit associated with intensive and sustained LDL-C reduction, underlies the "the lower, the better" paradigm. Cardiovascular risk stratification is the prerequisite for defining treatment intensity. In the context of primary prevention, international guidelines recommend the use of validated scores for an objective definition of individual risk. This evaluation must be integrated by considering risk-amplifying factors not included in the algorithms, such as a family history of premature events, elevated lipoprotein(a) and triglyceride levels, and the presence of coronary artery calcium. Statin/ezetimibe combination therapy acts through complementary mechanisms, reducing hepatic synthesis and intestinal absorption of cholesterol, respectively. Evidence indicates greater efficacy in achieving LDL-C targets compared with statin intensification alone, along with favorable treatment adherence. Despite clear recommendations regarding target LDL-C levels, real-world data highlight persistent undertreatment and a low percentage of patients with LDL-C levels consistent with guideline recommendations. In both primary and secondary prevention, the statin/ezetimibe combination represents an effective and safe strategy to achieve recommended therapeutic goals and its early implementation contributes to reducing therapeutic inertia.

title: [Role of statin/ezetimibe fixed-dose combination in lipid risk management in the cardiovascular disease continuum].
abstract: Prolonged exposure to high LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) levels represents a time-dependent driver of atherosclerotic risk. Available evidence shows that maintaining low LDL-C levels over time is associated with a reduction in cardiovascular events both in primary and secondary prevention. In this setting, combination therapy with statin and ezetimibe allows for a more effective LDL-C reduction compared with the statin titration alone, thanks to the complementary mechanism of action of the two drugs and improved treatment adherence. Clinical studies have demonstrated that early initiation of combination therapy increases the likelihood of achieving LDL-C goals and of reducing cardiovascular events. In parallel, recent real-world evidence downplays the incidence of complete statin intolerance, suggesting that a significant proportion of reported symptoms is attributable to nocebo effects. Therefore, the fixed-dose statin/ezetimibe combination represents an effective, simple, and generally well-tolerated therapeutic strategy to optimize lipid control. In patients requiring pronounced LDL-C reductions, combination with high-intensity statins contributes to achieving therapeutic goals while limiting the use of more complex and expensive injectable therapies.

title: Age, Gender, and Adherence in Low-density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Reduction with Statin Therapy: A Real-world Cohort Study.
abstract: Current guidelines recommend achieving ≥50% reduction in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) in high-risk patients. Real-world data on response patterns, age and gender differences, and determinants of nonresponse remain limited. The aim of the study is to evaluate LDL-C reduction following statin therapy in routine clinical practice and to examine the influence of age, gender, and medication adherence on treatment response and cardiovascular outcomes. In this observational cohort study, adults initiated on statin therapy with documented baseline and follow-up lipid measurements were included. LDL-C levels were recorded at baseline and follow-up. The primary outcome was achievement of ≥50% LDL-C reduction. In a total study population of 652 patients, statin therapy was associated with substantial early reductions in LDL-C that were largely maintained at 1 year. More than half of the patients achieved a ≥50% reduction, and nearly one-third achieved LDL-C levels 45 years demonstrated greater sustained LDL-C reduction compared with younger individuals. Numerical differences in LDL-C response were observed between men and women, although these were not statistically significant. Failure to achieve ≥50% LDL-C reduction appeared to be more closely associated with lower medication adherence rather than treatment intensity within this uniformly treated cohort. Greater proportional LDL-C reduction was associated with lower cardiovascular event rates during follow-up. In routine practice, approximately half of patients achieved ≥50% LDL-C reduction with high-intensity statin therapy. Adherence emerges as an important determinant of response. Age was associated with sustained response, whereas gender differences were not statistically significant. Nonresponse is primarily associated with modifiable treatment-related factors.

title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Whether a retinal artificial intelligence (AI) risk score reclassifies SCORE2 cardiovascular risk stratification in statin-naive adults across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary is uncertain. We evaluated the retinal AI risk score for 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prediction. In 40,672 statin-naive UK Biobank participants (aged 40-69, without diabetes), cardiovascular risk categories and treatment recommendation status (Class I or IIa vs neither) were defined using the 2025 ESC/EAS focused-update framework. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) adjusted for SCORE2 or for established risk factors. The incremental predictive value of adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. Over a 10.0-year median follow-up (914 ASCVD events), the very high retinal AI risk group independently predicted ASCVD (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.32 vs low risk; p<0.001). Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 reclassified risk across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary (statin-eligibility NRI [net reclassification improvement] 0.012, p<0.001); reclassification was statistically significant but modest (continuous NRI 0.445, p<0.001), without C-index or net-benefit gain. In the statin-indicated subgroup, retinal AI risk groups further stratified risk (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.16; p<0.001). Statin-not-indicated participants in the high or very high retinal AI risk groups had numerically similar observed 10-year risk to all statin-indicated, untreated participants (p=0.758). There was no evidence of effect modification by clinically detectable retinal disorder (interaction p=0.93). Incremental value was greater in women than men (sex interaction p<0.001). Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 produced modest bidirectional risk reclassification across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary; these findings warrant prospective validation.Abstract word count: 250 words.

title: A study using the REIN registry suggests a statin therapy benefits for secondary prevention in patients receiving dialysis.
abstract: While statins are effective for cardiovascular prevention in the general population, their benefit in patients with CKD G5D (kidney failure treated by dialysis) remains uncertain. Previous randomized controlled trials included mixed populations for primary and secondary prevention while excluding patients with recent cardiovascular events, leaving a knowledge gap regarding statin effectiveness for secondary prevention immediately following an atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event. Here, we address this gap by providing real-world evidence. We conducted a landmark-based observational study, informed by the target trial framework using the French Renal Epidemiology and Information Network (REIN) registry and merged with data from the French national healthcare system database from 2010 to 2023. We included adults with CKD G5D who experienced an ASCVD event. Results focus on the relative and absolute risk difference and the life expectancy gain using delta restricted mean survival time (dRMST). title: Disproportionality analysis of adverse event reporting with aspirin, statins, and their co-exposure in FAERS, 2004-2025.
abstract: To characterize and compare adverse-event reporting patterns for aspirin without statins, statins without aspirin, and aspirin-statin co-exposure in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), and to explore statistical reporting-interaction signals. We analyzed FAERS reports from 2004 Q1 through 2025 Q1. Active-comparator disproportionality analyses compared aspirin-statin co-exposure with aspirin-without-statin and statin-without-aspirin reports using the reporting odds ratio (ROR), proportional reporting ratio (PRR), Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN), and empirical Bayesian geometric mean (EBGM), followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) correction. Candidate preferred terms (PTs) common to both active-comparator analyses underwent adjusted statistical interaction analyses using four exposure groups, including a neither-drug reference. Primary models retained missing age, sex, and reporter type as explicit Unknown categories, and a complete-case sensitivity analysis excluded reports with missing adjustment covariates. After deduplication, 18,932,599 unique FAERS reports were retained. The active-comparator analysis included 134,479 aspirin-without-statin reports, 202,565 statin-without-aspirin reports, and 70,806 aspirin-statin co-exposure reports. Among 9,332 and 9,736 PTs tested in the two active-comparator analyses, 119 and 254 PTs remained after prespecified signal-detection criteria and BH-FDR correction, respectively; 42 PTs were common to both comparisons. Adjusted interaction models were reliably estimable for 40 candidates, and 31 PTs met both additive and multiplicative reporting-interaction criteria. Missingness was substantial for age (42.33%), sex (12.12%), and reporter type (4.35%). The complete-case dataset retained 53.83% of reports, and 21 of the 31 primary both-scale-positive PTs remained jointly positive. Aspirin-statin co-exposure showed distinct adverse-event reporting patterns in FAERS. The identified signals are exploratory statistical reporting interactions and do not establish increased incidence, clinical risk, causality, or pharmacological drug-drug interactions. Only 21 of the 31 primary both-scale-positive PTs remained jointly positive in the complete-case sensitivity analysis, reinforcing the need for cautious interpretation and validation in denominator-based pharmacoepidemiologic datasets.

title: Calcium Density as a Marker of Coronary Plaque Stabilization in Primary Prevention: The CAUGHT-CAD Trial.
abstract: Despite primary prevention statin treatment, a substantial proportion of individuals remain at residual risk for cardiovascular events. Coronary computed tomographic angiography (CTA) enables the quantification of compositional changes in calcified plaque. The aim of this study was to examine whether increases in coronary calcified plaque volume and density associated with statin therapy could be used as a marker of plaque stabilization in asymptomatic individuals undergoing serial coronary CTA. In the CAUGHT-CAD trial, asymptomatic, statin-naive, intermediate-risk individuals were randomized to a primary prevention strategy (including statin treatment) vs usual care. Participants underwent coronary CTA at baseline and 3 years. In this post hoc analysis, volumes of 5 plaque subtypes were quantified: noncalcified (≤350 HU), low-density calcium (351-500 HU), intermediate-density calcium (501-700 HU), high-density calcium (701-1000 HU), and very high density calcium (>1,000 HU). The primary outcome was the per-lesion level change in volumes of calcified plaque subtypes. Eight hundred forty lesions were included from 338 participants (mean age: 58.3 ± 6.9 years, 57.1% men, 161 [47.6%] statin treated). Statin treatment was associated with greater progression in intermediate-density (β = 0.89, SE = 0.39; P = 0.02) and high-density (β = 0.79, SE = 0.24; P = 0.001) calcium, alongside regression of noncalcified plaque (β = -9.83, SE = 1.64; P < 0.001), following adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) level, and baseline plaque volume. Among statin-treated participants, LDL-C reduction ≥30% was associated with greater progression of high-density (β = 1.11, SE = 0.49; P = 0.03) and very high density (β = 1.68, SE = 0.85; P = 0.04) calcium. In asymptomatic, intermediate-risk individuals, statin treatment was associated with a shift toward higher density calcium within coronary plaques, most marked with effective lowering of LDL-C. (Coronary Artery Calcium Score: Use to Guide Management of Hereditary Coronary Artery Disease [CAUGHT-CAD]; ACTRN12614001294640).

title: Association of Non-Cytochrome P450 3A4-Metabolized Statins Versus Atorvastatin With Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Patients With Cancer Receiving Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors: A Propensity Score-Matched Target Trial Emulation.
abstract: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) often undergo CYP3A4 (cytochrome P450 3A4) metabolism. Atorvastatin is a CYP3A4 substrate, whereas rosuvastatin and pitavastatin largely bypass this pathway. We evaluated whether statin choice was associated with major adverse cardiovascular events in TKI-treated patients with cancer. Using TriNetX, we conducted an active-comparator, new-user target trial emulation among adults with cancer receiving their first TKI. The index date was the first statin dispensation; outcome ascertainment began on Day 30 and continued up to 3 years. Separate 1:1 propensity score-matched comparisons included rosuvastatin versus atorvastatin (primary; 2215 per group), pitavastatin comparisons, and a pooled non-CYP3A4 statin comparison. Among 10 843 eligible patients (mean age, 66.7 years; 60.7% male), rosuvastatin was associated with a lower major adverse cardiovascular events rate than atorvastatin (624 versus 769 events; hazard ratio [HR], 0.84 [95% CI, 0.76-0.93]). The proportional-hazards assumption was violated (P=0.042), so the HR was interpreted as a time-averaged association. The pooled comparison was concordant (HR, 0.87 [95% CI, 0.78-0.96]). The early-persistence Day-180 estimate was imprecise (HR, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.73-1.09]). Rosuvastatin use was associated with lower major adverse cardiovascular events than atorvastatin in TKI-treated patients with cancer. This observational finding is compatible with, but does not establish, a CYP3A4-mediated interaction. Residual confounding, nonaligned TKI and statin timing in part of the primary cohort, and lack of individual-level event-time data require prospective confirmation.

title: Statin Prescribing and Guideline Concordance Among Adults With HIV Aged 40-75 Years in a Single Urban Outpatient HIV Clinic, 2024.
abstract: People with HIV (PWH) have elevated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk. Following the REPRIEVE trial, 2024 HHS Adult and Adolescent Antiretroviral Guidelines recommend at least moderate-intensity statins for adults with HIV aged 40-75 years with 10-year ASCVD risk 5% to <20%. The 2026 ACC/AHA Dyslipidemia Guideline expands eligibility, supporting statins for all adults aged 40-75 years with HIV for primary prevention, regardless of LDL-C. We evaluated statin prescribing and HHS guideline concordance for primary prevention in this population. Single urban outpatient HIV clinic in the United States. Retrospective electronic health record review of adults with HIV aged 40-75 years with an outpatient HIV visit on or after February 27, 2024. Statin prescribing was an active prescription at the index visit. ASCVD risk was abstracted from clinical documentation; virologic suppression was HIV RNA <50 copies/mL. Primary-prevention eligibility followed the February 27, 2024 HHS framework: LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL plus ASCVD risk ≥5% or diabetes mellitus. Of 753 patients reviewed, 414 met inclusion criteria. Statins were prescribed for 212 (51.2%). Statin-prescribed patients were older (median 62 vs. 54 years) with higher median ASCVD risk (13% vs. 7%). ASCVD risk was unavailable for 100 (24.2%). Among 242 patients eligible for primary-prevention statin therapy, 128 (52.9%) had an active statin prescription at the index visit. In multivariable modeling (n=314), higher ASCVD risk, higher CD4 count, and virologic suppression were independently associated with prescribing. Only half of statin-eligible adults with HIV were prescribed statins, with the largest gap among those eligible by ASCVD risk 5% to <20% without diabetes. The 2026 ACC/AHA guideline expands eligibility to all adults aged 40-75 years with HIV. These findings highlight opportunities to improve implementation of guideline-directed cardiovascular prevention through improved cardiovascular risk assessment, clinician education, and electronic clinical decision support.

title: Development and Validation of a Coronary Artery Calcium Volume and Density Score.
abstract: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring is a useful tool for coronary heart disease (CHD) risk prediction. The current standard method, the Agatston score, weights plaque area upward by density. However, higher density is inversely associated with CHD. We aimed to develop and validate a CAC score accounting for the inverse association of density with CHD, and the nonlinear association between CAC volume and density in a prospective cohort study. A CAC volume and density score was developed, which adjusts CAC volume for density based on whether the volume level was 3. We used data from the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) to develop and assess the score, including all participants with CAC>0 and follow-up for CHD events. Score performance for CHD risk prediction was compared with the pooled cohort equations and the Agatston score using Cox proportional hazards models and Harrell C-index and continuous and categorical net reclassification improvement. Analyses were also stratified by Agatston score, age, sex, race/ethnicity, and statin use. Finally, performance was evaluated in 4 longitudinal cohorts for external validation. The MESA cohort included 3360 individuals. CAC volume and density score improved the C-index for CHD to a greater degree over the pooled cohort equation (0.699 [95% CI, 0.675-0.723]) compared with the Agatston score (0.687 [95% CI, 0.663-0.711]) and resulted in greater continuous net reclassification improvement (0.54 [95% CI, 0.43-0.64]) compared with the Agatston score (0.45 [95% CI, 0.34-0.56]) when added to the pooled cohort equation. The greatest improvement in risk prediction was in those with lower burden of CAC (Agatston <300). Consistent results were seen in stratified analyses and external validation cohorts. The CAC volume and density score, which adjusts CAC volume downward for higher density, and can be calculated from existing CAC reports, significantly improves risk discrimination and reclassification compared with the Agatston score.

title: Risk-Guided Statin Initiation in People Living with HIV: Clinical Utility of a Cardiovascular Risk Prediction Model in a Malaysian Cohort.
abstract: BackgroundOptimal statin initiation strategies for people living with HIV (PLHIV) remain uncertain. We evaluated whether the D:A:D reduced (D:A:Dr) model improves primary prevention statin initiation decisions among Malaysian PLHIV compared with non-risk-based strategies.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study followed statin-naïve PLHIV adults from an infectious diseases centre over five years for incident cardiovascular events. Decision curve analysis compared the net benefit of a D:A:Dr-guided strategy against four alternatives: LDL-cholesterol ≥3.0 mmol/L, age ≥40 years, treat-all, and treat-none.ResultsAmong 5,741 PLHIV, 48.9% were moderate-to high-risk. The 5-year event rate was 2.0%, ranging from 0.5% (low-risk) to 8-9% (high-risk). D:A:Dr-guided strategy yielded superior net benefit at >2% - 10% threshold probabilities. Age ≥40 years lost benefits as thresholds increased whereas LDL-cholesterol-based strategy offered minimal utility.ConclusionD:A:Dr risk-based statin initiation offers superior clinical utility at >2% to 10% threshold probabilities, enabling targeted, resource-efficient prescribing in resource-constrained settings.

title: A Review of the Vascular Pathophysiology of Migraine: Should We Consider Statins as a Treatment Option?
abstract: Migraine is a primary headache disorder that affects more than a billion people worldwide and can severely impact quality of life. Inflammation and endothelial dysfunction in the trigeminovascular system are the suggested underlying mechanisms. Statins, beyond their lipid-lowering effects, exhibit pleiotropic properties including anti-inflammatory, antioxidative, and endothelial-modulating effects, which may be relevant to migraine pathophysiology. This narrative review evaluates current evidence on the efficacy of statins in migraine prophylaxis, treatment, and prevention of associated vascular events. A literature search was conducted using MEDLINE (via PubMed) for English-language articles published between 1997 and June 2026 using the terms "migraine," "statins," "pathophysiology of migraine," "neuroinflammation," and "migraine treatment". The majority of studies endorse the use of statins in individuals with migraines, noting that their positive impact on migraines and cardiovascular risk outweighs any adverse effects. Considering the increased cardiovascular risk in migraine sufferers compared with those without migraine, statins may play a beneficial role in both migraine management and cardiovascular risk reduction. It is surprising that the role of statins in a common disease like migraine, which is also associated with an increased risk of vascular events, does not include definitive evidence. Statins might be considered for migraine treatment and prevention in individuals with chronic migraine, aura, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, a family history of cardiovascular disease, or other cardiovascular risk factors. We hope that the present article will encourage further research to establish if statins have a definite role in the treatment of migraine.

title: Sex-Based Disparities in Statin Use and Intensity among Women with Peripheral Artery Disease: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a manifestation of systemic atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and is associated with substantial cardiovascular and limb-related morbidity. High-intensity statin therapy is recommended for patients with PAD, yet statin treatment remains underused, and sex-based differences in lipid-lowering therapy may further contribute to inequities in secondary prevention. This systematic review evaluated sex-based disparities in statxin use and statin intensity among adults with PAD. A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL was performed from database inception through June 6, 2026. Eligible studies included adults with PAD, reported PAD-specific statin or lipid-lowering outcomes, and compared outcomes by sex. The primary outcome was high-intensity statin use among women versus men with PAD. Secondary outcomes included any statin use, no statin therapy, guideline-concordant lipid-lowering or vascular-protective therapy, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) goal achievement. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity in study design, PAD definition, clinical setting, and outcome reporting. Eleven observational studies met inclusion criteria. Only two studies reported high-intensity statin use by sex, and both found lower use among women than men. In the Medicare cohort of patients with critical limb ischemia, high-intensity statin use was lower among women than men. Similarly, in the Veterans Affairs cohort, women with PAD had lower rates of high-intensity statin use, any statin use, and statin adherence. Across studies reporting secondary lipid-lowering outcomes, women were generally less likely than men to receive statins or guideline-concordant vascular-protective therapy, including in primary care, hospital discharge, revascularization, administrative claims, and vascular registry settings. LDL-C goal achievement was not reported in the included studies. Women with PAD are less likely than men to receive statin therapy and guideline-concordant vascular-protective treatment, and the limited available evidence suggests lower use of high-intensity statins among women when statin intensity is reported. These findings highlight a persistent sex-based gap in secondary prevention for PAD. Future studies should report statin intensity, adherence, LDL-C goal achievement, treatment escalation, and standardized measures of statin tolerance or intolerance separately by sex. Quality-improvement efforts should also focus on improving statin prescribing for women with PAD.

abstract_sections.label: Background
abstract_sections.text: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a manifestation of systemic atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and is associated with substantial cardiovascular and limb-related morbidity. High-intensity statin therapy is recommended for patients with PAD, yet statin treatment remains underused, and sex-based differences in lipid-lowering therapy may further contribute to inequities in secondary prevention. This systematic review evaluated sex-based disparities in statxin use and statin intensity among adults with PAD.

abstract_sections.label: Methods
abstract_sections.text: A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL was performed from database inception through June 6, 2026. Eligible studies included adults with PAD, reported PAD-specific statin or lipid-lowering outcomes, and compared outcomes by sex. The primary outcome was high-intensity statin use among women versus men with PAD. Secondary outcomes included any statin use, no statin therapy, guideline-concordant lipid-lowering or vascular-protective therapy, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) goal achievement. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity in study design, PAD definition, clinical setting, and outcome reporting.

abstract_sections.label: Results
abstract_sections.text: Eleven observational studies met inclusion criteria. Only two studies reported high-intensity statin use by sex, and both found lower use among women than men. In the Medicare cohort of patients with critical limb ischemia, high-intensity statin use was lower among women than men. Similarly, in the Veterans Affairs cohort, women with PAD had lower rates of high-intensity statin use, any statin use, and statin adherence. Across studies reporting secondary lipid-lowering outcomes, women were generally less likely than men to receive statins or guideline-concordant vascular-protective therapy, including in primary care, hospital discharge, revascularization, administrative claims, and vascular registry settings. LDL-C goal achievement was not reported in the included studies.

abstract_sections.label: Conclusion
abstract_sections.text: Women with PAD are less likely than men to receive statin therapy and guideline-concordant vascular-protective treatment, and the limited available evidence suggests lower use of high-intensity statins among women when statin intensity is reported. These findings highlight a persistent sex-based gap in secondary prevention for PAD. Future studies should report statin intensity, adherence, LDL-C goal achievement, treatment escalation, and standardized measures of statin tolerance or intolerance separately by sex. Quality-improvement efforts should also focus on improving statin prescribing for women with PAD.

title: Known Unknowns: Unpacking Controversies and Uncertainties in the 2025 Guidelines for Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes.
abstract: The 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for managing patients with acute coronary syndromes (ACS) is the first major update since the 2013-2015 ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and non-ST elevated myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) guidelines. It brings both conditions together into a single framework. This review covers the most important new and revised recommendations and points out where evidence is still lacking. New findings show that several significant updates are based on recent large-scale trials. The use of bivalirudin with high-dose infusion after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is now given a Class I recommendation for primary PCI in the case of STEMI, as a result of the BRIGHT-4 trial. Complete revascularization is also now recommended as Class I for stable STEMI patients who have multivessel disease, according to the COMPLETE trial. For a selected group of patients with refractory cardiogenic shock resulting from a myocardial infarction, the percutaneous microaxial flow pump has received a new Class IIa recommendation from the DanGer Shock trial, while the intra-aortic balloon pump and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation are classified as Class III for routine use. Intracoronary imaging (intravascular ultrasound and optical coherence tomography) is now given a Class I recommendation for complex PCI, based on the data of the RENOVATE-COMPLEX-PCI, OCTOBER, and OCTIVUS trials. The guidelines also suggest specific low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) targets, and non-statin drugs should be added if the LDL-C level remains above 70 mg/dL even when maximum statin therapy is used. Regarding antiplatelet therapy, ticagrelor or prasugrel is now preferred to clopidogrel in the case of ACS-PCI, and it is formally recommended to switch to P2Y12 monotherapy at one month in patients at high risk for bleeding as an alternative to standard DAPT. The updates indicate a shift towards more potent antiplatelet therapy at hospital presentation, use of radial access when feasible, more use of imaging-guided PCI, stricter lipid targets, and more refined antiplatelet approaches at the time of discharge. That said, significant gaps in the evidence still exist. It has not yet become clear whether physiology-guided revascularization of non-culprit arteries in patients with STEMI or NSTEMI is better than angiography-guided PCI-a question that is currently being investigated in the randomized COMPLETE-2 trial. The optimal time to provide mechanical circulatory supper in cases of cardiogenic shock remains uncertain. The recent neutral findings from intracoronary imaging studies such as OPTIMAL and IVUS-CHIP might alter the existing Class I recommendation. Lastly, new data from the HOST-EXAM, and SMART CHOICE 3, studies suggest that P2Y12 monotherapy may be better than aspirin for the long-term prevention of major adverse cardiovascular events, and this could influence future guideline recommendations for long term antiplatelet therapies in the chronic phase.

title: Clopidogrel Versus Aspirin Monotherapy According to Atherothrombotic Risk Profile.
abstract: Clopidogrel monotherapy has shown superior efficacy compared with aspirin after completion of dual antiplatelet therapy following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). However, whether treatment effects differ according to overall atherothrombotic risk integrating clinical and angiographic factors remains unclear. This post hoc analysis of the SMART-CHOICE 3 (Smart Angioplasty Research Team: Choice of Optimal Anti-Thrombotic Strategy in Patients Undergoing Implantation of Coronary Drug-Eluting Stents 3) randomized trial included patients who completed guideline-directed dual antiplatelet therapy after PCI. Atherothrombotic risk was defined using the a Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention and complex PCI. Patients with Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention ≥3 or complex PCI were classified as higher risk, and those with a Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention <3 without complex PCI were classified as lower risk. The primary end point was major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (death, myocardial infarction, or stroke). Bleeding was defined as Bleeding Academic Research Consortium type 2, 3, or 5. Among 5506 patients, 4486 (81.5%) were at higher risk and 1020 (18.5%) were at lower risk. Over a median 2.3 years, the incidence of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events was higher in the higher-risk group (6.1% versus 3.1%; hazard ratio, 1.83 [95% CI, 1.17-2.78]; P=0.007). In higher-risk patients, clopidogrel reduced major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events compared with aspirin (4.6% versus 7.4%; hazard ratio, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.50-0.89]; P=0.006), with no difference in lower-risk patients (3.0% versus 3.2%; hazard ratio, 1.03; P=0.945; interaction P=0.242). Bleeding was similar between groups. After completion of dual antiplatelet therapy following PCI, clopidogrel monotherapy was associated with lower ischemic risk than aspirin in patients with higher atherothrombotic risk, without increased bleeding. title: Comparative Safety and Efficacy of Oral Anticoagulants in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation and Prior Ischemic Stroke: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized-Controlled Clinical Trials.
abstract: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and prior ischemic stroke represent a high-risk population facing competing risks of recurrent thromboembolism and hemorrhagic complications. Although direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are recommended over vitamin K antagonists for stroke prevention in AF, no randomized controlled clinical trial has directly compared individual DOACs to each other in this population. We conducted a systematic review and frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis of randomized-controlled clinical trials enrolling patients with AF and prior ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack. MEDLINE, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception until May 2026. The primary outcome was any stroke. Secondary outcomes included ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, major bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality. Treatment effects were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs. The evidence network comprised 6 trials (18 395 patients) in a star-shaped structure. Each DOAC was informed by a single warfarin-controlled trial, and 2 trials used aspirin as the comparator. All between-DOAC comparisons were indirect. In the network meta-analysis, compared with warfarin, apixaban was the only agent to significantly reduce both any stroke (RR, 0.72 [95% CI, 0.53-0.97]) and major bleeding (RR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.54-0.99]). Dabigatran, apixaban, and edoxaban each significantly reduced hemorrhagic stroke and ICH versus warfarin, whereas rivaroxaban did not reach significance for any bleeding outcome. Edoxaban was the only agent associated with significantly lower cardiovascular (RR, 0.79 [95% CI, 0.65-0.97]) and all-cause mortality (RR, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.72-0.99]). Based on indirect comparisons only, no differences between individual DOACs were observed. In patients with AF and prior ischemic stroke, individual DOACs reduced intracranial and systemic bleeding relative to warfarin, although not uniformly across agents. Apixaban alone significantly reduced both any stroke and major bleeding versus warfarin, but differences between individual DOACs could not be established given the small number of trials. URL: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/; Unique identifier: CRD420261404062.

title: Rationale for Early Discontinuation of Aspirin After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation: Design of the SOLOTAVI Randomized Trial.
abstract: Trans-aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become the first line treatment of aortic stenosis, a condition predominantly affecting elderly patients. In absence of a specific indication for antithrombotic therapy, lifetime aspirin is recommended after TAVI while it may be discontinued 3 months after bioprosthetic surgical valve replacement. Primary prevention, using aspirin compared to placebo among elderly patients is associated with an increased risk of major bleeding and no reduction rates of thrombotic events. Hence, there is a gap of knowledge on whether aspirin should be continued >3 months after TAVI. SOLOTAVI is a multicenter, open label, blinded endpoint assessment, 1:1 randomized, non-inferiority trial comparing aspirin discontinuation 3 months after TAVI (experimental) to long-term therapy (control). Adult patients with successful transfemoral TAVI for symptomatic aortic stenosis and no indication or contraindication for long-term antithrombotic therapy will be enrolled. Randomization is stratified on center and valve type. The primary endpoint is the 12-month composite of all cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and non-procedure-related major or disabling bleeding. A hierarchical analysis is performed for the primary and 3 principal secondary endpoints. The sample size is computed for demonstrating the non-inferiority of the experimental strategy compared with the control strategy, with a conservative non-inferiority margin of 6.5%. A total of 1400 patients will be enrolled. The SOLOTAVI trial will assess the non-inferiority of a 3-month duration of aspirin compared to the long-term therapy after successful transfemoral TAVI in terms of thrombotic and bleeding events. NCT06518317 clinicaltrials.org.

title: Aspirin-Based Thromboprophylaxis Versus Anticoagulant Regimens After Total Hip or Knee Arthroplasty: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Aspirin is widely used for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis after total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA); however, uncertainty remains regarding its efficacy and safety compared with anticoagulant regimens. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated aspirin-based thromboprophylaxis versus anticoagulant regimens following THA or TKA. Materials and Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were searched through July 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing aspirin-based prophylaxis with anticoagulant regimens. The primary outcomes were any deep vein thrombosis (DVT), symptomatic DVT, and symptomatic venous thromboembolism (VTE). Secondary outcomes included pulmonary embolism (PE), proximal and distal DVT, bleeding outcomes, wound complications, blood transfusion, and mortality. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Additional risk-difference sensitivity analyses incorporated CRISTAL's published cluster-adjusted estimates. Results: Sixteen trials involving 21,265 participants were included. Aspirin was associated with higher risks of symptomatic DVT (RR 1.79, 95% CI 1.35-2.38), symptomatic VTE (RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.33-2.18), PE (RR 1.89, 95% CI 1.33-2.68), and distal DVT (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.06-2.06). Aspirin was associated with lower risks of minor bleeding (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.31-0.71) and ecchymosis or bruising (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.93). No statistically significant differences were detected for the other assessed outcomes. Additional analyses incorporating CRISTAL's cluster-adjusted risk differences did not identify statistically significant differences for the three primary outcomes or PE. Conclusions: The main pooled analyses associated aspirin-based thromboprophylaxis with higher risks of symptomatic thromboembolic events. However, the symptomatic DVT and symptomatic VTE associations were no longer statistically significant after exclusion of CRISTAL or restriction to trials at low risk of bias. The low-risk analysis identified a significantly higher risk of any DVT with aspirin. Aspirin reduced minor bleeding and bruising without a statistically significant reduction in major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding. These findings require cautious interpretation given dependence on CRISTAL, sensitivity to trial inclusion and analytical approach, and differences in prophylactic strategies and outcome definitions.

title: Association Between Long-Term Blood Pressure Patterns and Onset of Stroke: A Nested Case-Control Study of a Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Elevated blood pressure (BP) and its variability are established stroke risk factors; however, whether long-term BP patterns are associated with stroke onset in patients with type 2 diabetes remains unclear. As a post hoc analysis, we conducted a nested case-control study among 2535 patients in the Japanese Primary Prevention of Atherosclerosis with Aspirin for Diabetes (JPAD) trial. During follow-up, 117 patients developed cerebral infarction (CI), and 35 developed intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Controls for these cases were matched for sex, aspirin allocation, age, and diabetes duration. Systolic, diastolic, and mean BP values were collected at baseline, annually during the trial, and every two years after the completion of the trial. Sequential BP levels and coefficient of variations (CVs) were compared between cases and controls. In both CI and ICH subsets, the median intervals from the most recent BP measurement to stroke onset were similar between cases and controls (CI: 300 vs. 288 days, p = 0.46; ICH: 481 vs. 448 days, p = 0.76). The most recent BP measurements before stroke were similar between cases and controls for both CI (systolic BP, 135 vs. 133 mmHg, p = 0.15; diastolic BP, 74 vs. 74 mmHg, p = 0.85) and ICH (systolic BP, 137 vs. 134 mmHg, p = 0.40; diastolic BP, 75 vs. 72 mmHg, p = 0.17). CVs were also comparable. Among patients with type 2 diabetes enrolled in a clinical trial, we found no clear evidence of an association between long-term BP patterns and subsequent stroke onset, suggesting that other factors triggering stroke onset warrant investigation.

title: Predictors of recurrent stroke among patients with lacunar stroke receiving intensive blood pressure control: a secondary analysis of the secondary prevention of small subcortical strokes trial.
abstract: Intensive systolic blood pressure (SBP) lowering to <130 mm Hg is recommended in contemporary secondary stroke prevention guidelines; however, it did not significantly reduce overall recurrent ischemic stroke in the Secondary Prevention of Small Subcortical Strokes (SPS3) trial. In this post hoc secondary analysis of participant-level SPS3 trial data, we sought to identify baseline predictors of recurrent ischemic stroke among patients with lacunar stroke assigned to the lower SBP target in SPS3. This post hoc secondary analysis included SPS3 participants randomized to the lower SBP target (<130 mm Hg). The primary outcome was centrally adjudicated recurrent ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke. Candidate predictors were evaluated with multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression and reported as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Among 1501 participants (41.1% aged ≥ 65 years; 60.8% were men), 120 (8.0%) experienced recurrent ischemic stroke over a median follow-up of 3.49 years (interquartile range, 1.80-5.08), corresponding to an incidence rate of 2.43 events per 100 person-years. In unadjusted comparisons, recurrent ischemic stroke was associated with diabetes mellitus (44.2% vs 34.2%; p = .036), coronary artery bypass grafting/coronary stent (9.2% vs 4.1%; p = .018), Black race (24.2% vs 14.4%; p = .007), elevated serum creatinine (14.2% vs 7.7%; p = .022), aspirin or clopidogrel use at the qualifying lacunar stroke (44.2% vs 28.5%; p p = .004), and lower prevalence of a subcortical qualifying stroke (21.7% vs 46.1%; p p = .009) and large-vessel atherosclerosis (HR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.08-2.413; p = .020) were independently associated with recurrence. Randomization to aspirin plus clopidogrel was not associated with recurrent ischemic stroke (HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.75-1.57; p = .661). In SPS3 participants assigned to intensive SBP control, 8.0% experienced recurrent ischemic stroke. Aspirin or clopidogrel use at the qualifying lacunar stroke and large-vessel atherosclerosis remained independent predictors of recurrence. These findings may help identify patients who require preventive strategies beyond intensive SBP lowering.

Randomization to aspirin plus clopidogrel was not associated with recurrent ischemic stroke (HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.75-1.57; p = .661).

abstract_sections.text: In SPS3 participants assigned to intensive SBP control, 8.0% experienced recurrent ischemic stroke. title: Impact of Fixed-Dose Combination Therapies on Cardiovascular Mortality and Major Cardiovascular Events.
abstract: Fixed-dose combination therapy (the polypill) was developed to reduce treatment complexity and improve adherence to evidence-based cardiovascular therapies. This review evaluates contemporary evidence for its effects on major cardiovascular events and cardiovascular mortality across primary prevention, secondary prevention, and emerging heart failure applications, while addressing implementation barriers and remaining evidence gaps. Early pharmacodynamic and adherence trials established that co-formulation preserves the effects of individual components and improves medication adherence. Event-powered trials subsequently demonstrated clinical benefit: PolyIran and TIPS-3 reduced major cardiovascular events in predominantly primary prevention population, whereas SECURE reduced recurrent events after myocardial infarction. Individual-participant and aggregate-data meta-analyses showed relative reductions of approximately 20% to 40% in composite cardiovascular outcomes and a reduction in cardiovascular mortality, with larger benefits among patients with greater adherence and in aspirin-containing strategies. POLY-HF extended the approach to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, improving left ventricular ejection fraction and uptake of guideline-directed therapy; reductions in heart failure events were secondary findings that require confirmation in larger outcome trials. These findings supports fixed-dose combination therapy as an effective strategy for improving adherence and reducing cardiovascular events, with a cardiovascular mortality benefit supported by pooled analyses. Its greatest potential may be in high-risk populations and resource-limited settings, where treatment complexity impedes implementation. Broader adoption will require formulation standardization, sufficient dosing flexibility, longer-term safety data, and effective integration into clinical guidelines and health systems.

title: Biomarker Modulation by Aspirin and Metformin for Colorectal Cancer Prevention: Results from the ASAMET Randomized Phase II Trial.
abstract: Aspirin (Asa) and metformin (Met) have shown preventive efficacy in colorectal cancer (CRC). Preclinical data suggest convergence on NFκB/PI3K-mTOR signalling and potential synergy. The ASAMET phase II trial tested this hypothesis in patients with resected stage I-III CRC. In a 2 × 2 factorial, multicentre, double-blind study (EudraCT 2015-004824-77; NCT03047837), 51 patients were randomized to placebo, Asa 100 mg qd, Met 850 mg twice daily, or AsaMet for 12 months. Biopsies of normal colonic mucosa and fasting blood samples were obtained at baseline and 12 months. NFκB (primary endpoint), Ki67, EGFR, and pS6K were assessed by immunohistochemistry. After 12 months, compared with placebo, Met reduced global NFκB by -9.04 (95% CI, -17.55 to -0.54; p = 0.04), whereas Asa alone was inactive (-3.58; 95% CI, -12.15 to 4.99; p = 0.41), and AsaMet showed a non-significant reduction (-8.88; 95% CI, -18.86 to 1.10; p = 0.08). Pooled analyses confirmed a Met-driven effect (Met vs non-Met: -7.29; 95% CI, -13.79 to -0.79; p = 0.03), with no impact of Asa (p = 0.73). Ki67 and pS6K were unchanged globally; however, AsaMet increased right-sided Ki67 (12.48; 95% CI, 0.45 to 24.51; p = 0.04). No treatment modulated pS6K. Toxicity was manageable, and no serious adverse events occurred. Met reduces NFκB expression in normal colorectal mucosa of CRC survivors, supporting its potential as a low-toxicity preventive agent. Aspirin did not favourably affect mucosal biomarkers. These findings support tissue-based endpoints and further evaluation of metformin for CRC prevention.

title: Eligibility and prescribing of low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention under two international guidelines: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: The primary objective was to compare eligibility for low-dose aspirin prophylaxis according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommendations. Secondary objectives were to evaluate aspirin prescribing among eligible women and preeclampsia outcomes according to guideline eligibility. This retrospective cohort study included 1,064 pregnant women with complete clinical data from a tertiary referral hospital in Türkiye. Eligibility was determined according to ACOG and NICE criteria. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's kappa and McNemar's test. Aspirin prescribing and preeclampsia outcomes were also evaluated. According to the ACOG criteria, 311 women (29.23 %, 95 % CI, 26.58-32.03 %) were eligible for aspirin prophylaxis, whereas 130 (12.22 %, 95 % CI, 10.39-14.32 %) met the NICE criteria. The overall agreement between the two guidelines was 82.9 %, with moderate concordance (Cohen's kappa=0.50). McNemar's test demonstrated a significant difference in patient classification (p<0.001). Aspirin was prescribed to only 25.4 % of ACOG-eligible women and 48.5 % of NICE-eligible women. Overall, preeclampsia occurred in 38 of 1,064 women (3.57 %; 95 % CI, 2.61-4.86 %). Among women eligible for aspirin prophylaxis, preeclampsia developed in 23 of 311 women (7.4 %; 95 % CI, 4.98-10.85 %) according to ACOG criteria and in 16 of 130 women (12.3 %; 95 % CI, 7.72-19.06 %) according to NICE criteria. Although the ACOG guideline identified substantially more women as eligible for aspirin prophylaxis than the NICE guideline, documented aspirin prescribing remained considerably lower than guideline-defined eligibility, highlighting an implementation gap in routine clinical practice.

title: Real-world impact of coronary artery calcium scoring on primary prevention management in a community cardiology practice.
abstract: To evaluate the impact of coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring on lipid-lowering therapy intensification, aspirin initiation, and downstream cardiac testing in primary prevention patients in a community cardiology setting. Retrospective observational study. Single community cardiology practice. Four hundred consecutive patients undergoing CAC scoring in 2022. CAC scoring used for risk stratification and clinical decision-making. Changes in lipid-lowering therapy, aspirin initiation, and downstream cardiac testing across CAC categories (0, 1-99, 100-399, ≥400); risk reclassification using Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) and Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) risk scores. Among 400 patients (mean age 60.2 ± 10.6 years; 46.5% male), 30% had CAC = 0, 37% CAC 1-99, 18% CAC 100-399, and 16% CAC ≥400. Lipid therapy modification increased across categories (7.7%, 33.3%, 69.0%, 81.7%; p p p p < 0.001). CAC changed MESA risk category in 192/348 patients (55.2%): 87 upward and 105 downward. CAC burden was independently associated with graded intensification of lipid-lowering therapy, aspirin initiation, and downstream testing after multivariable adjustment, extending prior descriptive literature with persistent, quantified associations in real-world community practice. Improvement in clinical outcomes cannot be assessed from this retrospective, six-month implementation study.

title: Tirofiban vs standard antiplatelet therapy in acute branch atheromatous disease-related stroke: a multicenter, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint, parallel-group, phase III clinical trial.
abstract: Tirofiban is sometimes used empirically for branch atheromatous disease (BAD)-related stroke, but its benefit in this population remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of intravenous tirofiban administered within 48 h of onset in patients with acute BAD-related stroke. This multicentre, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint clinical trial enrolled patients with BAD-related stroke within 48 h of onset from 25 hospitals in China between 9 November 2023 and 22 November 2025. Eligible patients were randomly assigned to the tirofiban group (intravenously, 0.4 μg/kg per minute for 30 min, followed by a 0.1 μg/kg per minute for 47.5 h) or standard antiplatelet therapy group (oral aspirin with or without clopidogrel) for 48 h. The primary endpoint was an excellent functional outcome, defined as a score of 0 or 1 on the modified Rankin Scale at 90 days. Safety outcomes included major bleeding within 90 days. This trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06037889). Among 516 patients randomized, 513 were included in the primary analysis (258 with tirofiban and 255 with standard antiplatelet therapy). An excellent functional outcome was observed in 181 of 258 patients (70.2%) in the tirofiban group and 178 of 255 (69.8%) in the standard antiplatelet therapy group (risk ratio, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.90-1.13]; P = 0.93). Major bleeding occurred in 0 of 259 participants in the tirofiban-exposed safety population and 1 of 245 (0.4%) in the standard-antiplatelet-exposed safety population. Among patients with acute BAD-related stroke, intravenous tirofiban administered within 48 h of onset without concomitant oral antiplatelet therapy was not superior to standard antiplatelet therapy for achieving an excellent functional outcome at 90 days. These findings should not be extrapolated to substantially earlier treatment or to other tirofiban-based antiplatelet strategies.
