title: The Gap Between Perceived and Objective Diet Quality in Patients with Lynch Syndrome.
abstract: Lynch syndrome (LS) confers a substantially elevated lifetime risk of colorectal cancer (CRC). While enhanced endoscopic surveillance and aspirin chemoprevention are the cornerstones of management, evidence suggests modifiable lifestyle factors like diet may help mitigate or modify hereditary cancer risk. Because specific LS dietary guidelines are lacking, general CRC prevention recommendations are often substituted. Therefore, the aim of this study was to conduct a detailed and comprehensive examination of dietary habits, cancer-related dietary beliefs, and overall cancer-related worry in individuals with Lynch syndrome who attend a Gastrointestinal (GI) Risk Management Clinic. A cross-sectional study was conducted using data collected between June 2025 and June 2026 from individuals with a confirmed LS diagnosis attending a tertiary Gastrointestinal Risk Management Clinic in Melbourne, Australia. Participants completed electronic questionnaires capturing demographics, clinical history, a Food Frequency Questionnaire, the 14-item Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener (MEDAS), and the Cancer Worry Scale (CWS). Self-reported dietary beliefs regarding the relationship between food and cancer risk were captured. Lifestyle behaviors were benchmarked against the Australian Bowel Cancer Risk Reduction Recommendations. The MEDAS was primarily analysed as a population-specific top-vs-bottom half ("better adherence"), and secondarily as a priori "good" adherence (MEDAS > 7). A total of 94 LS patients completed the study (65% female, median age ~51). A striking paradox was observed: 73.3% of participants believed they maintained a healthy diet, yet the cohort demonstrated poor objective adherence to a Mediterranean pattern (median MEDAS: 5 [IQR 4, 7]; range 0-10), with only 14.9% achieving a "good adherence" score (>7). Cancer worry was prevalent, with 60.9% having a CWS > 13, consistent with significant worry about future cancer, with no sex-based differences. However, higher cancer worry (CWS > 11: aOR 1.59, 95% CI 0.48-5.28) and a personal history of cancer (aOR 0.69, 95% CI 0.24-1.97) were not significantly associated with better dietary adherence. Aspirin use was a strong predictor of better Mediterranean diet adherence, yielding an aOR of 3.09 (95% CI: 1.10-8.68), likely reflecting improved overall engagement in health promotion. Only one participant (1.1%) met all objective bowel cancer prevention guidelines. Of the cohort, 37% intentionally restricted foods (primarily processed/red meats) and 21% intentionally included specific foods to prevent cancer; their primary information sources were doctors and the internet. A substantial gap exists between perceived diet quality and objective adherence to evidence-based cancer prevention recommendations among individuals with Lynch syndrome. High levels of cancer-related worry and a willingness to modify dietary choices do not automatically translate into optimal nutrition. These findings highlight a critical need for interventional trials to provide LS patients with evidence-based dietary guidelines to reduce their lifetime risk of CRC that are tailored to this highly motivated but clinically underserved population.

title: Aspirin for primary prevention in patients with high lipoprotein(a): A promising therapeutic option while awaiting future therapies?
abstract: Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined cardiovascular risk factor, linked to both atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and aortic valve stenosis. Plasma Lp(a) levels between 30-50mg/dL suggest a moderate risk, while levels of 51-180mg/dL indicate high risk, and concentrations exceeding 180mg/dL are linked to a very high cardiovascular risk. Currently, there are no approved therapies specifically indicated to lower Lp(a). Recent evidences indicate a role of aspirin in reducing cardiovascular events in primary prevention in patients with high Lp(a). In this review, we discuss the results of the studies that explored the impact of aspirin in reducing cardiovascular events in primary prevention in patients with increased Lp(a) while waiting for the results from large-scale research initiative exploring the impact of RNA-targeting Lp(a)-lowering therapies in reducing cardiovascular risk. In conclusion, waiting for the ongoing trials on emerging RNA-based therapies, the use of aspirin in a subgroup of patients with high atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk, with very high Lp(a) levels and without important bleeding risk could be an interesting strategy. Emerging RNA-targeted therapies might offer in future increased protection against the occurrence of major atherosclerotic cardiovascular events compared to standard lipid management agents in these patients.

title: When prevention constrains cure: Institutional lock-in and gene therapy access for beta-thalassemia.
abstract: On 16 November 2023, the United Kingdom Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first CRISPR-based gene therapy for a genetic disease, offering patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) freedom from lifelong monthly transfusions. Yet in China, which carries the world's largest TDT patient population, no patient has received the therapy through the public health system, and the access gap is not explained by price or manufacturing economics alone. This paper argues that prevention-era institutional architecture constrains cure-era access through three lock-in mechanisms: cognitive (the direction of genetic information flow), infrastructural (the spatial distribution of treatment capacity), and fiscal (the structure of payment responsibility). Drawing on a structured comparison of four countries selected to represent distinct institutional pathway types (Cyprus, ecclesiastical-public certification; China, administrative filing; Thailand, public health universal coverage; India, federal fragmentation), the analysis proposes a typology of barrier configurations and illustrates them through four exploratory cases. The administrative-filing pathway is associated with high barriers across information, geographic, and economic dimensions; trust-intention is not assessable on current evidence. The ecclesiastical-public pathway is associated with medium information and low geographic barriers with medium fiscal and low-confidence trust barriers; the universal-coverage pathway provides a balanced platform that remains under-activated for gene therapy; and the federal-fragmented pathway fails the precondition of patient identification. No pathway simultaneously optimizes all four readiness dimensions. Presented as a hypothesis-generating typology rather than a tested diagnostic model, the framework relates pathway type to barrier configuration and offers testable hypotheses for pathway-specific intervention design and for extension to sickle cell disease, hemophilia, and other genetic conditions entering the curative era.

title: Precision Medicine in Sickle Cell Disease: From Molecular Pathways to Curative Strategies.
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a monogenic β-globin disorder characterized by hemoglobin S polymerization, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion, yet it exhibits remarkable clinical heterogeneity. Despite advances in supportive care and disease-modifying therapies, substantial variability in severity, treatment response, and long-term outcomes persists. Therefore, this review aims to examine the biological and clinical foundations of precision medicine in SCD, emphasizing genomic modifiers, molecular pathways, and phenotype-driven therapeutic strategies. Key pathogenic pathways including hemoglobin polymerization, vascular adhesion, and inflammatory and oxidative amplification have enabled the development of targeted agents such as hydroxyurea, voxelotor, crizanlizumab, and L-glutamine, each demonstrating domain-specific targets. Pharmacogenomic insights, particularly involving fetal hemoglobin regulatory loci (e.g. BCL11A and HBS1L-MYB), further elucidate variability in disease expression and therapeutic response. Emerging curative approaches, including allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, lentiviral gene addition, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing, represent transformative applications of precision hematology. Collectively, these advances support a paradigm shift from generalized symptom management toward biologically informed, individualized care. title: Future-proofing thalassaemia care: harnessing scalable therapies, artificial intelligence, and global collaboration.
abstract: Advances in the treatment of thalassaemia have led to major improvements in survival and quality of life over the past 30 years. In addition to developments in stem-cell transplantation, transfusion safety, iron overload monitoring, and iron-chelation therapy, novel disease-modifying and gene therapies are also emerging. However, substantial disparities in access to specialised care and novel therapies persist, particularly in low-income and middle-income countries, where most people with thalassaemia reside. This Series paper explores complementary strategies aimed at improving global thalassaemia outcomes beyond conventional therapeutic innovation. We discuss the emerging role of repurposed low-cost therapies, particularly hydroxyurea and thalidomide, as disease-modifying options in resource-limited settings. We further examine opportunities to democratise access to curative gene therapies through technological developments, decentralised manufacturing, regional collaborations, and simplified treatment platforms. In addition, the rapidly expanding role of artificial intelligence in screening, diagnosis, prediction of complications, and remote care delivery is reviewed. Finally, we highlight the importance of international collaborations, multidisciplinary training, and research networks in strengthening equitable global thalassaemia care.

title: The expanding therapeutic landscape of β-thalassaemia.
abstract: β-thalassaemia is characterised by ineffective erythropoiesis, chronic anaemia, haemolysis, and progressive iron-related and non-iron-related morbidity. Although transfusion, iron chelation, multidisciplinary care, and allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation have substantially improved outcomes, major gaps persist in treatment burden, access, safety, adherence, and curative feasibility. Over the past decade, the therapeutic landscape has expanded rapidly, with disease-modifying agents targeting erythroid maturation and red cell metabolism, including luspatercept and mitapivat, now available as options for both transfusion-dependent and non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia. In parallel, gene addition and gene editing therapies, particularly beti-cel and exa-cel, have established proof of curative potential independent of donor availability. However, optimal patient selection, response definitions, long-term outcome assessment, affordability, and equitable global access remain central challenges for wide implementation. In this Series paper, we discuss advances in β-thalassaemia treatment over the past decade, including newly approved and late-stage therapies and their future implications, and highlight remaining research gaps.

title: Clinical translation of CRISPR-Cas9 therapeutics in cancer and inherited genetic disorders.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9, adapted from the bacterial Type II CRISPR adaptive immune system, functions as a programmable RNA-guided endonuclease that employs a single-guide RNA to direct Cas9 to specific genomic loci. CRISPR-Cas9 has transformed targeted genome editing by replacing complex protein engineering with programmable Watson-Crick base pairing between the guide RNA and target DNA. This review was developed following a structured literature search of major biomedical databases and clinical trial registries to synthesize current evidence on the therapeutic applications of CRISPR-Cas9 in oncology and inherited genetic disorders. Clinical studies of ex vivo BCL11A-enhancer editing have shown fetal hemoglobin reactivation, with most evaluable participants with sickle cell disease remaining free of severe vaso-occlusive crises for the prespecified period and most evaluable participants with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia achieving sustained transfusion independence. In vivo reductions in circulating transthyretin protein levels have been achieved for transthyretin amyloidosis via lipid nanoparticle delivery, while clinically meaningful improvements in selected measures of visual function were observed in a subset of patients receiving subretinal AAV-delivered CRISPR editing for CEP290-associated Leber congenital amaurosis type 10. Preclinical and early clinical studies have further investigated CRISPR-engineered T cells designed to improve antitumor activity, persistence, or resistance to inhibitory signaling. Despite these advances, key translational hurdles include the risk of off-target mutations and large-scale chromosomal rearrangements. Furthermore, immune responses against bacterial Cas9 nucleases and viral delivery vectors may limit the long-term efficacy of CRISPR-based therapies, while technical barriers surrounding delivery to extrahepatic tissues, such as skeletal muscle and the central nervous system, continue to hinder broader clinical success. Ethical concerns regarding germline modifications and the high cost of individualized therapies present additional translational challenges. Consequently, emerging DSB-independent technologies, such as base editing and prime editing, may reduce selected DSB-associated liabilities, but each introduces distinct editing, delivery, and genotoxicity risks that require product-specific evaluation.

title: Development of CRISPR_SCD001, an autologous hematopoietic stem cell gene therapy for sickle cell disease.
abstract: We developed CRISPR_SCD001, an autologous cellular therapy in which the pathogenic HBB sickle allele is corrected by CRISPR-Cas9-mediated homology-directed repair, using a single-stranded oligodeoxyribonucleotide as DNA donor template. The drug product (DP) from plerixafor-mobilized peripheral blood CD34+ cells from sickle cell disease patients and healthy donors were used for (1) pharmacodynamic assessments to interrogate therapeutic potential, (2) evaluation of genotoxicity, and (3) in vivo characterization by a non-GLP toxicology study in NBSGW mice. Large-scale DP lots yielded 89% ± 5% CD34+ purity and had a viability of 84% ± 6%. Mean gene correction at HBB was 22% ± 4% of alleles, with 51% ± 6% of allelic disruption. Edited erythroid cultures produced 39% ± 5% adult hemoglobin and 40% ± 6% fetal hemoglobin, reducing sickle hemoglobin from 89% to 22% ± 6%. In NOD,B6.SCID Il2rg -/- KitW41/W41 (NBSGW) mice, CRISPR_SCD001 engrafted robustly (59% ± 25%), maintained editing frequencies comparable to injected cells (∼20% gene correction), and showed polyclonal distribution of the edited cells; no noteworthy treatment-related toxicity or pathologic evidence was found by a blinded histopathology assessment. Our protocol generates a clinical-grade, cryopreserved CD34+ cell product that corrects the sickle mutation, restores anti-sickling hemoglobins, and meets pre-clinical safety criteria, establishing a reproducible manufacturing process suitable for clinical translation. These data support initiation of a first-in-human phase 1 trial of CRISPR_SCD001 for sickle cell disease patients presenting with severe pathology.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing: technological advances, delivery strategies and precision engineering of primary cells for therapeutic application in genetic disorders and diabetes mellitus.
abstract: The CRISPR-Cas9 system has revolutionized modern life sciences, driving a paradigm shift in biomedical research and becoming an indispensable tool in molecular biology due to its remarkable precision, efficiency, and simplicity. Originating from a bacterial adaptive immune mechanism, CRISPR-Cas9 has evolved rapidly, providing a versatile framework for manipulating genetic material and addressing a wide spectrum of human diseases. Recent progress includes the discovery of novel Cas orthologs and the rational engineering of Cas9 variants to enhance editing fidelity, broaden target range, and minimize off-target effects. Structural and functional optimization of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) has further improved target binding affinity, stability, and Cas9-sgRNA complex formation, thereby increasing overall editing performance. The development of high-fidelity Cas9 derivatives and next-generation platforms such as base editors and prime editors has enabled precise single-nucleotide substitutions and small insertions or deletions without generating double-stranded DNA breaks. Advanced delivery systems-including viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, and ribonucleoprotein electroporation-have facilitated efficient CRISPR-mediated editing across in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo models. Remarkable therapeutic milestones have been achieved in treating monogenic disorders such as sickle cell disease, β-thalassemia, and cystic fibrosis, where long-term clinical benefits have been documented. Furthermore, CRISPR-Cas9 technology is redefining diabetes research by enabling precise modeling of disease mechanisms, uncovering molecular pathways involved in glucose homeostasis, and opening new avenues for cellular and gene-based therapies. This review highlights recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing, emphasizing breakthroughs in primary cell editing and the development of translational models for genetic diseases and diabetes mellitus.

title: Sickle cell disease and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: donor expansion, gene-modified grafts and prenatal horizons.
abstract: To review advances from the past 18 months in allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and autologous gene-modified stem cell transplantation for sickle cell disease (SCD), and to relate these developments to stem cell biology, conditioning and emerging prenatal strategies. Matched sibling HSCT remains the clinical benchmark, but recent studies show age- and regimen-dependent trade-offs between durable engraftment, graft-versus-host disease and toxicity. Haploidentical platforms using posttransplant cyclophosphamide, thiotepa or intensified low-dose irradiation have widened donor access, although infection, graft failure and chronic graft-versus-host disease remain important. Autologous CRISPR-edited and lentiviral grafts can nearly eliminate severe vaso-occlusive events, but still require stem cell collection, individualized manufacture and myeloablative conditioning. New work identifies inflammation, lineage skewing, reduced GATA1 and premature senescence as determinants of sickle stem cell fitness, while culture-sparing editing and antibody-directed conditioning offer routes to safer transplantation. Curative SCD therapies are converging on the same challenge: establishing durable healthy hematopoiesis with acceptable toxicity. Progress will depend on graft quality, safer niche creation, patient-centred outcomes and equitable delivery. In vivo and prenatal approaches remain preclinical and require a substantially higher maternal-foetal safety threshold.

title: The landscape and trajectory of global CRISPR therapeutics.
abstract: With the first regulatory approval in 2023 of a CRISPR-based therapy for sickle cell disease followed by the recent demonstration of an accelerated, personalized CRISPR treatment for congenital severe carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency, CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has progressed from a laboratory technology into a clinical reality in just over a decade. While enthusiasm for deploying CRISPR-Cas9 to treat a range of human genetic diseases continues to grow, broad clinical application remains constrained due to technical, regulatory, manufacturing and economic challenges. Here, scientists from the European Cooperation in Science and Technology (COST) action Genome Editing to Treat Human Diseases (GenE-HumDi) provide a comprehensive global overview of the CRISPR therapeutic landscape. We systematically analyze CRISPR-based therapeutic trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and the EU Clinical Trials Register, providing a thorough assessment of the current clinical activity and the trajectory of CRISPR technology as it advances toward routine clinical interventions.

title: Translating CRISPR to Practice in the Clinic: Transformative Therapy in Hemoglobinopathies and Emerging Applications in Malignancies.
abstract: Exagamglogene autotemcel, the first clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based gene-editing therapy to enter clinical practice, has established genome editing as a curative-intent option for eligible patients with severe sickle cell disease (SCD) and transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (TDT). Ex vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing of autologous CD34-positive hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells to reactivate fetal hemoglobin has produced durable freedom from severe vaso-occlusive crises in SCD and sustained transfusion independence in TDT. This approach offers a donor-independent alternative to allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation without graft rejection or graft-versus-host disease. Hemoglobinopathies, therefore, provide the first clinically validated delivery model for CRISPR therapeutics. Successful implementation, however, requires more than editing efficacy. It depends on structured referral, candidacy assessment, organ function review, mobilization and collection, centralized manufacturing, pharmacokinetic-guided myeloablative conditioning, transplant-level supportive care, fertility preservation, psychosocial support, and prolonged surveillance coordinated among primary hematologists and cellular therapy programs. Key barriers include stem cell collection, conditioning-related toxicity, cost, reimbursement friction, and persistent inequities in access. Long-term follow-up and registry participation are necessary to evaluate outcomes beyond pain crises, identify late toxic effects, and compare real-world effectiveness across gene editing, gene addition, and allogeneic transplantation. In oncology, CRISPR-based therapy remains investigational, with early clinical feasibility demonstrated in relapsed or refractory B-cell malignancies, T-cell malignancies, AML, multiple myeloma, and selected solid tumors. For hematologists, oncologists, and transplant and cellular therapy programs, the central challenge is to integrate CRISPR into practice with the rigor required for any high-risk curative therapy: careful patient selection, disciplined delivery, and long-term accountability.

title: Addressing the slow uptake of gene therapy for sickle cell disease: a lack of interest, a high cost, or a more complex issue?
abstract: The approval of Gene Therapy (GT) for sickle cell disease (SCD) marks a major milestone in hematology, offering curative potential for SCD without the need for a allogeneic transplantation. Yet early real-world uptake has been slow. This delay in integration is likely due to complex intertwined barriers that require further elucidation. We conducted a structured review of the literature, searching PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov through April 2026 for evidence on the economic, institutional, clinician-level, and patient-level barriers limiting adoption of GT for SCD, as well as global disparities in access. Slow uptake of GT reflects the expected challenge of introducing a complex, resource-intensive intervention into a fragmented care system for an underserved population with a chronic debilitating illness. Addressing these barriers requires coordinated efforts from payers, institutions, clinicians, and patient communities. Without deliberate structural reform, GT risks widening existing health disparities rather than alleviating them.

title: Sickle Cell Disease: From Ancient Origins to Modern Breakthroughs in Gene Therapy.
abstract: Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) is a hereditary hemoglobinopathy arising from a single-nucleotide transversion (GAG → GTG) at codon six of the HBB gene on chromosome 11, substituting glutamic acid with valine in the β-globin chain and producing hemoglobin S (HbS). Under hypoxic conditions, HbS polymerizes and distorts erythrocytes into the characteristic sickle shape, initiating a cascade of vaso-occlusion, chronic hemolytic anemia, and progressive multi-organ damage that defines the clinical burden of this disease. Although SCD has ancient origins in sub-Saharan Africa, the Indian subcontinent, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean, regions where it conferred heterozygous resistance to malaria, the ease of human migration has long since made it a global health concern, affecting an estimated 300,000-400,000 newborns annually. Advances in molecular and genomic research have deepened our understanding of SCD pathophysiology, revealing the central contributions of hemoglobin polymerization, oxidative stress, endothelial inflammation, and nitric oxide depletion to disease progression. Current management rests on supportive pharmacological interventions, including hydroxyurea, chronic transfusion therapy, L-glutamine, and multimodal pain management, complemented by lifestyle modifications. Curative approaches have advanced substantially: hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) remains the established standard of cure, while the regulatory approvals in late 2023 of the CRISPR/Cas9-based exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy) and the lentiviral vector-based lovotibeglogene autotemcel (Lyfgenia) represent the most transformative development in the history of SCD therapeutics. This review traces the disease from its ancient origins and molecular characterization through to its clinical manifestations, inheritance patterns, screening strategies, and the full spectrum of current and emerging therapies. Persistent challenges, prohibitive treatment costs, healthcare inequities, the ethical dimensions of genome editing, and the urgent need for long-term safety data, are examined critically, with a view to informing the research and policy agenda that must accompany these remarkable scientific advances.

title: Gene Therapy for β-Haemoglobinopathies: From Molecular Correction to Curative Medicine.
abstract: β-haemoglobinopathies, including sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia, are among the most common monogenic disorders worldwide and represent a major global health burden. Conventional treatments, such as blood transfusions, iron chelation, fetal haemoglobin induction, and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, have improved outcomes but remain limited by treatment-related toxicity, donor availability, and incomplete curative potential. A narrative literature review was conducted using PubMed up to 2025. Search terms included "sickle cell disease," "sickle cell anemia," "β-thalassemia," "transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia," "gene therapy," "gene addition," "gene editing," "CRISPR-Cas9," "lentiviral vector," "children," "paediatric," and "pediatric." Relevant clinical trials, reviews, consensus statements, and guidelines were selected and qualitatively analysed. Gene therapy for β-haemoglobinopathies is based mainly on two strategies: gene addition and gene editing. Gene addition uses lentiviral vectors to introduce functional or modified β-globin genes into autologous haematopoietic stem cells, whereas gene editing targets regulatory pathways, particularly BCL11A, to reactivate fetal haemoglobin synthesis or correct disease-causing mutations. Clinical studies have shown encouraging outcomes, including transfusion independence in many patients with β-thalassaemia and marked reduction or elimination of vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease. Paediatric and adolescent data are increasingly promising, although still limited. Gene therapy is reshaping the treatment landscape of β-haemoglobinopathies by offering a personalised and potentially curative approach. However, long-term safety, conditioning toxicity, fertility preservation, accessibility, costs, and implementation in high-prevalence regions remain critical challenges. Further studies are needed to optimise patient selection and expand equitable access.

abstract_sections.label: Background
abstract_sections.text: β-haemoglobinopathies, including sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia, are among the most common monogenic disorders worldwide and represent a major global health burden. Conventional treatments, such as blood transfusions, iron chelation, fetal haemoglobin induction, and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, have improved outcomes but remain limited by treatment-related toxicity, donor availability, and incomplete curative potential.

abstract_sections.label: Methods
abstract_sections.text: A narrative literature review was conducted using PubMed up to 2025. Search terms included "sickle cell disease," "sickle cell anemia," "β-thalassemia," "transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia," "gene therapy," "gene addition," "gene editing," "CRISPR-Cas9," "lentiviral vector," "children," "paediatric," and "pediatric." Relevant clinical trials, reviews, consensus statements, and guidelines were selected and qualitatively analysed.

abstract_sections.label: Results
abstract_sections.text: Gene therapy for β-haemoglobinopathies is based mainly on two strategies: gene addition and gene editing. Gene addition uses lentiviral vectors to introduce functional or modified β-globin genes into autologous haematopoietic stem cells, whereas gene editing targets regulatory pathways, particularly BCL11A, to reactivate fetal haemoglobin synthesis or correct disease-causing mutations. Clinical studies have shown encouraging outcomes, including transfusion independence in many patients with β-thalassaemia and marked reduction or elimination of vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease. Paediatric and adolescent data are increasingly promising, although still limited.

abstract_sections.label: Conclusions
abstract_sections.text: Gene therapy is reshaping the treatment landscape of β-haemoglobinopathies by offering a personalised and potentially curative approach. However, long-term safety, conditioning toxicity, fertility preservation, accessibility, costs, and implementation in high-prevalence regions remain critical challenges. Further studies are needed to optimise patient selection and expand equitable access.

title: Oligonucleotide Synthesis Errors Are a Source of Untoward Variation in HDR-Mediated Gene Editing.
abstract: Single-stranded oligonucleotides (ssODNs) are used as donor templates for therapeutic gene editing by CRISPR-Cas9 cleavage and homology-directed repair (HDR). Although ssODN sequence fidelity is critical to the safety and efficacy of editing, standard quality control methods cannot resolve individual nucleotide errors. We performed deep sequencing of ssODNs from three manufacturers and amplicons from edited hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells. We find that synthesis errors are present in all ssODNs tested at rates that vary more than two-fold among manufacturers, at positions that are dependent on sequence context. These synthesis errors are propagated into the genome by HDR at frequencies proportional to their abundance in the ssODN. In our sickle cell mutation correction protocol, the most prevalent SNEs are predicted to produce benign β-globin variants, while the less frequent frameshift deletions are predicted to generate β-thalassemia-like alleles. Current quality control standards are insufficient to detect these errors, and deep sequencing of ssODNs should be incorporated into regulatory submissions for clinical gene editing programs.

title: Post-COVID Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction: A Focus on Persistent Diarrhea.
abstract: Persistent gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection include diarrhea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, constipation, nausea, and other disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs), but these entities should not be treated as interchangeable. In a meta-analysis of long-COVID studies, any GI symptom was reported in approximately 22% of patients and diarrhea in 10%, although heterogeneity was very high. In a large US Veterans Affairs cohort, post-acute COVID-19 was associated with incident diarrhea (hazard ratio {HR}: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.52-1.65; excess burden 7.99 per 1,000 persons at one year) and irritable bowel syndrome (HR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.28-1.86). Prospective Rome IV cohorts report lower absolute rates of formally diagnosed DGBIs; one study found persistent DGBI symptoms in 6.6% at six months, with functional diarrhea in 2.2% and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in 2.5% at three months. Mechanistic evidence supports intestinal involvement during acute infection and demonstrates associations with epithelial/angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) perturbation, immune activation, barrier dysfunction, altered microbial taxa, and impaired microbial metabolite production. However, persistent viral RNA or antigen, dysbiosis, and gut-lung signaling remain proposed or associative mechanisms rather than established causes of chronic diarrhea. Treatment evidence specific to post-COVID functional diarrhea is sparse. A large synbiotic trial improved a broad "gastrointestinal upset" domain in post-acute COVID syndrome, but did not enroll a defined chronic diarrhea or Rome-positive population; probiotic and fecal microbiota transplantation trials showing GI effects were largely conducted during acute COVID-19. Therefore, current care should first exclude organic and medication-related causes, then apply phenotype-based management extrapolated from established diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) and functional-diarrhea practice while clearly acknowledging the limited post-COVID-specific evidence. Standardized definitions, pre-infection GI data, appropriate controls, functional microbiome measures, and dedicated randomized trials are priorities for future research.

title: Vaccination and hybrid immunity is associated with SARS-CoV-2 protection but not shedding duration in rural Guatemalan households.
abstract: Essential agricultural workers in Central America and their households faced a high force of infection during the COVID-19 pandemic. Here, we evaluated if pre-existing seropositivity and vaccination (hybrid immunity) influenced SARS-CoV-2 infection risk and duration of shedding in an agricultural community in rural Guatemala. Individuals from 70 households were enrolled in a community cohort. From September 2021 to December 2022, all participants reported symptoms twice-weekly and provided saliva weekly for SARS-CoV-2 RNA testing by reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Following detection of SARS-CoV-2 in a household, all enrolled household members provided saliva tested three times weekly for four weeks for RT-PCR testing to determine the duration of viral shedding among infected participants. We selected 119 SARS-CoV-2 PCR-positive individuals and 101 month-matched controls to measure nucleocapsid IgG and Omicron neutralizing antibody (NAb) titers. Compared to uninfected controls, SARS-CoV-2 cases were more frequently female (60.5% vs. 48.5%, p = 0.08), had fewer vaccine doses (p = 0.07), and were less likely to have hybrid immunity (p = 0.08). Compared to controls, SARS-CoV-2 cases had lower median titers of nucleocapsid IgG (cutoff index [COI] = 9.6 vs. 23.6, p = 0.12) and Omicron NAb (28.4 vs. 50.4, p = 0.15). SARS-CoV-2 cases also had lower NAb than controls among those vaccinated with 1 (16.1 vs. 182.7, p = 0.01), 2 (11.9 vs. 87.0, p = 0.04), or 3 doses (13.4 vs. 232.5, p = 0.004), and those considered up-to-date on vaccination (13.1 vs. 155.6, p = 0.0001). Nucleocapsid IgG and Omicron NAb were similar between individuals with short (≤ 7 days) vs. long (> 7 days) viral shedding durations. In a household cohort of Guatemalan agricultural workers, cumulative vaccine doses associated with lower odds of infection. Among those previously vaccinated, lower titers of nucleocapsid IgG and Omicron NAb were associated with elevated infection risk, highlighting the importance of hybrid immunity in COVID-19 protection in this population.

title: SARS-CoV-2-specific monoclonal antibody AER002 in Long COVID: an exploratory randomized phase 2a mechanistic trial.
abstract: Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 has been proposed as a biological driver of Long COVID, a disabling chronic illness with no proven treatments. We conducted an exploratory, placebo-controlled, double-blind, 2:1 randomized mechanistic trial (NCT05877508) of the SARS-CoV-2-specific monoclonal antibody AER002 in 36 participants who met the World Health Organization case definition of Long COVID. After baseline characterization, participants received a single infusion and were followed for 360 days. The primary endpoint was the PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score (PHSS) at 90 days; secondary and exploratory endpoints included patient-reported and objective measures of physical and neurocognitive function as well as blood-, imaging-, and tissue-based biomarkers. While AER002 was safe and well tolerated, no significant differences in physical health, quality of life, objective measures of physical function or cognition, or blood-based biomarkers were demonstrated between the treatment and control arms. In a post-hoc analysis, participants with a lower baseline SARS-CoV-2 antibody level and higher drug exposure were more likely to perceive treatment benefit based on the Patient Global Impression of Change scale (p < 0.05 for anti-S, S1, and RBD). Although AER002 was not efficacious in this proof-of-concept study, our findings could inform future trials using monoclonal antibodies to target viral persistence in Long COVID.

title: Metformin at the Time of COVID-19 Infection and Risk of Long COVID: A Target Trial Emulation Study.
abstract: Our objective was to evaluate metformin prescribed at the time of SARS-CoV-2 infection on the risk of developing Long COVID (LC) in electronic health record data. We conducted a new user analysis of metformin prescribed within 6 days of documented infection with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) versus experimental control: prescription for fluvoxamine, fluticasone, ivermectin, or montelukast. a clinic visit in the 0-6 months and the 6-12 months before infection. metformin or control within 12 months. LC or death (LC/D), to address death as a competing risk, among patients prescribed drug within Days 0-6 of infection. LC was defined by diagnosis code or computable phenotype. We used entropy balancing to estimate the average treatment effect with a weighted log-linear model. After weighting, there were 248 in the metformin and control groups; the average age was 53 (16); 16% were Black; and 16% were Hispanic. In the primary analysis, 10/248 (4.0%) in the metformin group developed LC/D versus 21/248 (8.5%) in the control group, adjusted risk ratio (aRR) 0.47 (95% CI 0.25-0.89, p = 0.02). For prescriptions on Days 0-1 relative to infection, aRR was 0.39 (95% CI 0.12-1.24); for prescriptions on Days 0-14, the aRR was 0.75 (95% CI 0.52-1.08). In this observational analysis, metformin prescribed within a week of documented SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with a 53% lower risk of LC over 6 months than comparator medications. With the aRR of 0.47 (95% CI 0.25-0.89), any risk reduction between 75% and 11% is highly compatible with our data. This analysis of electronic health record diagnoses is important for the reproducibility of clinical trial results that ascertained the same outcome but via participant-report.

title: The Rising Burden of Atrial Fibrillation and Respiratory Failure Mortality in the United States: A 25-Year Nationwide Retrospective Analysis of Death Certificate Data.
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and respiratory failure (RF) frequently co-occur in critically ill patients, but long-term national trends in deaths recording both remain unknown. CDC WONDER multiple-cause-of-death data identified U.S. adults aged ≥ 55 years with both AF (including atrial flutter) and RF listed on death certificates from 1999 to 2024. Age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs) and annual percent changes (APCs) were estimated using joinpoint regression. Sensitivity analyses included adults aged ≥ 25 years, exclusion of COVID-19-related deaths, and stratification by co-listed heart failure (HF). A total of 462 284 deaths listed both AF and RF. The AAMR increased roughly five-fold (7.84 to 41.76 per 100 000), rising steadily through 2018 (APC 7.81), accelerating through 2021 (APC 18.78), and declining thereafter (APC -5.90). Excluding deaths listing COVID-19, the 2018-2021 acceleration was not detected, and AAMRs rose through 2024 (2017-2024 APC 5.25). AAMRs for deaths without HF recorded rose over fourfold. Mean AAMRs were higher in males (26.19) than in females (19.04) and in non-Hispanic (NH) White adults (24.06) than in other groups. The West and nonmetropolitan areas had the highest rates. The 2018-2021 surge was steepest among Hispanic (APC 25.62) and NH Black adults (APC 24.06). Population mortality rates for deaths recording both AF and RF increased substantially over 25 years, beginning before the COVID-19 pandemic, persisting after excluding deaths listing COVID-19, and occurring with and without HF recorded. These data cannot separate changes in disease occurrence from changes in diagnosis or coding.

title: Self-reported long COVID associated with sleep problems and poor sleep quality among adults in Germany: results of the German Health Update 2023 (GEDA 2023).
abstract: Long COVID refers to various long-term health impairments following a SARS-CoV-2 infection, including physical, cognitive, and psychological symptoms. Sleep problems are among the most prevalent neuropsychiatric symptoms of long COVID and can negatively affect daily functioning and quality of life. This study aims to investigate sleep onset problems, problems maintaining sleep and poor sleep quality in associations with long COVID among adults in Germany. Analyses are based on data from the cross-sectional nationwide telephone interview survey "German Health Update" (GEDA 2023). Between March 2023 and February 2024, 9,310 adults (50.8% female, median age = 60.8 years) answered questions on any prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and long COVID status, as well as on sleep onset problems, problems maintaining sleep and poor sleep quality over the past 4 weeks. Weighted prevalence estimates for each sleep variable were calculated by self-reported SARS-CoV-2 infection and long COVID status. Multivariable logistic regressions were conducted, adjusted for age, sex, level of education, chronic conditions, depressive symptoms, COVID-19 vaccination status, and multiple SARS-CoV-2 infections. Participants with self-reported current long COVID reported higher proportions of sleep onset problems (32.6%), problems maintaining sleep (47.8%) and poor sleep quality (44.8%) compared to participants without a SARS-CoV-2 infection (20.0%, 30.8 and 24.1%, respectively) or prior infected participants without long COVID (13.8%, 23.8 and 20.0%, respectively). In multivariable logistic regression analyses, participants with self-reported current long COVID had an increased likelihood of experiencing problems maintaining sleep (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 1.73; 95% CI = 1.23-2.44) and a higher likelihood of poor sleep quality (aOR = 1.81; 95% CI = 1.29-2.55) compared to non-infected individuals; however, sleep onset problems were not associated with long COVID. Our findings from general population data suggest that adults with current long COVID have 1.7- to 1.8-fold higher odds of problems maintaining sleep and poor sleep quality than non-infected individuals. Given the potential impact on quality of life and physical and psychological functioning, sleep-related symptoms may represent an important target for clinical assessment and management in individuals with long COVID.

title: Glycemic dysregulation and insulin resistance across acute and post-acute COVID-19: a systematic review and meta-analysis of etiologic and prognostic evidence.
abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can disrupt glucose regulation through inflammation, adipose-tissue dysfunction, impaired insulin signaling, and variable β-cell compensation. These evidence domains remain incompletely integrated. To synthesize evidence on glycemic dysregulation and insulin resistance or insulin sensitivity across acute and post-acute COVID-19, including metabolic trajectories and associations with adverse clinical outcomes. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect were searched. Eligible studies evaluated glucose regulation and at least one insulin-resistance or insulin-sensitivity measure during or after COVID-19. Etiological and prognostic evidence was analyzed as related but distinct domains. Prognostic meta-analysis evaluated study-defined acute hyperglycemic phenotypes; insulin-resistance or insulin-sensitivity assessment was a study-level eligibility criterion rather than part of a participant-level composite exposure. Unadjusted risk ratios (RRs) from event counts were pooled using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Non-combinable evidence was synthesized according to Synthesis Without Meta-analysis principles. Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate tools, and certainty was evaluated with GRADE. The protocol and analytical plan were retrospectively registered in OSF on August 21, 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU). Twenty independent studies represented by 23 reports. Acute hyperglycemic phenotypes were associated with increased short-term all-cause mortality (four studies; 1,079 participants; RR 2.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.21-3.64; I2=31.3%; 95% prediction interval 0.96-4.56) and invasive mechanical ventilation (three studies; 679 participants; RR 3.64, 95% CI 1.74-7.61; I2=0%). Mortality estimates remained directionally stable in sensitivity analysis. Adding a large study using peak in-hospital glucose preserved the mortality association but produced substantial heterogeneity for ventilation. Etiological evidence showed no uniform post-COVID trajectory: insulin resistance or glycemic abnormalities resolved in some populations, persisted in others, and progressed toward newly diagnosed diabetes in a subset. Mechanistic evidence implicated inflammatory stress, adipose-tissue dysfunction, impaired insulin signaling, and variable β-cell responses. Study-defined acute hyperglycemic phenotypes were associated with adverse COVID-19 outcomes in studies that also assessed insulin resistance or insulin sensitivity. These unadjusted estimates should not be interpreted as effects of a combined phenotype or as causal associations. Persistent metabolic abnormalities occurred heterogeneously, supporting standardized participant-level definitions and controlled longitudinal studies. https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU, identifier 10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU.

title: Changes in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein testing and distribution across the COVID-19 pandemic: a 17-year laboratory-based study.
abstract: COVID-19 altered health care utilization and laboratory testing. We assessed changes in routine high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) testing and distributions across the pandemic. We retrospectively analyzed hs-CRP results from a tertiary-care medical center from 2007 through 2023. We included 314 106 episodes from 116 505 patients. Annual testing volume, median values, upper-tail percentiles, and threshold categories were assessed, and distributions were compared across the prepandemic (2007-2019), pandemic (2020-2022), and postpandemic (2023) periods. The hs-CRP distribution was right skewed (median, 0.050 mg/dL; 95th and 99th percentiles, 0.440 mg/dL and 1.060 mg/dL, respectively). Annual median values remained stable, but upper percentiles and the proportion of hs-CRP results 0.3 mg/dL or higher declined (annual odds ratio, 0.985 [95% CI, 0.983-0.988]). During 2020-2022, hs-CRP values below 0.1 mg/dL were more frequent and values at or above 0.3 mg/dL less frequent than before the pandemic. Pandemic-period differences occurred against a preexisting decline in upper-tail hs-CRP values. These findings should be interpreted in their long-term context, considering testing volume and result distributions.

title: Stem Cell Educator Therapy for Ex Vivo Immune Modulation of Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells in Patients with Long COVID.
abstract: Long COVID, generally defined as clinical symptoms persisting for 3 months or longer following severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection, affects multiple organs and systems. At least 400 million people globally are living with long COVID, with symptoms including persistent fatigue and brain fog. Currently, long COVID care mainly consists of symptomatic management and supportive approaches, with no validated effective treatments available that address the underlying inflammation. Stem Cell Educator (SCE) therapy is a treatment developed to modulate immune responses. This protocol describes SCE therapy and its application in patients with long COVID to evaluate safety, clinical outcomes, and immunological changes. During SCE therapy, a patient's peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) are collected by leukapheresis and co-cultured with adherent cord-blood-derived multipotent stem cells (CB-SC) in vitro, after which the "educated" PBMC are returned to the patient's circulation via infusion. SCE therapy has previously been evaluated in clinical studies for type 1 diabetes and other autoimmune diseases. Twenty-five patients with long COVID (15 males and 10 females) received SCE therapy. Five patients experienced mild adverse effects during apheresis, and one patient reported itching during infusion. Brain fog and fatigue disappeared in 21 of 25 patients following treatment, and most participants reported feeling refreshed, energized, and mentally clear. Flow cytometry demonstrated reductions in inflammatory markers, including interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β)-positive cells and C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 16 (CXCL16)-positive cells. These findings demonstrate the application of SCE therapy in patients with long COVID and provide preliminary clinical and immunological observations supporting further evaluation of this approach.

title: Associations between salivary HHV-6 and long COVID severity in a cross-sectional, case-control analysis.
abstract: Reactivation of human herpesviruses (HHVs), particularly EBV, is associated with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of Long COVID (LC). Reactivation of HHVs has been previously implicated in hormonal dysregulation, which has also been observed in LC, suggesting a potential link. This study aims to examine the relationship between LC symptoms and salivary HHV DNA, cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol levels. Our cross-sectional, case-control study enrolled 45 participants with LC, and 45 age-sex-matched controls. Surveys and validated health questionnaires were used to collect demographics, medical history, and symptom profiles. Saliva was self-collected at waking, 15, 30, and 45 min, and 8 and 16 h after waking, across two consecutive days. Salivary cortisol, testosterone and oestradiol were measured, and extracted nucleic acid was tested for EBV, HSV 1/2, HCMV and HHV-6 A/B using multiplex qPCR, and for SARS-CoV-2 and RNaseP using RT-qPCR. Detection of salivary EBV and HHV-6 DNA copies was highest early in the morning. There were no significant differences in salivary cortisol, testosterone, or oestradiol, or in EBV or HHV-6 DNA between the LC and control groups. However, salivary HHV-6 DNA levels were positively associated with a greater aggregated LC propensity score (r = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.02-0.44, p = 0.015, adj. p = 0.030), as well as anxiety (β = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.02-1.36, p = 0.045) and depression (β = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.05-0.42, p = 0.013) scores. The observed correlation between salivary HHV-6 DNA and symptom severity suggests HHV-6 may contribute to post-acute disease, though mechanisms remain unclear. While we did not identify a relationship between salivary EBV DNA and LC, EBV may still play a role at earlier time points in the disease course, or in compartments not sampled in this study. These findings highlight the potential importance of HHV-6 in LC pathophysiology and underscore the need for longitudinal, multi-compartment studies of herpesvirus reactivation in LC. National Institutes for Health (NIH) funding sources supported AT, SB and CM.

title: Post-COVID neurological manifestations are associated with neuroinflammation, increased autoantibody burden, and persistent complement activation.
abstract: Neurological manifestations represent commonly persistent features of post-COVID conditions (PCC), but mechanisms underlying their pathogenesis remain unclear. In this study, participants with neuro-PCC (n = 29), mostly presenting with persistent headache, fatigue, sleep disturbances, anosmia/dysgeusia, cognitive complaints, and/or paresthesia, recovered from COVID-19 (n = 32), and non-infected controls (n = 32), all matched for sex and age, had paired serum samples from acute phase (0-14 days) and two time points of convalescence (3-6 months and 9-12 months) assessed for antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens (ENA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and autoantibodies against cytokines using Luminex assays. Biomarkers of neuroinflammation, including neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), total Tau protein, and neurogranin were quantified by Ella ELISA and complement activation was determined by increased C5b-9 levels. Patients with neuro-PCC showed a greater number of neurological symptoms during acute phase, with increased frequency of headache and fatigue, and a higher prevalence of obesity and cardiovascular comorbidities. GFAP remained elevated for up to one year after infection, independently of symptom persistence. However, only patients with neuro-PCC exhibited a transient increase in NfL levels during acute phase, and persistent complement activation throughout follow-up. No specific autoantibody was associated with neuro-PCC, but these patients exhibited a higher cumulative autoantibody burden. Multivariable logistic regression analysis showed that hospitalization and the neurological burden during the acute phase were associated with neuro-PCC, whereas anti-cytokine autoantibody counts showed an inverse trend. Increased complement activation and a higher autoantibody burden suggest a broad and nonspecific immune activation that may contribute to a sustained low-grade neuroinflammatory state, potentially driving the persistence of neurological symptoms after COVID-19.

title: Revised estimates of types and duration of long COVID symptoms based on claims records from 245 million US patients.
abstract: COVID-19 has been reported to cause multisystem effects lasting years [Z. Al-Aly, E. Topol, Science 383, 830-832 (2024)]. These findings are primarily based on cohort studies comparing test-positive COVID-19 patients to controls without known COVID-19 infection, tested or untested [M. Cai, Y. Xie, E. J. Topol, Z. Al-Aly, Nat. Med. 30, 1564-1573 (2024)]. However, such comparisons can be biased by the reasons people were tested. Using 14.4 billion insurance claims from 244.7 million US patients, we find that most long-term effects attributed to COVID-19 by unrestricted control designs likely reflect bias due to selective testing of individuals with non-COVID conditions, causing long-term effects of those conditions to be misattributed to COVID-19. We removed this bias by analyzing only tested individuals, comparing test-positive to test-negative patients. Across 614 clinical outcomes followed over 2 y, the test-based design resulted in 83.5% fewer symptoms being attributable to COVID-19 between 30 to 119 d after infection (43 attributable symptoms vs. 262 for the unrestricted control design), a 98.2% reduction at 120 to 359 d (5 vs. 286), and a 100% reduction at 360 to 719 d (0 vs. 369). The unrestricted control design also attributed unrelated outcomes (e.g., firearm injuries) to COVID-19 at a high rate, whereas the testing-based design did not. The test-based control design may modestly underestimate some effects. This study does not indicate that symptoms beyond one year are not genuine but that their attributability to COVID-19 is uncertain.

title: Control-Anchored QUBO Clustering Reveals Control-Distant Postural Control Patterns in Motion Capture Balance Signals After COVID-19.
abstract: Post-COVID-19 balance and postural control alterations have been reported after SARS-CoV-2 infection, but individual-level phenotyping remains challenging because post-acute sequelae are heterogeneous and often lack clear clinical ground truths. We analyzed motion capture balance data from 140 participants, including 114 post-COVID-19 participants and 26 control-group participants, who completed sensory organization/postural balance tasks under single-task and cognitive dual-task conditions. Relative joint angle trajectories were transformed into 0-5 Hz frequency-domain spectra, from which 13 balance-derived task contrasts were constructed to capture cognitive dual-task versus single-task differences, closed-eyes versus open-eyes task condition differences, and related task condition changes. Joint-wise spectral contrast features were encoded using a vector-quantized variational autoencoder. Control-distant subgroup discovery was then formulated as a control-anchored, graph-based QUBO clustering problem and solved using a quantum annealing workflow. Simulated annealing and tabu search were applied to the identical BQM/QUBO formulation as classical solver-level references, whereas Gaussian mixture modeling was retained as an unconstrained classical clustering reference. Consistent with the control-anchored design of the QUBO objective, QUBO clustering identified a selective subset of post-COVID-19 participants with control-distant latent balance profiles while largely preserving the control-group reference structure. Across all task contrasts, quantum annealing assigned 1 of 307 control-group participant-contrast assignments (0.3%) and 118 of 1366 post-COVID-19 participant-contrast assignments (8.6%) to the control-distant group. Simulated annealing and tabu search produced slightly larger but similar control-distant post-COVID-19 subsets, assigning 143 of 1366 post-COVID participant-contrast assignments (10.5%) and 0 of 307 control-group participant-contrast assignments (0.0%) to the control-distant group. In contrast, GMM assigned 63 of 307 control-group participant-contrast assignments (20.5%) and 266 of 1366 post-COVID-19 participant-contrast assignments (19.5%) to the control-distant group. Parameter sensitivity analysis showed high overall assignment agreement for the same BQM/QUBO formulation, but the exact membership of the sparse control-distant subset was more variable. Simulated annealing sensitivity analysis showed overall agreement of 98.3-100.0% and control-distant Jaccard indices of 0.836-1.000 relative to the baseline, whereas a representative QPU sensitivity analysis showed overall agreement of 93.6-100.0% and control-distant Jaccard indices of 0.443-1.000. Frequency band profiles further suggested that QUBO-derived control-distant assignments corresponded to contrast-dependent and exploratory interpretable postural control patterns, particularly in low-frequency postural sway-dominant and mid-low-frequency postural control bands. These findings support the feasibility of objective-driven, control-anchored QUBO-based quantum-assisted clustering for exploratory subgroup discovery in heterogeneous, label-limited biomedical datasets. The proposed framework does not establish diagnostic criteria for long COVID or evidence of quantum speedup but provides a hypothesis-generating approach for interpretable post-COVID-19 neuromotor phenotyping and related medical data analysis applications.

title: Neuromuscular Phenotype in Long COVID Is Associated with Inflammation, Mineral Homeostasis, and Muscle Metabolism.
abstract: Neuromuscular dysfunction in long COVID remains poorly understood, and conventional biomarkers of muscle injury often fail to account for persistent symptoms. This study aimed to compare laboratory biomarkers and neuromuscular outcomes by sex, long COVID duration, and hospitalisation status, and examine the association between neuromuscular outcomes and laboratory biomarkers. In this cross-sectional study, 153 adults with long COVID underwent clinical, body composition, handgrip strength, surface electromyography, and laboratory assessments, including creatine kinase (CK), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), ferritin, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), haemoglobin, sodium, potassium, and calcium. Analyses were stratified by sex, disease duration, and hospitalisation. Significant between-group differences in laboratory and neuromuscular variables were more frequent among men than among women. Hospitalised women had lower muscle mass and higher body fat than non-hospitalised women. Men with longer long COVID duration differed in CK, ferritin, haemoglobin, and vastus lateralis electromyographic activity. Ferritin, calcium, potassium, haemoglobin, and LDH showed consistent, modest multivariate associations with neuromuscular outcomes. The haemoglobin-ferritin-ESR axis correlated most consistently with muscle mass and handgrip strength. These exploratory findings suggest a sex-specific pattern and a consistent haemoglobin-ferritin-ESR axis in long COVID, requiring confirmation in longitudinal studies.

title: Resveratrol for Post-COVID-19 Cognitive Dysfunction: From Molecular Basis to Clinical Translation.
abstract: Post-COVID-19 condition can include persistent cognitive symptoms, commonly described as impaired attention, memory difficulties, slowed processing, and "brain fog." Clinical and translational evidence implicates systemic inflammation, neurovascular dysfunction, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, and altered synaptic or network function; their relative contributions remain uncertain and may differ across patient subgroups. Resveratrol is a polyphenolic compound that modifies inflammatory, redox, metabolic, endothelial, and antiviral pathways in experimental systems. This focused narrative review examines whether those actions provide a mechanistic basis for the use of resveratrol in post-COVID-19 cognitive dysfunction. Evidence was considered according to biological proximity to the intended indication, distinguishing human post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) studies from acute-COVID-19, non-COVID-19 clinical, animal, organoid, and cell-based evidence. The review identifies candidate neurovascular, immune, and metabolic processes, evaluates where resveratrol evidence intersects with those processes, and distinguishes molecular observations from clinical questions that remain to be tested for to define the therapeutic potential of using resveratrol to treat post-COVID-19 cognitive impairment.

title: BRAF wild-type metastatic melanoma arising in a congenital melanocytic nevus initially reported as melanoma in situ, 4 years after negative sentinel lymph node biopsy: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Melanoma arising in a congenital melanocytic nevus is uncommon, and distant relapse years after a thin primary tumor and a negative sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is rarely documented in detail. A 34-year-old man underwent wide local excision of a bleeding congenital hairy nevus of the sacral skin. Histopathology showed melanoma in situ with a thin invasive component (<0.8 mm, nonulcerated, mitotic rate 7/10 high-power fields; recorded as pT1b), and BRAF testing was negative. After referral 2 years later, lymphoscintigraphy-guided SLNB was negative in all eight nodes from both groins and the right axilla. Four years after nodal staging, he presented with back pain, lower-limb weakness, and urinary retention from multiple vertebral metastases with an epidural component at L3, raising concern for cauda equina compression, together with solitary hepatic and pulmonary lesions, a pattern consistent with hematogenous dissemination. Liver and vertebral biopsies confirmed metastatic melanoma. Next-generation sequencing identified no variant of therapeutic or prognostic significance (BRAF wild-type) and a low tumor mutational burden (2.84 mutations/Mb). Palliative radiotherapy to L1-L4 (20 Gy in five fractions) restored ambulation, and denosumab and ipilimumab plus nivolumab, an accepted first-line option for BRAF wild-type melanoma, were started. In a lesion reported as melanoma in situ, the invasive component, not the in-situ component, confers metastatic potential. A negative SLNB does not exclude occult nodal disease or hematogenous dissemination. New skeletal or neurological symptoms in melanoma survivors warrant prompt imaging, even after a prolonged disease-free interval.

title: Absence of Viable Tumor Cells in Macroscopically Pigmented Regional Lymph Nodes after Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy in Duodenal Metastasis of Cutaneous Melanoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Malignant melanoma frequently metastasizes to the gastrointestinal tract, but duodenal metastasis is uncommon, and pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) for this indication is rare, particularly in the era of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Moreover, the histological consequences of ICI therapy within regional lymph nodes draining gastrointestinal metastasis remain poorly documented. A 67-year-old woman with a history of cutaneous malignant melanoma of the thumb developed metachronous ileocecal and duodenal metastases years after the initial resection, during treatment with ICIs. After ICI therapy, she underwent subtotal stomach-preserving PD for the duodenal metastasis. Although preoperative PET/CT showed no regional nodal uptake, the peripancreatic lymph nodes appeared macroscopically black, mimicking nodal metastasis. Histopathological examination revealed fibrosis with CD68-positive, melanin-laden macrophages and no viable tumor cells; Melan-A was negative, and Berlin blue staining excluded hemosiderin, confirming that the pigment was melanin. No viable tumor cells were identified within the regional lymph nodes. The postoperative course was uneventful. Macroscopically pigmented "black nodes" after ICI therapy may not represent viable metastasis, and detailed pathological evaluation is essential to avoid misinterpretation. This case also raises the possibility of an immunological role for tumor-draining lymph nodes during ICI therapy, although the implications for the timing of lymph node dissection remain uncertain.

title: PROTAC technology for sensitizing melanoma to immune checkpoint therapy.
abstract: Melanoma remains one of the most aggressive malignancies, with limited response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) due to primary or acquired resistance. Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) have emerged as a novel therapeutic modality that induces selective degradation of target proteins via the ubiquitin-proteasome system, offering distinct advantages over conventional inhibitors. This review summarizes the design principles and molecular mechanisms of PROTACs, and highlights their emerging role in sensitizing melanoma to immunotherapy. Specifically, PROTACs can restore tumor antigen presentation, reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by targeting regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and tumor-associated macrophages, and suppress key oncogenic signaling pathways. We also discuss combination strategies with PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 blockade, as well as current challenges including poor cell permeability, off-target effects, and acquired resistance. Finally, future perspectives on rational design, tissue-specific delivery systems, and clinical translation are addressed.

title: Gut Microbiome Signatures and Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Response in Gastrointestinal Cancers: Reproducibility and Translational Readiness.
abstract: Gut microbial features have been associated with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) outcomes, but whether these signatures are robust across gastrointestinal (GI) tumor types, treatment regimens, and populations remains uncertain. This critical narrative review assesses human evidence, experimental mechanisms, longitudinal sampling, and the criteria needed for clinical implementation. A gastric cancer cohort showed different response-associated microbial features for immunotherapy alone, chemotherapy alone, and combined treatment. Cross-cancer strain-resolved analyses found that signature transportability was strongly conditional on matching ICI regimens. A large primary liver cancer cohort analyzed 315 patients and 777 serial samples and explored a baseline score derived from on-treatment species selection; later samples were available only in a selected subgroup, complicating interpretation. Experimental studies link selected microbes and metabolites with antitumor immunity, but these mechanistic findings do not establish therapeutic efficacy in humans. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) studies in melanoma demonstrate feasibility yet do not establish benefit in GI malignancies. Stool profiles may not represent mucosal or tumor-adjacent communities in upper GI cancer. No stool microbiome signature is currently validated to select ICI therapy in GI oncology. Meaningful translation requires standardized assays, non-ICI comparators to establish treatment-effect prediction, strict separation of discovery and external validation, prospectively handled missingness, and randomized clinical-utility studies.

title: The Place of Therapeutic Apheresis in Severe Immune-Related Adverse Events: A Scoping Review of Literature.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized the management of patients with cancer. However, they can induce breakdowns in immunologic tolerance, leading to autoimmune diseases, or immune related adverse events (irAEs). These irAEs can sometimes be life threatening, requiring aggressive management, such as immunosuppressant (IS) or even therapeutic apheresis (TA). TA, an extracorporeal circulation technique, may represent a therapeutic option for severe irAEs, reducing their severity and duration by removing ICIs, pathogenic antibodies or inflammatory cytokines, although its role in this situation remains underreported. We made scoping review to better identify the use of TA for managing severe irAEs. From January 2022 to August 2025, three databases were reviewed, for articles mentioning the use of TA in the event of immunotoxicity. Only case reports or case series were retained. A descriptive summary was produced in table forms. Between 2022 and 2025, 162 articles were identified, 34 articles concerning 42 patients treated for severe irAE via TA were included. The underlying cancers were mainly non-small cell lung cancer and melanoma, and 78% of patients were treated with monotherapy anti-PD(L)1. The main indications for TA were neurological (40.6%), overlap manifestations (23.8%), and hepatitis (21.4%), mainly highly severe. TA was most often used in rescue situations, that is, after failure of several lines of IS. Complications of TA were rare. Clinical improvement was reported in most patients, usually within days of TA, with 24% complete resolution, and 45% partial resolution. Despite revolutionizing cancer treatment, ICIs induce severe irAEs, with poorly defined therapeutic options. TA may be a therapeutic option for life threatening irAEs, with data in the literature assuming its effectiveness. However, details on its use remain poorly defined. Further studies are required to emphasize its use as in irAEs.

title: Canine and Feline Melanoma: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prognosis.
abstract: Melanocytic tumors are clinically important in veterinary oncology because their biological behavior, diagnosis, and prognosis vary substantially by species and anatomical site. Canine oral melanoma is characterized by aggressive local invasion and early metastatic spread, whereas melanocytic tumors at other canine sites and in cats show distinct clinicopathologic features that require different diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. This narrative review was based on a structured literature search of PubMed, with searches organized around epidemiology and biological behavior, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. A total of 1887 records were identified after removal of duplicates, and 111 publications were ultimately included following title, abstract, and full-text screening. This review summarizes current evidence on the epidemiology, molecular biology, diagnosis, clinical staging, treatment, and prognosis of canine and feline melanocytic neoplasms. Diagnostic approaches include cytology, histopathology, immunohistochemistry for amelanotic tumors, advanced imaging, sentinel lymph node mapping, and emerging molecular methods. Therapeutic options include surgery, radiation therapy, electrochemotherapy, chemotherapy, therapeutic vaccination, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and targeted therapies. Prognostic factors include tumor location and stage, histologic grade, mitotic count, nuclear atypia, pigmentation, tissue invasion, and molecular biomarkers. Surgical excision remains the cornerstone of treatment for localized disease, but effective systemic therapies for advanced melanoma remain limited. Ongoing molecular characterization, genomic profiling, and comparative oncology research may improve prognostic stratification and support more precise therapeutic strategies.

title: Precision Microbiome Interventions in Oncology: From Predictive Biomarkers to Therapeutic Modulation of Immunotherapy Outcomes.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment of multiple malignancies, yet durable clinical responses remain limited to a subset of patients. Accumulating evidence identifies the gut microbiome as a regulator of antitumour immunity that can influence treatment efficacy and toxicity through microbial metabolism, epithelial barrier integrity, inflammatory signalling, and host immune responses. This review critically evaluates the microbiome as both a predictive biomarker and therapeutic target in precision oncology. It moves beyond descriptive taxonomic associations by assessing emerging functional and mechanistic models that integrate microbial metabolites, ecological interactions, strain-level variation, and host-microbiome communication. Clinical and translational evidence from melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and urothelial carcinoma reveals marked differences in the reproducibility and clinical maturity of reported microbial signatures. Emerging microbiome-targeted strategies, including dietary modulation, faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), live biotherapeutic products (LBPs), and defined microbial consortia, may enhance ICI responsiveness, with responder-derived FMT providing important early clinical proof of concept. However, inter-individual variability, donor-recipient compatibility, microbial engraftment, the lack of standardised analytical approaches, and unresolved safety and regulatory requirements continue to limit clinical translation. Pending prospective validation, reasonable clinical practice is to avoid unnecessary microbiome-disrupting antibiotics, systematically document diet and concomitant medications, evaluate FMT and LBPs within regulated clinical trials, and interpret microbiome profiles alongside established tumour and host biomarkers rather than as stand-alone tests. Current evidence therefore supports a cautious shift towards functional microbiome-guided precision oncology, providing a foundation for personalised strategies to improve cancer immunotherapy outcomes.

title: Reprogramming the Melanoma Tumor Microenvironment: From Cellular Crosstalk to Cellular Immunotherapy.
abstract: Melanoma is the most aggressive and rapidly metastasizing malignant neoplasm of the skin and mucous membranes, arising from melanocytes of neuroectodermal origin. Despite substantial advances in immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapy, a significant proportion of patients develop primary or acquired resistance, which is largely attributable to the complex interactions between tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment (TME). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the cellular and molecular components of the melanoma TME and their contribution to immunosuppression, tumor progression, and therapeutic resistance. The role of keratinocytes as the primary niche-forming cells in the epidermis is examined, including their reprogramming during melanomagenesis and their involvement in drug resistance. Particular attention is given to cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which orchestrate stromal remodeling, promote immune exclusion, and limit the efficacy of immunotherapy. The phenotypic and functional heterogeneity of innate and adaptive immune cells-macrophages, granulocytes, natural killer cells, dendritic cells, T and B lymphocytes-is discussed in the context of their dual role in antitumor immunity and immune escape. A detailed analysis of immune editing mechanisms, including defective antigen recognition, resistance to apoptosis, and the establishment of an immunosuppressive microenvironment, is provided. The review further summarizes the current landscape of cellular immunotherapy for melanoma. Clinically established approaches, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and CAR-T cells, are discussed with reference to completed phase II-III clinical trials, whereas emerging strategies such as CAR-macrophages and dendritic cell vaccines are presented as largely preclinical or early-phase investigational platforms. It is concluded that the melanoma TME functions as a unified immunosuppressive network rather than a collection of individual cell populations. Based on currently available comparative clinical evidence, reprogramming this network through the combination of cellular platforms with immune checkpoint inhibitors, stromal modulators, and macrophage-repolarizing agents, supported by personalized assessment of TME composition, represents a rational and actively investigated therapeutic direction.
