title: Safety and efficacy of dual immune checkpoint inhibition for melanoma brain metastases and its comparison to ICI monotherapy: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Melanoma brain metastases remain a major cause of morbidity and death despite advances in systemic therapy. Dual immune checkpoint inhibition has shown promising intracranial activity, but the overall evidence is heterogeneous and its benefit relative to monotherapy remains clinically important to define. We performed a PRISMA-based systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective and retrospective studies evaluating dual immune checkpoint inhibition in adults with cutaneous or mucosal melanoma brain metastases. PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched from inception to November 5, 2025. Random-effects models were used to pool intracranial progression-free survival, overall survival, intracranial response outcomes, and adverse events. Comparative analyses versus monotherapy were performed when data were available. Twenty-four studies involving 3518 patients were included. In the overall dual ICI cohort, pooled intracranial progression-free survival was 51.9% at 6 months, 44.1% at 12 months, 40.5% at 2 years, and 38.8% at 3 years. Pooled intracranial objective response rate was 42.5%, increasing to 48% in first-line dual ICI recipients. Outcomes were more favorable in asymptomatic patients than in symptomatic patients, with pooled overall survival at 3 years of 52.3% versus 31.5%. Comparative analyses favored dual ICI over monotherapy for overall survival at 6 months, 12 months, and 2 years, while no significant difference was seen at 3 years. Elevated LDH was associated with worse survival, whereas BRAF mutation was not significantly associated with outcome. All-grade treatment-related adverse events occurred in 78% of patients, grade 3 or higher events in 48.2%, and all-grade immune-related adverse events in 65.5%. Across studies reporting adverse events for patients receiving dual and mono ICI, dual ICI therapy was consistently associated with higher rates of treatment-related and immune-related toxicities, which is consistent with the established safety profile of nivolumab plus ipilimumab and highlights the need for close monitoring, and early management of immune-related complications. Dual immune checkpoint inhibition provides meaningful and durable intracranial benefit in melanoma brain metastases, particularly in asymptomatic patients and when used early. Comparative analyses favored dual ICI over monotherapy at 6 months, 12 months, and 2 years. However, the 3-year survival advantage remains uncertain because of limited data and substantial heterogeneity. Symptomatic disease remains a major unmet need, and the potential survival benefit must be balanced against substantial toxicity.

title: Radiotherapy for skin tumors and soft-tissue sarcomas: Current state of the art and recent advances.
abstract: Radiotherapy plays a pivotal role in the management of skin cancers and soft-tissue sarcomas in both curative and adjuvant settings. Over recent years, several clinical trials and international guidelines have refined its indications and identified new strategies that are likely to influence clinical practice. This review provides an updated overview of the role of radiotherapy in basal cell carcinoma, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, cutaneous melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, cutaneous lymphoma, and soft-tissue sarcoma. Recent evidence highlights the potential benefit of consolidation radiotherapy following hedgehog inhibitors in locally advanced basal cell carcinoma, improved outcomes with the combination of cemiplimab and radiotherapy in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, integration of stereotactic radiotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors for melanoma brain metastases, the importance of minimizing the interval between surgery and postoperative radiotherapy in Merkel cell carcinoma, the limitations of ultra-low-dose radiotherapy for indolent cutaneous lymphomas, and the emergence of hypofractionated preoperative radiotherapy schedules for soft-tissue sarcoma. By distinguishing established indications from emerging evidence, this review summarizes the developments most likely to influence contemporary radiation oncology practice and highlights areas where further prospective studies are warranted.

title: NRAS Mutations in Different Melanoma Histotypes: Molecular and Clinical Implications.
abstract: Melanoma is a highly aggressive skin malignancy with increasing incidence and mortality worldwide. Among its key genetic alterations, NRAS mutations occur in approximately 15-25% of melanomas, defining a distinct molecular subset associated with aggressive tumor behavior and poor prognosis. Unlike BRAF mutations, NRAS alterations remain largely undruggable, posing significant therapeutic challenges. This review examines the histotype-specific distribution of NRAS mutations in melanoma and discusses their molecular and clinical implications. Most NRAS mutations involve codon 61 and result in constitutive activation of the MAPK and PI3K signaling pathways, thereby promoting tumorigenesis and disease progression. Although NRAS-mutant melanomas are associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, they also exhibit high immunogenicity, suggesting potential sensitivity to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). To further characterize the molecular landscape of NRAS-mutant melanoma, we analyzed data from the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC), providing insights into the prevalence, distribution, co-mutation patterns, and functional consequences of NRAS alterations across different melanoma histotypes. NRAS mutations represent a major driver of melanoma progression and define a biologically and clinically distinct subset of the disease. Despite encouraging responses to immunotherapy, clinical outcomes remain suboptimal, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic approaches. A deeper understanding of NRAS-driven oncogenesis, histotype-specific mutation patterns, and their impact on therapeutic response is essential for advancing precision medicine and improving outcomes for patients with melanoma.

title: Frequency of Bloodwork in Patients on Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are widely used to treat solid tumours. Prolonged use leads to increased bloodwork to monitor for adverse events (AEs). We explored the safety of decreasing bloodwork frequency while administering an ICI. Data was collected on patients receiving ICIs without chemotherapy for solid tumours from 2015 to 2020 at an academic cancer centre in Canada. Demographics, cancer diagnosis, ICI use, and pre-treatment bloodwork were extracted. The control group comprised all patients with all detected AEs. We modelled a decreased frequency of bloodwork by assuming that those same patients had bloodwork taken only every second or third cycle. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with a missed bloodwork-related AE of grade 2 or higher. Descriptive statistics were used. Among 735 patients, median age was 67, 65% were male, and most had lung cancer (39.6%) or melanoma (38.9%). Most (90.5%) received monotherapy. When neutropenia and lymphopenia were excluded, grade 2+ bloodwork-related AEs occurred in 20.9 to 27.7% of patients prior to cycle 2 of the ICI. When bloodwork is omitted every two or three cycles, respective AE miss rates were as high as 5.2 and 8.3% for thyroid abnormalities, 4.6 and 8.1% for hyperglycemia, and 1.6 and 2% for hepatitis. During the first period of bloodwork omission, overall grade 2+ AE miss rates were 10.4 to 12.4% when bloodwork was done every two cycles, and 17.9 to 23.8% when bloodwork was done every three cycles, varying by cycle duration. Miss rates were lower in later cycles. ICI bloodwork-related grade 2+ AE miss rates exceed 10% when bloodwork is omitted, suggesting that bloodwork should be obtained with each cycle of an ICI administered.

During the first period of bloodwork omission, overall grade 2+ AE miss rates were 10.4 to 12.4% when bloodwork was done every two cycles, and 17.9 to 23.8% when bloodwork was done every three cycles, varying by cycle duration. Miss rates were lower in later cycles.

title: The Psychosocial Burden of the 'Lazarus Effect': A Systematic Review of Survivor Guilt, Identity Shift, and Discontinuation Anxiety in Exceptional Responders to Cancer Immunotherapy.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have transformed oncology by inducing unexpected and sustained remissions in some patients; however, this atypical survival may be accompanied by significant psychosocial and existential challenges. The objective was to synthesize the available scientific evidence on the psychosocial burden of the 'Lazarus Effect', characterized by survivor guilt, identity shift, and discontinuation anxiety. A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA2020 guidelines, based on a preregistered protocol on the OSF. Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and APA PsycINFO using PICOS-based eligibility criteria. Seven primary empirical studies were included, and their methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the MMAT 2018. Survivor guilt stems interpersonally from peer deaths and intrapersonally from perceived autonomy loss. Identity shift involves transitioning into an "existential limbo," re-establishing self-identity while off active treatment. Discontinuation anxiety relates to recurrence fears, absence of curative biomarkers, and uncertainty regarding treatment duration. Interactively, these dimensions drive broader psychosocial burden, including social isolation, "scanxiety," and a discrepancy between physical recovery and emotional vulnerability. Current evidence-limited to seven heterogeneous studies concentrated in high-income settings-indicates exceptional responses to immunotherapy may involve nuanced psychosocial challenges. Given small sample sizes, melanoma overrepresentation, potential report retrieval bias, and non-standardized assessment tools, findings require cautious interpretation. They offer an exploratory foundation for future research rather than definitive clinical conclusions, supporting preliminary psycho-oncological screening during treatment transitions.

title: Nanotechnology-Enabled Immunotherapy for Colorectal Cancer: Overcoming the "Cold" Tumor Microenvironment in Microsatellite-Stable Disease.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the management of mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the ~95% of patients with mismatch repair-proficient/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) disease derive little benefit owing to an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME), poor T-cell infiltration, myeloid dominance, TGF-β-enriched stroma, and the systemically immunosuppressive milieu imposed by hepatic metastases. Clinically tested combinations-multikinase inhibitor plus anti-PD-1, Fc-enhanced dual checkpoint blockade, chemotherapy- or antiangiogenic-ICI regimens-have so far produced modest, largely non-durable response rates that are further attenuated in liver-metastatic disease, motivating approaches that pharmacologically remodel the TME rather than only release checkpoint restraint. To provide an evidence-stratified synthesis of nanotechnology-enabled immunotherapy in CRC that explicitly separates (a) clinically established evidence, (b) strategies under early-phase clinical investigation, and (c) concepts that remain preclinical or are extrapolated from other tumor types, and to derive from this appraisal a biomarker-enriched translational research agenda. Narrative, integrative (non-systematic) review. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ASCO/ESMO/AACR proceedings were searched from January 2010 through April 2026. Each strategy was appraised according to the highest available level of evidence, the tumor type and model system in which the evidence was generated, and its demonstrated CRC specificity. In current clinical practice, nanomedicine in CRC is essentially limited to nanoparticle-formulated cytotoxics exploited for pharmacokinetic advantage (e.g. liposomal irinotecan), whereas nano-enabled immunotherapy is confined to a small number of early-phase trials-most notably lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccines in ctDNA-positive resected CRC and hafnium-oxide nanoparticle radioenhancers-none of which has yet demonstrated a progression-free or overall survival benefit in MSS CRC. Against this background we critically appraise six classes of strategy: (i) LNP-based mRNA neoantigen vaccines; (ii) polymeric and inorganic nanocarriers for STING and TLR agonists; (iii) tumor-associated macrophage-repolarizing nanoparticles; (iv) nano-radiosensitizers and photothermal/photodynamic platforms priming immunogenic cell death; (v) nano-formulated checkpoint inhibitor delivery; and (vi) locoregional nano-strategies directed at hepatic metastasis-specific immunosuppression. For categories (ii)-(vi) the supporting evidence is predominantly murine (largely subcutaneous CT26/MC38 models) or extrapolated from immunologically "hot" tumors such as melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer, in which both the underlying biology and the checkpoint backbone differ materially from MSS CRC. Recurrent translational barriers include low, highly heterogeneous nanoparticle accumulation in human tumors, dense TGF-β-rich stroma and elevated interstitial pressure, mononuclear phagocyte system clearance, liver-metastasis-specific tolerance that subcutaneous models do not reproduce, unresolved manufacturing/CMC and regulatory pathways, and the absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers of intratumoral immune conversion. Nanotechnology offers a mechanistically coherent and experimentally testable-but at present clinically unproven-set of strategies for converting "cold" MSS CRC into immune-responsive disease. We therefore position nano-enabled immunotherapy as a research priority rather than an imminent standard of care, and argue that its clinical value can only be established through biomarker-enriched, paired-biopsy early-phase trials with pharmacodynamic endpoints of immune conversion and prospective stratification by metastatic site (particularly hepatic involvement) and consensus molecular subtype. This is a narrative rather than systematic review; it is therefore subject to selection and publication bias, and much of the evidence synthesized is preclinical and of limited direct translational certainty.

title: Predictors of Immediate Therapeutic Lymph Node Dissection Instead of Index Lymph Node After Neoadjuvant Checkpoint Inhibitors: Lessons Learned from the PRADO Trial.
abstract: In the PRADO trial, a multicenter phase II study, patients with macroscopic stage III melanoma received neoadjuvant ipilimumab and nivolumab followed by resection of the marked index lymph node (ILN). Patients without a major pathological response (MPR) underwent therapeutic lymph node dissection (TLND), although some required TLND for other indications. We investigated whether baseline clinicopathological and preoperative response parameters identify patients benefiting from immediate TLND rather than ILN resection followed by potential secondary TLND. Data were collected from PRADO case report forms. Group differences were assessed using Fisher's exact, chi-square, or Mann-Whitney U tests. Logistic regression identified predictors of TLND, with a subgroup analysis restricted to pathology-positive TLND. Model performance was assessed using (cross-validated) area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Ninety-nine patients were included; 36 underwent TLND: 20 (56%) with pathological nonresponse, eight (22%) with partial response, and eight (22%) for other indications (nodal recurrence after MPR, n = 3; extranodal extension, n = 1; suspicious nodes on imaging, n = 2; or infeasible ILN resection due to immune-related adverse events, n = 2). Age < 40 years (odds ratio 7.91, 95% confidence interval 1.35-46.30; P = 0.022) and radiographic increase in tumor size (odds ratio 1.15; 95% confidence interval 1.07-1.24; P < 0.001) were associated with TLND. Age younger than 40 years and unfavorable radiological response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy were associated with TLND, suggesting these parameters may identify patients at risk of residual nodal disease and subsequent need for TLND.

title: A fibril-selective single-domain antibody targets pathogenic amyloid-β assemblies and protects human neurons.
abstract: Alzheimer disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-β deposition that contributes to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Although anti-amyloid-β antibodies reduce plaque burden, their use requires monitoring for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. Here, phage display against immobilized Aβ40 fibrils representing a patient-relevant polymorph identified J8, a fibril-selective, Fc-free single-domain antibody. J8 bound fibrils with high apparent affinity, showed no detectable binding to monomeric Aβ40, decorated fibril surfaces, and recognized plaque-associated amyloid in Alzheimer disease brain tissue. During concurrent fibril exposure, J8 reduced apoptotic signaling in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and forebrain organoids. Single-nucleus profiling of pooled organoids identified fibril-associated stress programs and opposite-direction expression patterns in the FibJ8 condition; fibril-associated changes showed the strongest directional concordance with advanced disease pathology. These findings identify J8 as a fibril-selective candidate and support organoid-based evaluation of anti-amyloid reagents as a fit-for-purpose preclinical tool.

title: Current capacity of Portuguese specialized dementia centers in the era of anti-amyloid antibodies.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains a major cause of cognitive decline and societal burden. The recent approval of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) lecanemab and donanemab represents a paradigm shift in AD treatment. We assessed the preparedness of Portuguese centers to implement DMTs. A nationwide survey-based cross-sectional service-capacity study targeted memory clinics, focusing primarily on National Health System (NHS) centers. Data were collected on clinical capacity, diagnostic access, treatment capability, and research activity. Among 51 responding units, 20 had organized memory clinics (17 in the NHS), covering 60.7% of the population. In 2024, these centers conducted 21,721 consultations, representing expert care for <10% of the total AD patients estimated to exist in Portugal. Bottlenecks included long waiting times and limited biomarker access (26.2% underwent cerebrospinal fluid or amyloid positron emission tomography). Nationwide, from experts' estimates, 701 patients could currently start treatment. Portugal's current NHS capacity appears insufficient for broad DMT implementation, requiring major investment in diagnostics, training, infrastructure, and research to ensure equitable and effective treatment access.

title: Real-Time Single Molecule Imaging Reveals Pathway-Selective Action of Aducanumab on Amyloid-β Aggregation.
abstract: Aducanumab is an anti-amyloid-β (Aβ) antibody that binds aggregated Aβ species and has been reported to inhibit secondary nucleation on fibril surfaces. However, how antibody binding influences aggregate dynamics at the molecular level remains incompletely understood. Here, we used high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM) to directly visualize the interactions between aducanumab and Aβ42 aggregates in real time at single-molecule resolution. Aducanumab extensively decorated oligomers, protofibrils, and fibrils, with fibril binding depending on local surface structure. Consistent with its reported inhibition of secondary nucleation, bulk thioflavin T assays showed slowed aggregation. Nevertheless, in the continued presence of the antibody, protofibril formation proceeded─a pathway distinct from secondary nucleation. These observations reveal a pathway-selective mode of action: extensive surface binding and the suppression of secondary nucleation do not extend to protofibril formation, which proceeds in the continued presence of the antibody.

title: Spectrum of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities associated with aducanumab treatment: a case series report.
abstract: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) observed on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are known adverse events associated with beta-amyloid plaque-lowering monoclonal antibodies. A spectrum of radiographic and clinical presentations of ARIA have been observed. ARIA-E refer to vasogenic edema in the brain parenchyma and/or leptomeningeal/subpial sulcal effusion; ARIA-H refer to hemosiderin deposits including cerebral microhemorrhage and localized superficial siderosis. With clinical availability of anti-amyloid therapies for treatment of early clinical stage Alzheimer's disease, there is an important need for better awareness of ARIA and education among a diversity of clinicians and practice settings. To illustrate the wide spectrum of ARIA, we present the clinical history, course, and MRI findings as well as summarize learnings and implications of 10 ARIA-E cases from the aducanumab phase 3 clinical trials EMERGE and ENGAGE (ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers NCT02484547 and NCT02477800). Monitoring and management of ARIA, including criteria and timing of MRI, and drug dosing actions were defined per protocol and based upon radiographic severity and clinical symptoms associated with ARIA. ARIA were detected by MRI performed at pre-specified intervals or in response to symptoms or for safety follow-up reasons. The majority of ARIA-E events were asymptomatic. Most ARIA-E events occurred within the first 8 aducanumab doses and generally resolved within 3-4 months whether dosing was continued (i.e. when ARIA-E was asymptomatic and of mild radiographic severity) or whether dosing was suspended or discontinued. Occasionally, ARIA-E were recurrent. ARIA-H (microhemorrhages and superficial siderosis) most commonly occurred concurrently with ARIA-E. However, ARIA-H without ARIA-E, termed isolated ARIA-H, occurred at a similar frequency in aducanumab- and placebo-treated groups. 10% of participants with ARIA in the 10 mg/kg group had accompanying symptoms. When present, symptoms of ARIA most frequently included headache, nausea, fatigue, dizziness, confusional state, and visual disturbance. Serious symptoms associated with ARIA were uncommon (occurring in 0.3% of the participants treated with the 10 mg/kg dose regimen). These illustrative cases provide learnings into the nature and factors associated with ARIA that can increase knowledge for clinicians and trialists regarding the varied radiographic and clinical presentations and evolution of ARIA. Clinical Trials NCT02484547, registered June 18, 2015, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02484547 . Clinical Trials NCT02477800, registered June 18, 2015, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02477800 .

title: Neuromodulatory interventions for Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent an escalating global public health challenge with major socioeconomic consequences. Although anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies have introduced disease-modifying treatment options for early symptomatic AD, their benefits remain modest and must be balanced against cost, monitoring burden, and safety risks. Neuromodulatory interventions have therefore emerged as promising investigational strategies that may complement existing therapeutic approaches. This narrative review evaluates current clinical and neurophysiological evidence for seven major neuromodulation approaches: 40 Hz gamma rhythm sensory stimulation, also known as gamma entrainment using sensory stimulation (GENUS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), focused ultrasound (FUS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM). Integrating clinical findings with mechanistic evidence, we examine synaptic plasticity, neuroinflammation, glymphatic clearance, oscillatory entrainment, and cholinergic signaling as candidate therapeutic mechanisms. A comparative matrix summarizes target specificity, invasiveness, stimulation parameters, and translational status. Finally, we discuss key barriers, including biological heterogeneity, protocol standardization, durability of benefit, caregiver burden, and the uncertain implications of continuous network stimulation for future personalized and closed-loop interventions.

title: Ethical challenges in the clinical translation of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies for Alzheimer's disease: a scoping review.
abstract: The development and evaluation of anti-amyloid beta monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease have been accompanied by extensive ethical debate spanning clinical trials, regulatory processes, prescribing practices, and healthcare delivery. This scoping review examined literature published between 2006 and 2026 to identify and clarify the landscape of ethical considerations surrounding the implementation, prescribing, and delivery of anti-amyloid mAbs across both research and clinical settings. We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Ovid EBM Reviews (including CENTRAL and CDSR) from 2006 to March 2026 using a structured search strategy. Eligible publications focused on ethical issues associated with the clinical translation of anti-amyloid mAbs. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full-text articles, with duplicate extraction performed on an initial subset of publications. The review was conducted using JBI guidance and reported according to PRISMA-ScR. We identified 84 publications from 23 countries published between 2014 and 2026, including 12 original research studies, 1 systematic review, and 71 commentaries, narrative reviews, legal analyses, or practice guidelines. Analysis identified 32 subthemes, which were synthesized into 7 overarching themes: (1) beneficence and nonmaleficence, (2) respect for persons, (3) equity and accessibility, (4) evidence and trial integrity, (5) governance and stewardship, (6) relational and social impacts, and (7) health system readiness and sustainability. Among the 32 subthemes, uncertain clinical benefit and risk of harm (both within the beneficence and nonmaleficence theme) were discussed most frequently within the literature, each appearing in 61 publications. The biomedical literature documents a broad range of ethical considerations relating to anti-amyloid mAbs. Despite this growing literature, it is primarily based on commentary, with few empirical studies, and even fewer incorporating the perspectives of patients, families, and clinicians. Doing so may add further context and nuance to ethical discussion about mAbs in the years ahead.

Despite this growing literature, it is primarily based on commentary, with few empirical studies, and even fewer incorporating the perspectives of patients, families, and clinicians. Doing so may add further context and nuance to ethical discussion about mAbs in the years ahead.

title: Amyloid-β Immunotherapy in Alzheimer's Disease: Challenges and Opportunities.
abstract: Passive anti-amyloid-β immunotherapy has shifted from repeated phase 3 failure to reproducible, although modest, clinical slowing in biomarker-defined early Alzheimer's disease. We review lessons from first-generation antibodies, including inadequate target engagement, late-stage enrollment, and limited outcome sensitivity. We then compare second-generation agents (i.e., aducanumab, lecanemab, and donanemab) highlighting amyloid-β species selectivity, plaque clearance kinetics, and durability, and we discuss emerging delivery innovations. Safety is dominated by amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, likely reflecting cerebrovascular amyloid vulnerability, and requires timely baseline magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) screening; APOE-informed counseling; and standardized, front-loaded MRI surveillance with symptom-triggered evaluation. We summarize prevention trials in autosomal dominant and sporadic preclinical populations and consider prospects for combination or sequential regimens with tau-targeting therapies. Finally, we focus on biomarker-guided implementation: blood-based prescreening, confirmation pathways, monitoring of biological response, and treat-to-clear or stopping concepts, alongside unresolved issues of health-system readiness, equity, and budget impact. Registry-enabled learning is emphasized to generate real-world safety and effectiveness evidence.

title: Updated Italian intersocietal recommendations for the appropriate use of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: With the European authorisation of lecanemab and donanemab, Italy is entering the era of disease-modifying therapy for early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. The Italian Expert Panel on Alzheimer (EPA), which convened 21 scientific societies and patient associations and published a first set of intersocietal recommendations in 2025, was reconvened in Rome on 24 January 2026 (EPA2) to address the operational gaps that had emerged during the implementation of that document. A modified Delphi process was adopted to formalise consensus on the most controversial points raised during the meeting. Thirty-six declarative statements covering five domains, namely the tiered organisation of the Centres for Cognitive Disorders and Dementia (CDCD), clinical staging and treatment monitoring, eligibility considerations in mild cognitive impairment and atypical phenotypes, composition of the multidisciplinary team, and magnetic resonance imaging thresholds, ARIA monitoring and biomarker pathway, were submitted to a multidisciplinary panel of experts. Strong agreement was reached on the large majority of statements, providing quantitative endorsement for a competence-based reorganisation of the CDCD network, the harmonised use of the Clinical Dementia Rating, an explicit composition of the multidisciplinary team, trial-aligned magnetic resonance imaging eligibility criteria with a move towards risk-adapted ARIA monitoring, and a stepwise biomarker pathway integrating plasma assays, cerebrospinal fluid analysis on automated platforms and amyloid positron emission tomography. The document provides Italian regional and national health systems, prescribing centres and reimbursing authorities with a quantitative blueprint for the appropriate, equitable and sustainable use of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies in clinical practice.

title: Symptomatic lobar intracerebral hemorrhage during extended lecanemab treatment: A case report.
abstract: Lecanemab is an anti-amyloid-β protofibril antibody that slows cognitive decline in early Alzheimer's disease. Although amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) occur predominantly early in treatment, reports of hemorrhagic events during extended treatment beyond 18 months remain limited. A 77-year-old woman completed a standard 1.5-year lecanemab regimen without ARIA on surveillance MRIs. The day after her 42nd infusion, she acutely developed confusion and incomprehensible speech. MRI revealed a 2.5-cm left parietal subcortical hemorrhage. This case highlights that symptomatic lobar hemorrhage may occur even during extended lecanemab therapy, underscoring the importance of continued safety monitoring during extended treatment.

title: Steroid-responsive inflammatory leptomeningeal encephalitis temporally associated with lecanemab therapy: A case report.
abstract: Lecanemab is an anti-amyloid-β monoclonal antibody used for the treatment of early Alzheimer's disease. Herein, we report a 46-year-old woman who developed headache, fever, disorientation, and impaired consciousness 10 months after starting lecanemab. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a small focal subcortical fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense lesion and bilateral occipital leptomeningeal enhancement without detectable hemorrhagic findings on T2*-weighted gradient-recalled echo imaging. Cerebrospinal fluid revealed mononuclear pleocytosis and markedly elevated interleukin-6. Infectious studies and neuronal surface antibodies were negative. High-dose corticosteroid therapy led to rapid clinical improvement. These findings support a diagnosis of steroid-responsive inflammatory leptomeningeal encephalitis temporally associated with lecanemab.

title: Targeting the P2X7 receptor in Alzheimer's disease: mechanistic insights and emerging therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide and is characterized by progressive cognitive decline, amyloid-β deposition, tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and neuronal loss. Current therapies provide only limited symptomatic benefit, and although anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies have demonstrated disease-modifying potential in selected patients, additional disease-modifying targets are still needed. The purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R), an ATP-gated ion channel predominantly expressed on microglia and astrocytes, has emerged as a key regulator of neuroinflammatory signalling and AD progression. This narrative review summarizes and critically discusses recent preclinical, translational, and clinical evidence published through 2026. Evidence from cellular and animal models, post-mortem human brain analyses, positron emission tomography (PET) imaging studies, and pharmacological investigations was evaluated to assess the role of P2X7R in AD pathogenesis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that extracellular ATP-mediated activation of P2X7R promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β and interleukin-18, thereby sustaining chronic neuroinflammation. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of P2X7R reduced amyloid plaque burden, attenuated tau hyperphosphorylation, improved synaptic function, and ameliorated cognitive deficits in experimental AD models. Human studies further revealed elevated P2X7R expression and increased neuroinflammatory activity associated with AD pathology. Emerging therapeutic approaches include selective P2X7R antagonists, natural-product modulators, RNA-based interventions, nanotechnology-assisted drug delivery systems, and combination therapies targeting multiple pathogenic pathways. P2X7R represents a promising candidate target for disease-modifying therapeutic strategies in AD, based on convergent in vitro, animal-model, human post-mortem, and imaging/biomarker evidence linking ATP-mediated danger signalling to neuroinflammation, amyloid and tau pathology, and neurodegeneration. However, its clinical efficacy in AD remains to be established, as no clinical trial data for P2X7R-targeted therapies in this disease are yet available. Future clinical translation will require improved CNS-penetrant antagonists, enhanced receptor selectivity, biomarker-guided patient stratification, and precision medicine approaches.

title: Intracranial metastasis as a mimic of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities.
abstract: This report describes a 79-year-old woman with biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer's disease who developed progressive vasogenic edema initially interpreted as amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) with edema during lecanemab therapy, but was ultimately found to have multifocal intracranial metastases from recurrent papillary thyroid carcinoma. The serial neuroimaging highlights the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing ARIA from alternative causes of vasogenic edema in the era of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody treatment. In addition, this case raises an important and underexplored question regarding whether anti-amyloid therapies may alter blood-brain barrier integrity in a manner that could influence metastatic spread in susceptible patients.

title: Estimating the eligible population for amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibody therapy in memory clinics: Application to lecanemab in France.
abstract: Lecanemab was the first amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibody approved by the European Commission for treating patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease (AD). While this marketing authorization led to heterogeneous situations across European countries, France declined reimbursement, citing limited clinical benefit and concerns about the healthcare system's capacity to implement this new care pathway. This capacity depends directly on the number of eligible patients, yet robust estimates remain limited and highly variable across studies. Our objective was therefore to estimate the population eligible for lecanemab in France. Using transportability methods based on inverse odds of selection weighting, we articulated the nationwide consultation data from the French National Alzheimer Database (BNA) with the deeply phenotyped MEMENTO clinical cohort. Eligibility for lecanemab followed the French appropriate use recommendations: 1) clinical eligibility (age 50-90 years, MCI with common AD phenotype or mild AD dementia, MMSE ≥22), 2) biological eligibility (amyloid confirmation determined sequentially using plasma p-tau217, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers and amyloid-PET), 3) absence of contraindications (APOEε4 homozygosity, anticoagulant use, MRI risk markers for ARIA). Among patients consulting French memory clinics, 19.5% met clinical eligibility criteria. Of these, 73.0% (95%CI: 67.6-77.9) were amyloid-positive, and 49.7% (95%CI: 44.0-55.5) remained eligible after applying safety criteria. Overall, 9.7% (95%CI: 8.6-10.8) of patients consulting memory clinics were estimated to be eligible for lecanemab, representing approximately 18,200 individuals nationally (annual average, 2022-2024). These results inform healthcare planning for disease-modifying therapy implementation in France and comparable countries.

title: Transitioning from Clinical Trial to Clinical Practice for Long-Term Lecanemab Treatment in Early Alzheimer's Disease: Perspectives from a Cohort Study from the Alzheimer's Research and Treatment Center.
abstract: Lecanemab, an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody, significantly reduces amyloid markers and slows clinical decline in early Alzheimer's disease (AD) clinical trials. We assessed our single-center experience with lecanemab, including evaluating efficacy and safety data as well as patient-reported outcomes of individuals from our single center treated with intravenous or subcutaneous lecanemab. We conducted a single-center, nested cohort study of early AD subjects on lecanemab (intravenous or subcutaneous) at our center. Participants had been initiated on lecanemab therapy as part of lecanemab Study 201 or Clarity AD, and then continued lecanemab treatment in our center. Data collection included patient demographic characteristics, efficacy (eg, CDR-SB), safety, and patient-reported outcomes from surveys. At our center, 136 people were randomized to receive either lecanemab or placebo in either lecanemab Study 201 (lecanemab:53; placebo:16) or Clarity AD (lecanemab:37; placebo:30). Patients receiving lecanemab were more likely to have higher rates of stable or improved disease across efficacy assessments relative to placebo. There were no new long-term safety signals, and the most common adverse events for lecanemab patients were infusion-related reactions (36.2%), ARIA-H (25.9%), and ARIA-E (13.8%). Survey responses demonstrated high satisfaction with the subcutaneous lecanemab administration, including with treatment satisfaction (97%) and convenience (97%). All patients preferred subcutaneous over IV dosing, citing quickness, ease, and comfort. Our single-center experience with long-term lecanemab treatment was similar to that observed in clinical trials. The subcutaneous lecanemab formulation was highly preferred by patients and care partners, with feedback highlighting reduced treatment burden and strong acceptability.

title: Progressive Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities After Discontinuation of Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer Disease in an APOE ε2/ε4 Carrier.
abstract: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) are the most relevant adverse events associated with anti-amyloid therapies in Alzheimer's disease. We report a case of progressive ARIA after discontinuation of lecanemab in a patient with early-onset Alzheimer's disease carrying the rare APOE ε2/ε4 genotype. After two infusions, mild ARIA-edema (ARIA-E) and ARIA-hemorrhage (ARIA-H) were detected on routine MRI, prompting treatment interruption. Despite partial radiologic regression, follow-up MRI 8 weeks after discontinuation demonstrated marked progression with multifocal ARIA-H displaying as superficial siderosis, while the patient remained clinically asymptomatic. Corticosteroid treatment was initiated and lecanemab permanently discontinued. This case highlights that severe ARIA may progress beyond active treatment exposure and emphasizes the importance of continued MRI surveillance even after therapy cessation. Furthermore, the APOE ε2/ε4 genotype may represent a distinct risk factor for cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related vascular fragility and hemorrhagic ARIA.

title: Enhanced acute absorption of vitamin D3 with a liposomal formulation (Cymbiotika) compared to a standard formulation in healthy adults: a randomized double-blind crossover study.
abstract: Vitamin D deficiency is increasingly prevalent and linked to impaired health and disease. While vitamin D3 supplementation is effective, variability in absorption can influence bioavailability and clinical responses, with formulation characteristics potentially contributing to this variability. The aim of this randomized, double-blind, crossover absorption study was to compare the absorption of a liposomal vitamin D3 formulation (Cymbiotika) with that of a conventional non-liposomal vitamin D3 formulation. Healthy adult participants received a single oral dose of both formulations in random order separated by a 2-week washout period. Blood samples were collected over 48 h post-dose and plasma cholecalciferol concentrations quantified. Absorption parameters including area under the concentration-time curve (AUC), maximum plasma concentration (Cmax), and time to peak concentration (Tmax) were calculated following baseline correction. Twelve participants completed the study (mean age 34.3 ± 9.7 years; BMI 24.8 ± 2.7 kg/m2). The liposomal formulation showed greater systemic absorption compared with the comparator formulation, with a 1.9-fold higher AUC (199 vs. 106 ng·h/mL). Peak concentration was also higher for the liposomal formulation (8.4 vs. 6.0 ng/mL). Circulating cholecalciferol concentrations remained elevated above baseline at 48 h in the liposomal formulation but returned to baseline in the comparator formulation. These findings suggest that the Cymbiotika formulation may enhance the acute absorption of orally administered vitamin D3. Whether this enhanced acute absorption translates into improved long-term vitamin D status requires investigation in longer-term supplementation studies. https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN39055102, identifier (ISRCTN39055102).

title: Comparative Effectiveness of Nutritional Strategies for Sarcopenia-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
abstract: This study compared the relative effects of distinct nutritional strategies on muscle mass, muscle strength, and physical performance in older adults with sarcopenia or at high risk of sarcopenia. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and CNKI were systematically searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Random-effects pairwise meta-analysis and network meta-analysis (NMA) were performed. The surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) was used to summarize relative rankings, and CINeMA was applied to assess the certainty of evidence. Twenty RCTs involving 2160 participants were included, forming 17 network nodes. Nutritional interventions collectively improved appendicular skeletal muscle mass index (ASMI), grip strength, and gait speed, whereas the pooled effect on the five-times sit-to-stand test (5STS) was not statistically significant. In the NMA, whey protein + vitamin D + leucine improved ASMI (SMD = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.06 to 0.52) and grip strength (SMD = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.13 to 1.50), and it reduced 5STS completion time (SMD = -1.41, 95% CI: -2.63 to -0.18). Omega-3 fatty acids + leucine + Lactobacillus paracasei PS23 improved ASMI (SMD = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.10 to 1.25) and grip strength (SMD = 1.84, 95% CI: 0.39 to 3.28), although this node was supported by a single RCT. Leucine + vitamin D + medium-chain triglycerides improved gait speed (SMD = 1.28, 95% CI: 0.13 to 2.43), although this node was also supported by a single RCT. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the magnitude and precision of some formulation-specific estimates varied with the exclusion of individual trials or restriction to participants with confirmed sarcopenia. The certainty of evidence for the principal comparisons ranged from low to very low. Nutritional supplementation showed overall benefits for ASMI, grip strength, and gait speed, while formulation-specific effects varied across outcomes. Whey protein + vitamin D + leucine showed favorable effects across several outcomes, whereas omega-3 fatty acids + leucine + Lactobacillus paracasei PS23 and leucine + vitamin D + medium-chain triglycerides showed additional formulation-specific signals based on single-study nodes. Given the sparse network and very low certainty of evidence for the principal comparisons, these findings should be regarded as candidate signals rather than evidence of a definitive treatment hierarchy.

title: An Exploratory Randomized Clinical Trial to Assess the Effects of Vitamin D and Leucine-Enriched Whey Protein Supplementation on Inflammaging and Gut Eubacterial Biomass in Cardiac Rehabilitation Patients.
abstract: Whey protein (WP) supplementation could affect low-grade inflammation (inflammaging) and gut microbiome dysbiosis, both of which play key roles in non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Twenty-seven cardiac rehabilitation patients were randomly allocated to two groups: the case group (CA) (n = 14) received 80 g/die vitamin D and leucine-enriched WP supplement, combined with a standard hospital diet, while the control group (CO, n = 13) received the standard hospital diet alone. Blood and stool samples were collected at baseline (T0) and after two weeks (T1). At T1, serum levels of interleukin 6 (IL-6) and C-reactive protein (CRP) significantly decreased in the CA group. Ferritin levels significantly decreased within both groups and between the two groups. No significant differences were observed for IL-1β, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), or IL-10. A clear difference in the bacterial intestinal microbiome composition between the case group at T1 (CAT1) and at T0 (CAT0), and control group at T0 (COT0) and at T1 (COT1), was observed. The eubacterial rpoB copy number, which was quantified by qPCR, significantly increased between CAT0 and CAT1, in contrast to the Lactobacillus spp. rpoB copy number. Our exploratory results showed that vitamin D and leucine-enriched WP supplementation could have a potential effect on chronic inflammation and gut microbiota composition in cardiac rehabilitation patients.

title: Combined TP53 Codon 72 Genotype and p53 Expression in Association with Vitamin D Benefit in Digestive Tract Cancer: A Post-Hoc Study of the AMATERASU Trial.
abstract: Accumulating evidence suggests that vitamin D may influence cancer prognosis. We aimed to explore whether the TP53 codon 72 polymorphism (p.Pro72Arg; rs1042522) may be associated with differential effects of vitamin D supplementation on digestive tract cancer prognosis. This post hoc analysis of the AMATERASU randomized controlled trial included patients in whom both germline TP53 codon 72 genotype and p53 immunohistochemistry (IHC) assessment were available. Patients were stratified according to TP53 codon 72 genotype and p53 IHC expression. The association between vitamin D supplementation and relapse-free survival (RFS) was evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression models within each subgroup. A total of 333 participants (79.9%) out of 417 in the AMATERASU trial were included in the analysis. RFS was comparable between the vitamin D and placebo groups across the TP53 codon 72 genotype subgroups. The vitamin D group was significantly associated with more favorable RFS compared with the placebo group in patients with both the Arg/Arg genotype and high p53 IHC expression (HR, 0.32; 95% CI, 0.12-0.87; p = 0.03). However, with a fragility index of 2 and a non-significant three-way interaction among vitamin D supplementation, p53 IHC expression, and the Arg/Arg genotype (p for interaction = 0.09), these findings remain fragile despite reaching statistical significance, warranting careful interpretation. Vitamin D supplementation was associated with more favorable RFS among patients with digestive tract cancer who had both the Arg/Arg genotype and high p53 IHC expression. These exploratory findings warrant further investigation in prospective studies.

title: Comparison of the efficacy of daily versus weekly vitamin D supplementation on GOLD classification in COPD patients with vitamin D deficiency: An open-label randomized clinical trial.
abstract: BackgroundChronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), characterized by irreversible airflow limitation, markedly reduces expiratory airflow. COPD patients commonly suffer from vitamin D deficiency, which is strongly associated with reduced forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC).AimThis study compared the effects of weekly versus daily vitamin D supplementation on lung function in COPD patients with low baseline vitamin D levels.MethodsIn this open-label randomized clinical trial, 49 patients with COPD and baseline serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels below 30 ng/mL were allocated to receive either daily 4000 IU or weekly 50,000 IU vitamin D3, in addition to standard COPD treatment, for 12 weeks.SummaryAfter the intervention, serum vitamin D levels increased in both supplementation groups, while lung-function measures also increased from baseline. Although the weekly group showed numerically higher post-intervention FEV1 and FEV1 percentage values, the between-group differences were not statistically significant after adjustment for baseline age (p = 0.079 for absolute FEV1; p = 0.981 for FEV1 percentage). We observed a significant association between post-intervention vitamin D levels and post-intervention FEV1 (R2 = 0.42, p < 0.001). These findings do not demonstrate superiority of the weekly regimen over the daily regimen, and larger randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether clinically meaningful differences exist between dosing schedules.

title: Iron Status During Early and Late Pregnancy in a Swedish Multiethnic Population.
abstract: While ethnic differences in maternal iron deficiency (ID) have been documented in other high-resource settings, such differences in Sweden remain unknown. This study assessed iron status and the prevalence of ID and anemia in pregnant women from different countries of birth in Sweden. This secondary analysis included women enrolled in the randomized controlled Pregnancy and Vitamin D Intervention study (2020-2024;). Blood samples were collected in Trimesters 1 (T1) and 3 (T3), and additional data were obtained from questionnaires and medical records. Women were categorized by region of birth: Europe, Asia, and Africa. Anemia was defined as hemoglobin (Hb) < 110 g/L, and ID was defined using two serum ferritin (SF) thresholds: < 15 and < 30 μg/L. A total of 128 women (median age 29.8 years) were included in TI, and 89 had blood samples at both T1 and T3. In those with data in both T1 and T3 (n = 89), median SF, serum iron, and Hb were significantly lower in T3 compared with T1 (all p p p n = 128) from Asia and Africa more often had transferrin receptor concentrations > 4.4 mg/L than women from Europe (p = 0.02) but tended only to have a higher prevalence of SF p = 0.06). Self-reported use of iron supplementation (n = 89) increased from early to late pregnancy. According to medical records, 16% of women had been prescribed iron supplements during gestational weeks 6-12 and 85% by Week 32. ID was common and increased throughout pregnancy in this population in a high-resource country. No statistically significant differences were observed by region of birth. Despite prescribed iron supplements, nearly one-quarter were anemic in late pregnancy. This may reflect timing of treatment initiation, adherence, supplement dose, iron absorption, or other unknown contributors, highlighting the need to optimize iron status management during pregnancy. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05329428.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Upacicalcet in Hemodialysis Patients with Secondary Hyperparathyroidism: Two Randomized Clinical Trials.
abstract: These 2 phase 3 trials assessed upacicalcet, an intravenous calcimimetic, in hemodialysis patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism. ≥30% reduction in intact parathyroid hormone levels occurred in 42% (Parathyroid Hormone [PTH] Attenuation Trial in Hemodialysis-1) and 44% (Parathyroid Hormone [PTH] Attenuation Trial in Hemodialysis-2) with upacicalcet versus 17% and 17%, respectively, with placebo (strata-adjusted; both P < 0.001). Asymptomatic hypocalcemia was more frequent with upacicalcet, and symptomatic hypocalcemia was infrequent; gastrointestinal events were similar to placebo. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a common complication in patients with CKD undergoing hemodialysis. We examined the efficacy and safety of upacicalcet, an intravenous calcimimetic, versus placebo on serum intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) levels in patients receiving hemodialysis. Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) Attenuation Trial in Hemodialysis (PATH)-1 and PATH-2 were identical, randomized, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials conducted in parallel in 768 patients receiving hemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism and serum iPTH levels ≥400 to ≤1500 pg/ml. Participants received intravenous upacicalcet (n=510) or placebo (n=258) after hemodialysis for 27 weeks; dosing was titrated using iPTH and corrected serum calcium. Calcium supplementation or changes in active vitamin D sterols for corrected serum calcium <8.3 mg/dl without hypocalcemia symptoms were restricted. The primary outcome was the proportion of participants achieving ≥30% decrease from baseline in mean iPTH during the efficacy assessment period, weeks 22-27. The strata-adjusted proportions of participants achieving the primary outcome were significantly higher with upacicalcet versus placebo: in PATH-1, 42.1% versus 16.8%, for a difference in proportions of 25.3% (95% confidence interval, 16.2 to 34.5, P < 0.001); in PATH-2, 43.5% versus 17.4%, for a difference in proportions of 26.1% (95% confidence interval, 17.4 to 34.8, P < 0.001). Serious adverse events were similar between upacicalcet and placebo (PATH-1, 26% versus 24%; PATH-2, 23% versus 22%). Rates of gastrointestinal symptoms were similar between treatment groups. Corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dl occurred in 31% versus 12% in PATH-1 and 45% versus 19% in PATH-2; dose interruptions occurred in 44% versus 24% and 52% versus 27%, respectively. Investigator-attributed symptomatic hypocalcemia was reported in 0.8% and 2% of upacicalcet-treated participants, respectively, and in no placebo patients. In 2 phase 3 trials, upacicalcet significantly reduced iPTH versus placebo. Asymptomatic hypocalcemia and dose interruptions were more frequent in patients receiving upacicalcet, while symptomatic hypocalcemia was infrequent and gastrointestinal adverse event rates were similar to placebo. title: Monthly high-dose cholecalciferol supplementation in prostate cancer patients (ProsD trial): A nested analysis of vitamin D metabolites, metabolic ratios, and biochemical safety.
abstract: The effects of intermittent, high-dose cholecalciferol supplementation on circulating vitamin D metabolites and related biomarkers remain unclear. The ProsD randomised controlled trial evaluated the effects of monthly oral supplementation with 50,000 IU cholecalciferol in males with prostate cancer and assessed longitudinal changes in vitamin D metabolite responses. To characterise vitamin D metabolites and ratios after a monthly dose of 50,000 IU cholecalciferol supplementation and to assess the effects on biochemical markers. ProsD recruited and randomised 123 men with prostate cancer; 118 participants (placebo n = 40; vitamin D n = 78) provided blood samples at baseline, and from remaining participants at 0, 6, 12, and 24 months, at follow-up visits. Plasma vitamin D metabolites-25(OH)D3, 1,25(OH)2D3, 24,25(OH)2D3, and 3-epi-25(OH)D3-and vitamin D metabolite ratios (VMRs) were quantified. Longitudinal changes and between-group differences were evaluated using age-adjusted generalised estimating equations with estimated marginal means. Routine biochemical markers were also assessed. Compared with placebo, monthly cholecalciferol supplementation increased peak between-group difference at 24 months for 25(OH)D3 (+30.10 nmol/L; p 2D3 (+12.44 pmol/L; p = 0.11), 24,25(OH)2D3 (+3.95 nmol/L; p 3 (+5.94 nmol/L; p 3:24,25(OH)2D3 VMR increased in the placebo group but remained constant in the intervention group, and between-group analysis showed consistently lower ratios in the vitamin D group. All routine biomarkers remained within normal ranges throughout follow-up. Monthly oral supplementation of 50,000 IU cholecalciferol in men with prostate cancer produced sustained increases across multiple vitamin D metabolites over 24 months, accompanied by adaptive shifts in metabolite ratios consistent with regulated catabolic activation, with no clinically meaningful abnormalities in biochemical markers. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ACTRN12616001707459), Date: 13 December 2016.

title: Exploring Vitamin D Metabolism in Gynaecological Malignancies: Redox-Dependent and Redox-Independent Anticancer Mechanisms From Preclinical Models to Clinical Evidence.
abstract: Gynaecological malignancies account for over 1.4 million new diagnoses, with outcomes constrained by late-stage presentation and chemoresistance. Dysregulated redox homeostasis is a hallmark of tumourigenesis. Tumour cells maintain elevated basal reactive oxygen species (ROS), which support proliferative signalling but may also increase susceptibility to further oxidative stress. Vitamin D, acting through the vitamin D receptor (VDR), has antiproliferative and pro-apoptotic effects across cancer models, but its ability to amplify ROS beyond an apoptotic threshold in gynaecological malignancies remains unresolved. We conducted a narrative literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov and the Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results databases, using terms related to vitamin D and its metabolites, ROS/oxidative stress, apoptosis and gynaecological malignancies. Preclinical evidence indicates that calcitriol and related compounds can induce ROS-mediated mitochondrial apoptosis, modulate autophagy and arrest the cell cycle. In ovarian cancer, non-HGSOC cell data suggest that mutant TP53 may alter calcitriol responses, requiring validation in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma models. In cervical cancer, calcitriol radiosensitises human papillomavirus-positive cell lines through autophagy suppression, whilst an in vivo calcitriol-cisplatin study reported improved survival. In endometrial cancer, thioredoxin-interacting protein induction is a candidate mechanism for selective ROS-mediated apoptosis, although this remains context-dependent. Clinical evidence is heterogeneous: higher 25-hydroxyvitamin D status has shown modest inverse associations with ovarian cancer mortality; small trials report regression or reduced recurrence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia; no randomised controlled trial evidence supports efficacy in invasive cervical cancer; and associations with endometrial cancer incidence are largely null. Current evidence does not support vitamin D supplementation as an oncology-specific intervention. Future research should prioritise biomarker-stratified trials incorporating VDR genotype, CYP24A1 profiling, pre-specified 25(OH)D targets and pharmacokinetically informed dosing.

title: Micronutrient status and host defense against infectious diseases: Mechanisms, clinical evidence, and context-dependent interventions.
abstract: Micronutrients support epithelial barrier integrity, innate immune activity, adaptive immune responses, and redox regulation. However, micronutrient deficiency and supplementation do not have uniform relationships with infectious-disease risk or clinical outcomes. This review examines the mechanisms linking micronutrient status with host defence and evaluates clinical evidence for micronutrient interventions across gastrointestinal, respiratory, systemic viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections. Vitamins A, C, D, and E, together with zinc, selenium, and iron, influence epithelial barriers, phagocyte activity, lymphocyte function, cytokine regulation, oxidative stress, and pathogen-host nutrient competition. Clinical evidence is context-dependent. In randomised trials in children in low- and middle-income settings, therapeutic zinc was associated with shorter diarrhoeal duration, whereas findings for respiratory infections vary according to population, baseline status, intervention, and outcome. Vitamin D supplementation was associated with a modest reduction in acute respiratory infection risk in some randomised trials, but effects are not uniform across settings, and later aggregate-data meta-analyses did not confirm the earlier subgroup findings. Iron needs particular caution because deficiency can impair host defence, whereas excess available iron was associated with increased infection risk in some settings. Evaluate micronutrient interventions by baseline nutritional status, infection type, dose, timing, concurrent treatment, outcome definition, and safety. Future studies should prioritise stratified trials, standardised outcomes, transparent reporting, and targeted supplementation over universal high-dose approaches.

title: Vitamin D Supplementation and Improvement in Insomnia Symptoms Among Malaysian Women With Vitamin D Deficiency: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Insomnia is a prevalent sleep disorder associated with adverse physical, psychological, and functional outcomes. Emerging evidence suggests that vitamin D deficiency may contribute to sleep disturbances. Women are more likely to have lower serum vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D]) levels than men, and they also report a higher prevalence of insomnia. Although several studies have proposed that vitamin D supplementation may improve insomnia symptoms, findings remain inconsistent, and evidence from Southeast Asian populations is limited. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of weekly vitamin D₃ supplementation in improving insomnia symptoms, sleep quality, sleep efficiency, and functional outcomes among Malaysian women with vitamin D deficiency. This study is a double-blind, parallel-group, randomized placebo-controlled trial conducted among women aged 19-50 years with serum 25(OH)D levels <20 ng/mL and insomnia symptoms. Participants are randomized to receive either vitamin D₃ capsules (50,000 IU/wk) or placebo (1 capsule/wk) for 9 weeks. The study is conducted in a community setting. Primary outcomes include insomnia severity assessed using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), sleep quality measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and sleep efficiency objectively assessed using actigraphy. Secondary outcomes include daytime sleepiness measured using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and functional outcomes assessed using the Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire (FOSQ-10). Assessments are conducted at baseline, midintervention, and postintervention. Participant recruitment commenced in December 2023 and is expected to conclude in December 2026. As of July 2026, 42 participants had been screened, 33 eligible participants had been enrolled, 22 had completed the study procedures, 4 were in the intervention phase, and 1 had withdrawn due to loss of contact. If the efficacy of vitamin D3 supplementation in alleviating insomnia symptoms is demonstrated, it might be proposed as a supplementary approach to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for insomnia. Screening for vitamin D deficiency may also be considered in individuals presenting with insomnia symptoms prior to initiating pharmacological treatment.

Participants are randomized to receive either vitamin D₃ capsules (50,000 IU/wk) or placebo (1 capsule/wk) for 9 weeks. The study is conducted in a community setting. Primary outcomes include insomnia severity assessed using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), sleep quality measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and sleep efficiency objectively assessed using actigraphy. Secondary outcomes include daytime sleepiness measured using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and functional outcomes assessed using the Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire (FOSQ-10). Assessments are conducted at baseline, midintervention, and postintervention.

abstract_sections.label: Results
abstract_sections.text: Participant recruitment commenced in December 2023 and is expected to conclude in December 2026. As of July 2026, 42 participants had been screened, 33 eligible participants had been enrolled, 22 had completed the study procedures, 4 were in the intervention phase, and 1 had withdrawn due to loss of contact.

abstract_sections.label: Conclusions
abstract_sections.text: If the efficacy of vitamin D3 supplementation in alleviating insomnia symptoms is demonstrated, it might be proposed as a supplementary approach to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for insomnia. Screening for vitamin D deficiency may also be considered in individuals presenting with insomnia symptoms prior to initiating pharmacological treatment.

title: Macronutrient and micronutrient requirements in sickle cell disease across age groups: a narrative review.
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a hereditary haemoglobinopathy characterised by chronic haemolysis, inflammation, oxidative stress, and increased metabolic demands. Nutritional deficiencies worsen disease severity, growth, immunity, and quality of life, but evidence on age‑specific needs is fragmented. This narrative review synthesises current evidence on macronutrient and micronutrient requirements, deficiencies, and interventions in SCD across age groups. A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar (January 2000-March 2025). Original studies evaluating nutritional status or interventions in confirmed SCD were included. Individuals with SCD are in a hypermetabolic state with elevated energy and protein requirements. Common micronutrient deficiencies include vitamin D (prevalence 56.2% in children, 75.5% in adults), zinc, vitamin B12, folate, and vitamin C. Zinc deficiency is associated with more vaso‑occlusive crises, infections, delayed growth, and hospitalisations. Omega‑3 fatty acids, L‑arginine, glutamine, zinc, and vitamin D supplementation show potential benefits in reducing pain severity, vaso‑occlusive events, inflammation, and hospital admissions, while improving growth, endothelial function, and quality of life. However, the certainty of the evidence is low to very low due to small sample sizes and heterogeneous methods; adult‑specific data are particularly scarce. Major gaps remain in standardised dietary recommendations and supplementation protocols. Large, high‑quality randomised controlled trials are urgently needed to establish evidence‑based nutritional guidelines for SCD.

title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
abstract: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA. This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year. At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups. The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01939-3.

title: Assessment of serum micronutrient concentration in chronic pancreatitis: insights from the nationwide COMBO randomised trial<sup></sup>.
abstract: In patients with chronic pancreatitis (CP), pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) and poor dietary intake may cause malnutrition. International guidelines recommend monitoring key micronutrients (MN), however clinical implications remain uncertain. This study aims to evaluate the prevalence, risk factors, complications, and longitudinal course of low serum MNs in patients with CP. This is a predefined analysis of the COMBO trial, a nationwide stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial on evidence-based CP management. Nutritional biochemical assessment included vitamins A, D, E, and K, iron, zinc, selenium, calcium, and magnesium during the 35-month study period. PEI symptom severity was assessed using the PEI-Questionnaire. Among 409 patients with CP, 327 (80%) had PEI. Low serum MNs were present in 184 patients (45%), including 63 (15%) with low levels of multiple MNs. Low vitamin K (59%) and D (38%) were most prevalent. Risk factors of low serum MNs included severe PEI symptoms (aOR 2.54; 95% CI 1.04 - 6.18, p = 0.04), and daily alcohol use (aOR 3.71; 95% CI 1.54 - 8.89, p = 0.003), but not smoking and abnormal BMI. Low vitamin K was not associated with increased INR. Osteoporosis was diagnosed in 47/166 patients (28%), and associated with low calcium, but not with low vitamin D or K. In most patients, low serum MNs normalised over time without targeted supplementation. Low serum MNs are common in CP and associated with severe PEI symptoms, and daily alcohol use, but often not with functional outcomes. These findings support targeted biochemical nutritional assessment in CP, guided by clinical risk factors.

title: Additive effects of active vitamin D3 or vitamin E administration on therapeutic lower-limb home exercise for knee osteoarthritis: A pilot prospective randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Quadriceps weakness, inflammation, and reduced physical function are common in knee osteoarthritis (OA), and lower limb exercise therapy is an established non-pharmacological treatment. Vitamin D3 (vit D3) and vitamin E (vit E) have been proposed as adjunctive therapies; however, clinical findings are inconsistent. We aimed to examine whether combining lower limb home exercises with oral active vit D3 or vit E supplementation provides additive benefits compared with home exercise alone in women with symptomatic knee OA. Eighty-eight postmenopausal women with knee OA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-4; 71.9 ± 5.6 years) were randomly assigned to receive therapeutic lower limb home exercise only, home exercise with active vit D3 administration, or home exercise with vit E administration. Participants performed isometric lower limb exercises twice daily for 24 weeks. Subsequently, they were assessed using the Japanese knee osteoarthritis measure (JKOM) as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were short-form health survey, grip strength, quadriceps muscle strength, 10-m walk test, inflammatory markers, bone mineral density, and body composition. For data analyses, we used paired and independent t tests, analysis of variance, and analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, body mass index, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade. Eighty participants completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements in JKOM score, quadriceps muscle strength, and 10-m walk test. Grip strength improved significantly only in the group that received active vit D. No significant between-group differences were observed in JKOM scores, short-form health survey-36, muscle strength, or physical performance. Inflammatory markers decreased significantly in the vit E group, although between-group differences were not observed. No other significant between-group differences were found, except in bone mineral density. Administering active vit D3 or vit E for 24 weeks as an adjunct to lower limb home exercises did not yield significant additive effects on symptoms, muscle strength, or physical performance in women with knee OA. Exercise therapy alone remained effective, and vitamin supplementation showed nutrient-specific trends.
